Appendix.Content: Camera view and clip-space pipeline
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A camera pose maps camera coordinates to world coordinates; its inverse is the view map. Projection produces homogeneous clip coordinates, clipping applies the API-specific inequalities, and valid perspective division produces NDC. Storage order supplies none of these coordinate contracts.
Reconstruction cue: A standard minus-Z perspective example needs a point in front of the camera and a meaningful clip w before division.

University course development

Extend the existing transform pipeline with the clipping and depth-precision decisions that make projection robust. A view frustum is the set of points a camera can see, bounded by near and far planes as well as image sides. Transforming the frustum into a canonical clip cube makes outside tests cheap; partially intersecting triangles must be clipped and triangulated so the rasterizer still receives triangles. The near plane also avoids geometry crossing the eye plane, while the far plane limits depth range. Floating-point depth values are unevenly distributed after perspective division, so an excessively tiny near distance paired with a huge far distance can make two nearby surfaces quantize to the same depth and produce z-fighting. Choose the narrowest useful depth interval and keep the view, clip, normalized, and screen coordinates distinct.
A scene description becomes an image · Cameras, projection, and calibration · Rasterization, coverage, and depth
Phase 11 camera development

A raster-to-ray camera maps a pixel to a geometric sample; In a pinhole model, invert projection and view transforms to recover a camera-space direction, then transform it to world space without applying translation as if it were a point. Pixel-center convention, viewport origin, handedness, clip-depth range, and normalization all affect the result. Offset a pixel to generate differential rays and estimate the surface footprint; that footprint grows with depth and changes with surface orientation. Keep ray generation distinct from raster projection while ensuring their conventions agree. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.

Appendix.title: Matrix norms and numerical error
Appendix.Content: Matrix norms and numerical error

The spectral norm is the largest 2-norm stretch and equals the largest singular value. The Frobenius norm measures aggregate squared entry energy. Residuals, orthogonality errors, and condition numbers need a declared norm and scale; a small residual alone need not imply a sensitive solution is accurate.
Use it when: setting scaled tolerances or interpreting numerical diagnostics.

Developed in Phase 8: The spectral norm measures worst-case amplification, while the Frobenius norm accumulates squared energy across entries. The chapter uses them to scale residuals, reconstruction errors, and orthogonality defects, and separates backward error in a nearby problem from forward error in the requested answer. norms and scale · residuals and error interpretation
Prerequisites
Norms lengths and induced distances, Singular value decomposition, Forward and backward error.
Used by
Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, Matrix functions, Sparse and iterative solvers.
Teaching path: norms and error.
A matrix norm can protect a geometry bound

A local sphere under a linear transform is generally an ellipsoid. The Frobenius norm times its original radius gives a safe, possibly loose enclosing radius. Taking only the longest matrix column can fail under shear. The culling example derives the bound, demonstrates the shear counterexample, and links its geometric figure. This connects numerical matrix norms to conservative rejection decisions.

Appendix.title: Bounding volume hierarchies
Appendix.Content: Bounding volume hierarchies
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) organizes primitives into a tree of enclosing boxes. An internal node’s box contains the boxes of its children; a leaf stores a small set of triangles. To trace a ray, test the root box, recurse only into intersected children, and compare triangle hits in reached leaves. A box miss safely rejects every primitive beneath it, so the hierarchy reduces expensive exact tests when geometry is spatially coherent. Construction chooses how to group primitives and where to split; a surface-area heuristic estimates expected traversal work, while simpler median splits are faster to build. Dynamic scenes may refit boxes after deformation or rebuild the hierarchy when overlap grows. Correctness requires every primitive to remain enclosed; performance depends on tree quality and ray distribution.

Appendix.title: ODE integration and stability
Appendix.Content: ODE integration and stability
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

An ordinary differential equation gives the rate of change of a state over time. Forward Euler uses the current derivative: , where is the time step. For decay , it multiplies each step by ; if the magnitude exceeds one, the numerical solution grows even though the true solution decays. Spring systems can be stiff because high-frequency modes force very small stable steps. Backward Euler evaluates the rate at the unknown new state and is more stable for decay but requires solving an equation and may add numerical damping. Symplectic Euler updates velocity then position and often keeps energy bounded for conservative mechanics. Choose an integrator according to stability, accuracy, conservation, and runtime rather than displayed frame rate alone.
Phase 9–10 development

An initial-value problem consists of a differential equation and a specified starting state. A numerical integrator replaces continuous evolution with finite updates, so accuracy and stability depend on both method and step size. Consistency concerns local approximation, stability concerns error growth under repeated steps, and convergence concerns the limiting solution as the step is refined. Stiff systems can force explicit methods to take very small steps even when the visible trajectory changes slowly. Symplectic methods preserve Hamiltonian structure but do not generally preserve exact energy at each step.

Appendix.title: PDE fields and discrete Laplacians
Appendix.Content: PDE fields and discrete Laplacians
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A partial differential equation constrains a field through spatial and temporal derivatives. Laplace’s equation seeks a harmonic field whose value matches its neighborhood average; Poisson’s equation adds a source term. On a regular grid, finite differences produce the five-point stencil with four neighbor weights and a negative center weight. On a triangle mesh, cotangent weights encode angles and a mass matrix normalizes by vertex area. Boundary conditions supply essential data: Dirichlet fixes values, Neumann fixes normal flux, and Robin combines them. Neumann Laplace systems require zero net flux and a pinned value or mean because constants lie in the nullspace. Explicit heat updates have a stability-limited time step; implicit updates solve a sparse system. PDE algorithms separate field representation, spatial operator, boundary conditions, and time integration.

Appendix.title: Edge localization and subpixel contours
Appendix.Content: Edge localization and subpixel contours
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

An edge is a rapid image-intensity change, often associated with a material or depth boundary. Differentiating a noisy image amplifies high-frequency noise, so edge detectors first smooth with a Gaussian-like filter and then compute a gradient. Gradient magnitude estimates edge strength; gradient direction estimates the local normal. Nonmaximum suppression keeps a candidate only if it is a local maximum along that normal, thinning a broad response to a contour. Thresholding and hysteresis connect strong responses through weaker neighboring pixels. Subpixel localization fits a local peak to gradient samples, estimating a contour position between pixel centers. Accuracy depends on sampling, blur, contrast, and the assumed edge profile. This makes edge detection a measurement problem whose output uncertainty should propagate into later line, pose, or shape fitting.

Appendix.title: Surface orientation from image brightness
Appendix.Content: Surface orientation from image brightness
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Shape-from-illumination methods infer surface orientation or depth from how light changes across an image. Photometric stereo observes a fixed camera view under multiple known light directions; for a Lambertian surface, measured intensity is proportional to albedo times the dot product between light direction and surface normal. Solving several such equations estimates the scaled normal, then integration recovers height up to boundary and scale ambiguities. A reflectance map plots brightness as a function of surface normal under fixed illumination and can reveal which orientations are visible. The extended Gaussian image maps each surface area to its normal on the unit sphere; its distribution summarizes orientation and convex shape properties. Shape-from-shading uses one image and must jointly reason about unknown lighting, albedo, and depth, so it is more ambiguous. Each method needs assumptions stated explicitly.

Appendix.title: Additive energy and approximate structure
Appendix.Content: Additive energy and approximate structure
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Additive energy measures how often two pairs from a set have the same sum: . A random-like set has relatively few repeated sums; a set with many additive coincidences often contains a structured subset. The Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers principle turns high energy into a large subset with small doubling, while Ruzsa-style inequalities and Freiman-type theorems describe how small doubling constrains approximate additive structure. In finite fields, sum-product results show that a set cannot remain simultaneously additively and multiplicatively concentrated unless it has special algebraic structure, such as subfield behavior. These implications are quantitative and depend on group or field hypotheses, subset size, and constants. High energy does not mean the entire set is a subgroup, and a small-doubling conclusion may apply only after discarding many elements. Energy is a counting diagnostic that guides structure theorems, not a complete classification by itself.

Appendix.title: Exceptional projections and dimension
Appendix.Content: Exceptional projections and dimension
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Projection usually lowers dimension, but a finite or fractal set may collapse unusually many points in special directions. For a finite planar set , count pairs whose orthogonal projections coincide in direction ; such pairs lie on lines parallel to the projection fibers. Averaging over directions gives a baseline, while exceptional directions produce larger fibers and encode geometric structure. For a density, the related transform integrates along each fiber, as in tomography; the Fourier-slice identity connects the transform of a projection to a slice of the original Fourier transform. Dimension and separation assumptions matter: finite point sets, thickened sets, measures, and finite-field analogues have different statements. A highly structured set can defeat naive random-grid intuition, and subfield examples in finite fields create strong obstructions. Results are estimates with hypotheses, not universal formulas for every dimension or projection family. This node connects geometric projection to incidence counting and harmonic analysis.

Appendix.title: Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting
Appendix.Content: Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A radiance field represents a scene by the color and density seen along each 3D viewing ray. NeRF maps a position and viewing direction through a learned function, then volume-renders samples using transmittance and opacity weights; multiple calibrated photographs supervise the result. This representation handles view-dependent appearance but can require many ray samples and careful camera alignment. 3D Gaussian splatting instead stores anisotropic colored Gaussian primitives in space and projects them to screen, sorting and blending their footprints for fast interactive views. 2D Gaussian splatting uses oriented surface-like splats to improve geometric consistency. These methods trade continuous function evaluation for explicit primitives and rasterization. Sparse or biased views leave unseen regions unconstrained; floaters, blur, aliasing, incorrect transparency ordering, or poor geometry can remain even when training views look convincing. Novel-view quality is not equivalent to a watertight mesh or physically correct material. Reconstruction quality depends on camera poses, coverage, calibration, and the scene’s changing illumination.

Appendix.title: Perception feedback and robot learning
Appendix.Content: Perception feedback and robot learning
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A robot learning system closes a loop: sensors produce observations, a policy chooses an action, the world changes, and new observations arrive. A policy maps states or observations to actions; a value function estimates expected future return and can help compare actions. Reinforcement learning updates behavior from outcomes, while imitation learning fits demonstrations. In visual robotics, the observation pipeline may include cameras, learned features, pose estimates, and spatial grounding; errors then affect movement rather than only a label. The training and deployment distributions can differ because the robot’s own actions change what it sees. Small perception errors can compound into different states and larger future errors, a form of covariate or distribution shift. Stable deployment therefore needs calibrated sensing, feedback timing, safety constraints, and evaluation on physical conditions. Demonstrations in simulation do not establish robust real-world manipulation; embodiment, contact, latency, and unmodeled dynamics matter. A successful policy is evidence for a task and setting, not general intelligence.

Appendix.title: Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance
Appendix.source: Concepts/Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance.md
Appendix.Content: Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Monte Carlo integration estimates an integral by averaging random samples with importance weights. For target integral and samples drawn from density , the estimator is . It is unbiased when samples cover every region where is nonzero and the density is correct. Its variance falls approximately as , so halving standard error takes about four times as many samples. Importance sampling chooses to follow the magnitude of the integrand; multiple importance sampling combines strategies such as light sampling and BSDF sampling with weights that avoid overtrusting a strategy that rarely finds a contribution. Path tracing applies these estimators to light paths, while rare caustics and narrow visibility openings remain high-variance cases.
Phase 9–10 development

For independent samples from density , the sample average estimates the integral using terms where is positive on the integrand support. Unbiasedness requires the support condition and integrability; finite variance additionally requires a finite second moment of . A variance estimate describes sampling spread, not systematic bias. Dependent samples add covariance terms, and multiple-importance weights combine proposal densities while preserving mixture support. A confidence interval is justified only when its sampling and moment assumptions are stated.

Appendix.title: Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
Appendix.Content: Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Phase 7 derives the affine block matrix, distinguishes a singular affine map from an invertible frame, and traces model → view → homogeneous clip → NDC using a declared projection. The worked figure keeps the divisor visible and checks the chosen near/far depth endpoints.

An affine homogeneous point has last coordinate one; a direction has zero. Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence, while dehomogenization divides by a nonzero final component. Clip representatives and projective classes have related but distinct semantics.
and describe one finite projective point. NDC normalization standardizes ranges, not vector length.

Extend the existing account with the geometric reason for the final divide. A 3D point is stored as ; after multiplying by a projective matrix it becomes . Dividing the first three components by maps the homogeneous representative to ordinary coordinates. Any nonzero scalar multiple of a homogeneous vector represents the same point, which is why this division is meaningful. For a perspective camera, is chosen to depend on depth, so apparent size shrinks with distance. A direction has homogeneous coordinate zero and is not translated like a point. Projection matrices encode the camera frustum before division; afterward, a viewport transform scales and shifts normalized coordinates to pixels and commonly flips the vertical axis because image rows increase downward. Keep clipping before division to avoid unstable behavior around .
Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Cameras, projection, and calibration
Phase 11 camera development

Homogeneous image coordinates represent a ray up to nonzero scale; perspective division produces normalized image coordinates. Monocular reconstruction has a separate physical scale gauge: multiplying all scene points and camera translations by the same positive factor preserves projections. Do not confuse representational scale with unknown metric scale. A known object dimension, baseline, or depth measurement can anchor metres; normalizing a homogeneous vector cannot. This assumes calibrated perspective projection without an external scale prior. The distinction explains why a numerically precise reconstruction can still lack physical units. Barycentric weights reconstruct a triangle point as an affine combination. The weights sum to one; nonnegative weights describe points inside or on a nondegenerate triangle. Dot-system solves on off-plane inputs describe their projection, not proven surface membership.

Extend the existing interpolation note with the geometric meanings that make triangle rasterization and camera calibration easier to reason about. For triangle vertices , a point inside can be written , where the weights sum to one and are nonnegative. Each weight is the area of the opposite subtriangle divided by the full triangle area; equivalently it is a signed edge-distance normalized by altitude. The weights therefore provide both a point-in-triangle test and attribute interpolation. They also reveal a limitation: screen-space weights do not linearly interpolate a 3D attribute after perspective projection. Interpolate reciprocal depth and attribute divided by depth, then divide the interpolated values to recover perspective-correct texture coordinates or colors.

Extend the existing color note with why image-processing arithmetic must distinguish encoded values from light. A display encoding such as sRGB uses a nonlinear transfer curve so code values allocate precision in a way that suits perception and storage. Averaging or adding those encoded numbers does not generally average or add emitted light. Decode to linear-light RGB before blending, filtering, estimating radiance, or compositing, then encode for display. If two equal-area samples contain linear intensities and , their physical average is ; averaging their encoded sRGB values and treating that result as light yields a different, brighter answer. Color primaries and a white point also define the coordinate system of RGB, so a numeric triplet is incomplete without its color space. Keep scene-referred radiance, display-referred color, and perceptual appearance separate.

Extend the current convolution note from a sliding kernel to image formation and resampling. A pixel integrates incoming image energy over a finite footprint; point sampling is only an approximation to that area integral. Convolution combines nearby values with weights whose spatial support is the kernel footprint, and its Fourier transform describes which spatial frequencies survive. Before reducing resolution, low-pass filtering suppresses frequencies the coarser grid cannot represent. In texture mapping, the screen-to-texture Jacobian maps a nearly square screen pixel to a texture-space parallelogram. If the two singular directions have very different lengths, an isotropic mip level blurs one direction too much; anisotropic filters take extra samples along the long axis. This same footprint reasoning links pixel reconstruction, antialiasing, texture filtering, and sensor blur without treating them as unrelated tricks.

Extend the existing frequency-domain treatment with visual interpretation and filtering consequences. A Fourier coefficient records how strongly a sinusoidal basis function occurs at a given frequency and phase. In images, the origin of a two-dimensional spectrum represents slow spatial variation; moving farther from it corresponds to finer variation. A broad bright center indicates low-frequency structure, while energy far from the center often represents edges and texture. Filtering multiplies each frequency by the filter response: a low-pass response suppresses fine detail, and a high-pass response emphasizes it. Aliasing folds unresolved high frequencies into lower ones because sampled sinusoids can share identical sample values. This explains moiré patterns and animated shimmer, and shows why a spectrum is useful for diagnosing sampling problems rather than only for theoretical signal processing.

Appendix.title: Reflectance and rendering equation
Appendix.Content: Reflectance and rendering equation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A BRDF relates incident irradiance to outgoing radiance with directional weighting. The surface rendering equation adds emission and cosine-weighted incoming contributions. Visibility and transport assumptions matter; blurring completed output does not avoid shading.
Prerequisites

Extend the existing light-transport note with the distinction between a material’s directional response and the incident illumination it receives. At surface point , outgoing radiance depends on emitted radiance plus an integral over incoming directions. The BRDF is reflected outgoing radiance per incident irradiance, with units of inverse steradians; it depends on incoming direction and viewing direction . A physically plausible BRDF is nonnegative and conserves energy, but can still have narrow glossy lobes that are difficult to sample. The rendering equation combines this local material response with visibility, incoming radiance, and the cosine foreshortening factor. This form explains why shading, direct lighting, global illumination, and Monte Carlo integration are connected parts of one transport calculation rather than independent image effects.

Appendix.title: Reflection refraction and shading directions
Appendix.Content: Reflection refraction and shading directions
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Plane reflection reverses a direction’s normal component. Refraction scales its tangent component by the incident/transmitted index ratio and solves for a unit normal component. A negative computed discriminant indicates total internal reflection under the stated model. Half-vectors require normalized outward light/view directions.
Incident reflects to across normal . Antiparallel light/view directions have no unique half-vector.
Prerequisites

Extend the existing direction note by separating geometric surface orientation from optical ray behavior. The normal vector is perpendicular to a local tangent plane; it determines the cosine term in diffuse shading and the directions of ideal reflection and refraction. For unit incident direction and unit normal , specular reflection mirrors the direction about the normal, while refraction changes direction according to the ratio of refractive indices and may undergo total internal reflection. Direction conventions matter: some texts define incoming vectors toward the surface, others point away from it, so signs must be checked before applying formulas. A shading normal may differ from the true geometric normal, as in normal mapping, but it cannot change silhouette or visibility. Distinguish shading perturbations from geometry displacement, and use consistent normals when evaluating BRDFs, ray offsets, and medium transitions.

Appendix.title: Quaternion rotation and double cover
Appendix.Content: Quaternion rotation and double cover
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

For a unit quaternion q, the sandwich q(0,v)conjugate(q) rotates v. q and minus q give the same physical rotation. Every nonzero quaternion also rotates without scale if its true inverse is used; substituting conjugate for inverse off the unit sphere scales by the squared norm.
Reconstruction cue: The scalar-first quaternion (sqrt(1/2),0,0,sqrt(1/2)) rotates the X axis to Y.

Extend the existing quaternion note with interpolation and sign handling in animation. A unit quaternion represents a 3D rotation, but and encode the same physical orientation. If two endpoint quaternions have a negative dot product, negate one endpoint before interpolation so the path follows the shorter arc on the unit four-dimensional sphere. Linear interpolation followed by normalization is inexpensive and often adequate for close orientations; spherical linear interpolation travels at constant angular speed for widely separated rotations. Quaternion interpolation acts on orientation, while translation and scale need their own rules. This matters in camera paths and articulated characters: interpolating four components without handling the double cover can create an unnecessary long spin, while interpolating Euler angles can encounter a gimbal singularity. Validate unit length after operations subject to floating-point drift.

Appendix.title: Singular value decomposition
Appendix.Content: Singular value decomposition

For any real rectangular matrix, . Right singular vectors are input directions, left singular vectors are output directions, and nonnegative singular values are principal stretches. Unlike eigenvectors, the two sets live in different spaces.
Use it when: revealing rank and conditioning, solving rank-uncertain least squares, compressing a matrix, or understanding PCA.

Developed in Phase 8: The SVD expresses a rectangular map using orthonormal input and output directions joined by nonnegative stretches. Full, thin, and compact shapes have different dimensions; bidiagonal reduction and Jacobi methods compute the factors, and reconstruction, orthogonality, and triplet residuals check them independently. factor shapes · SVD algorithms and validation

Matrix multiplication and composition order, Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Dot products and orthogonality.
Used by

Extend the existing factorization note with its role in estimation, conditioning, and geometry. For matrix , the decomposition separates orthogonal input directions, axis-aligned scaling, and orthogonal output directions. Singular values on the diagonal of quantify how strongly each independent direction is preserved; a zero or tiny value signals rank loss or poor conditioning. Least-squares fitting can use this structure to identify which parameter combinations are well constrained and to avoid amplifying measurement noise along nearly invisible directions. The same analysis explains why a camera calibration or bundle-adjustment system can have gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave image measurements unchanged. Singular values diagnose these ambiguities, while constraints or fixed reference poses remove them. Thus SVD links linear algebra to robust vision, not just matrix compression.

Appendix.title: Spline bases and curve evaluation
Appendix.Content: Spline bases and curve evaluation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A spline is a piecewise polynomial curve whose neighboring pieces join under explicit continuity constraints. A cubic Bézier segment uses four control points and Bernstein weights; the weights sum to one, so the curve lies in their convex hull. A B-spline uses local basis functions so moving one control point changes only nearby spans rather than the whole curve. Knots mark where polynomial pieces meet; repeated knots reduce continuity. Catmull–Rom curves interpolate their control points and can be convenient for motion paths, while Bézier curves expose endpoint tangents through their handles. To evaluate a curve, compute basis weights at parameter and take their weighted sum of control points. Position, first derivative, and parameterization speed matter separately: even a smooth path may speed up or slow down unless its parameter is adjusted.

Appendix.title: Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure
Appendix.source: Concepts/Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure.md
Appendix.Content: Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A polygon mesh is a combinatorial surface made of vertices, edges, and faces plus an embedding that assigns each vertex a position. Manifoldness is a local connectivity condition: an interior edge belongs to two faces, and the faces around each interior vertex form one cycle or fan. At a boundary, an edge belongs to one face and the vertex neighborhood forms one open chain; each boundary component closes into a loop. A bow-tie vertex with two disconnected fans is nonmanifold even if every face is an ordinary triangle. These conditions let algorithms define an unambiguous local tangent neighborhood, traversal, and surface orientation. Connectivity validity does not guarantee good geometry: valid topology can still self-intersect, collapse to a point, or contain poor skinny triangles. Keep topological and geometric quality checks separate.

Appendix.title: Half-edge mesh connectivity
Appendix.Content: Half-edge mesh connectivity
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A half-edge data structure stores each undirected edge as two opposite directed records. Each record points to its twin, the next directed edge around its face, its origin vertex, its edge, and its face; vertices, edges, and faces keep one representative half-edge. Repeatedly following next visits a face boundary. Following twin then next walks around a vertex fan. This makes local neighborhoods and edits proportional to local degree rather than requiring a scan of every face. Correctness depends on invariants: twin of twin returns to the original, a half-edge is not its own twin, and next pointers form closed face cycles. The representation naturally assumes manifold connectivity; it can encode flips, splits, and collapses by changing a bounded set of pointers, but careless updates can break the cycles and corrupt subsequent traversal.

Appendix.title: Subdivision surface masks
Appendix.Content: Subdivision surface masks
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Subdivision refines a control mesh and updates old and newly inserted vertices with local masks, producing a sequence that approaches a smooth limit surface. Loop subdivision targets triangle meshes: for an interior edge with endpoints and opposite vertices , its new point is . An old vertex of degree becomes , with the lecture’s simple weight for and otherwise. Catmull–Clark targets polygon meshes: face points are face-vertex averages, interior edge points average endpoints and two adjacent face points, and old vertices use face-average, edge-midpoint-average, and original-position terms. Boundary rules differ from interior masks and must be stated. Extraordinary vertices have nonregular valence and need deliberate treatment.

Appendix.title: Quadric error mesh simplification
Appendix.Content: Quadric error mesh simplification
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Quadric error simplification greedily collapses the edge with the least predicted geometric error. For each triangle plane with unit normal and offset , form and . A homogeneous point has squared point-to-plane error . Sum the matrices of incident planes at each vertex; an edge candidate combines endpoint matrices. Partitioning the combined quadratic gives , whose stationary point solves . If the system is singular or indefinite, test endpoints and midpoint and keep the least-cost candidate. After selecting a location, reject collapses that flip incident face normals. The metric is a local approximation, so topology preconditions and orientation checks remain necessary.

Appendix.title: Triangle rasterization and coverage tests
Appendix.Content: Triangle rasterization and coverage tests
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Rasterization converts triangle geometry into a finite set of image samples. A pixel’s ideal coverage is the area fraction inside the triangle; a center test approximates this integral with one binary answer and therefore creates jagged edges. A directed edge defines an inside half-plane, so three signed edge tests classify a point against a triangle. A consistent tie rule assigns samples exactly on shared edges to one triangle, preventing cracks and double coverage. Supersampling tests several locations per pixel and averages their coverage, trading cost for a better area estimate. Hardware often checks candidate samples in parallel within a bounding box, then rejects or accepts coarse blocks that are wholly outside or inside. Triangle coverage is also the basis for interpolating depth, color, normals, and texture coordinates.

Appendix.title: Depth buffering and visibility order
Appendix.Content: Depth buffering and visibility order
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A depth buffer stores the nearest depth seen so far for each image sample. When rasterizing a fragment, compare its depth with the stored value; if it is closer, update both depth and color, otherwise discard it. This per-sample test resolves opaque visibility without sorting all triangles. Perspective projection maps view-space depth nonlinearly, so the near and far clipping planes affect how floating-point precision is distributed. If they span an unnecessarily huge ratio, nearly coplanar surfaces may quantize to equal or inconsistent depths and flicker as the camera moves; this is z-fighting. Alpha-blended surfaces need additional ordering or order-independent methods because color composition is not commutative. Depth establishes visibility, while transparency determines how multiple visible layers contribute.

Depth gives ordering or camera-relative distance under a specific projection convention; it does not identify the surface that produced a sample. Reprojecting old color and depth can place history behind a newly visible surface. Validate with current depth, normal, object identity, or neighborhood checks; reject disocclusions and large reprojection errors. Reversed-Z and nonlinear perspective depth require consistent reconstruction before threshold comparisons. Valid visibility does not guarantee photometric stability after lighting, exposure, or material changes. Link depth semantics to temporal history validation. Appendix.title: Ray-triangle intersection
Appendix.Content: Ray-triangle intersection
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A ray is a parametric half-line , where is its origin, is its direction, and only lies ahead of the ray. To intersect a triangle, first intersect the ray with its plane, then express the hit point in barycentric coordinates and accept it only if the weights lie inside the triangle. An equivalent determinant test solves for ray distance and two barycentric coordinates together. The hit record should state whether the result is nearest, any, or all intersections; those are different query contracts. Parallel or nearly parallel rays, degenerate triangles, and hits near edges require care because small floating-point errors can change classification. Scale-aware tolerances and consistent orientation predicates reduce cracks and self-intersection artifacts.

Appendix.title: Lens optics and depth of field
Appendix.source: Concepts/Lens optics and depth of field.md
Appendix.Content: Lens optics and depth of field
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A pinhole camera maps every scene point to one image point through a single center, but a real lens has a finite aperture. Rays from one object point pass through different parts of the aperture and meet at a focused image point only for the chosen focus distance. Points nearer or farther from that plane form a blur disk called the circle of confusion. Stopping down the aperture narrows the cone of rays and increases depth of field, but reduces collected light and may require longer exposure or higher sensor gain. Focal length and focus distance also affect field of view and perspective magnification. A thin-lens model is an approximation; real lenses add aberrations and vignetting. The model helps explain why depth of field is both an optical effect and a sampling/integration process over aperture positions.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Camera view and clip-space pipeline
• Reflection refraction and shading directions

Appendix.Content: Full teaching explanation
Lens optics, focus, and image formation · Photographic composition, history, and communication · Photographic workflow and integrated decisions
Phase 11 camera development

A pinhole camera emits one ideal ray per image location. A finite-aperture lens samples a family of rays whose intersections form a blur disk away from the focal plane. A thin-lens camera therefore samples film and lens position, then aims through a focal point. Differentials from film offsets alone omit aperture variation unless the model includes it. Monte Carlo PDFs and camera weights must match the sampled film/aperture measure. The thin-lens model approximates real optics; aberrations and bokeh shape require richer models. Appendix.title: Exposure and sensor response
Appendix.Content: Exposure and sensor response
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A camera sensor converts arriving photons into electrical measurements. Exposure depends on scene radiance, lens transmission, aperture, shutter duration, and sensor sensitivity; changing these settings trades motion blur, depth of field, noise, and saturation. A pixel integrates light over a finite area and exposure interval before quantization. Sensor wells have finite capacity, so highlights clip, while low photon counts have shot noise and readout adds electronic noise. ISO gain amplifies the signal and its noise rather than collecting additional photons. The recorded raw values are not yet display colors: white balance, color transforms, tone curves, and transfer encoding turn measurements into an image. A camera model must distinguish photon capture, sensor response, and display rendering to explain dynamic range and exposure choices.

Appendix.title: Probability density and change of measure
Appendix.source: Concepts/Probability density and change of measure.md
Appendix.Content: Probability density and change of measure
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A probability density describes probability per unit of a chosen measure, not probability at a point. A density over area differs from a density over solid angle. When a mapping changes variables, its Jacobian converts density so total probability remains one: in one dimension, with the determinant of the inverse Jacobian in multiple dimensions. In rendering, choosing a point on a light and using its direction from a shading point requires an area-to-solid-angle conversion involving distance squared and the light’s projected cosine. Estimator formulas are only correct when the sampling density and integral use the same measure. This concept prevents missing factors in importance sampling, environment-map sampling, and camera-lens integration.
Phase 9–10 development

A density is meaningful relative to a measure and its support; its value at a point is not itself an event probability. For a continuous scalar variable, an interval probability is the integral of the density over that interval. Under a differentiable one-to-one change of variables, the transformed density includes the absolute determinant of the inverse Jacobian. Values outside the transformed support have zero probability. A mixed law can contain both point masses and a continuous part, so one PDF alone cannot describe every distribution. When a renderer changes a surface-area density into a solid-angle density, the geometric Jacobian must preserve the same probability.
Prerequisites

• Random variables and probability laws

Appendix.title: Optical flow and time to contact
Appendix.source: Concepts/Optical flow and time to contact.md
Appendix.Content: Optical flow and time to contact
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Optical flow is the apparent 2D motion of image features between frames. Under brightness constancy, a tracked point keeps approximately the same intensity as it moves, yielding the constraint , where spatial derivatives and temporal derivative are measured from the image and is image velocity. One equation cannot determine two unknown components at a single pixel, so algorithms add neighborhood smoothness, feature tracking, or multiple scales. Flow can reveal camera motion, object motion, and looming. For an object approaching at speed , its image size grows at a rate related to depth; the ratio of size to its time derivative estimates time to contact without separately knowing absolute scale under simplifying assumptions. Texture, occlusion, and illumination changes violate brightness constancy.

Appendix.title: Hough transform and geometric voting
Appendix.Content: Hough transform and geometric voting
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

The Hough transform detects a parametric shape by letting each image feature vote for compatible shape parameters. A line can be represented by normal angle and signed distance , avoiding the vertical-line singularity of slope-intercept form. Each edge point votes along a curve in space; a bin with many votes indicates a line supported by many image points. Circle detection adds center and radius parameters, increasing accumulator dimension and cost. Quantization controls a tradeoff: coarse bins merge nearby hypotheses but reduce precision; fine bins need more votes and memory. Gradient direction can restrict votes and reduce clutter. The transform tolerates missing edge segments because evidence accumulates globally, but unrelated edges can also create peaks, so candidates need geometric validation and robust fitting.

Appendix.title: Template matching and distance transforms
Appendix.Content: Template matching and distance transforms
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Template matching searches an image for a known pattern by comparing a small reference patch at candidate positions. Sum of squared differences penalizes intensity mismatch; normalized correlation compensates for brightness scale and offset. Direct search costs work proportional to image area times template area, while convolution or Fourier methods can accelerate broad searches. Rotation and scale changes require transforming the template or searching additional parameters. For contour-based matching, a distance transform stores each pixel’s distance to the nearest edge. A template edge point then receives a low cost when it lands near an observed contour even if the exact pixels do not align. The chamfer score sums these distances over template points. These methods suit industrial inspection where the target geometry is known, but need explicit thresholds for occlusion, deformation, and false positives.

Appendix.title: Camera calibration and bundle adjustment
Appendix.Content: Camera calibration and bundle adjustment
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Camera calibration estimates parameters that map 3D points to image coordinates. Intrinsics describe focal scale, principal point, and lens distortion; extrinsics describe camera pose relative to the scene. Known calibration targets provide 3D-to-2D correspondences, and a nonlinear least-squares objective minimizes reprojection error. Bundle adjustment jointly refines many camera poses and 3D feature points by minimizing all observed image residuals. The problem is sparse because each image sees only a subset of points. It also has gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave projections unchanged, so fix a reference pose or scale. Robust loss functions reduce the effect of mismatched features. Good initialization, parameter scaling, and Jacobian structure determine whether optimization converges.

Null directions are local ambiguities, while small eigenvalues indicate weak constraints. In calibrated monocular structure from motion, global frame choice and common scene scale are gauge freedoms. Appendix.title: Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry
Appendix.Content: Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Stereo reconstruction uses two or more views to infer depth from corresponding image features. A 3D point and the two camera centers define an epipolar plane; its intersection with each image plane is an epipolar line. Thus a feature in one image should match along a one-dimensional line in the other, reducing a 2D search to a constrained search. With calibrated cameras, triangulation intersects the two viewing rays; noise means they are skew, so estimate the 3D point minimizing reprojection or ray distance. Depth uncertainty grows rapidly when the viewing rays are nearly parallel, which happens for distant points or small baselines. Rectification rotates images so epipolar lines become horizontal scanlines. Occlusion, repetitive texture, and calibration error can still produce mismatches, so confidence and consistency checks are essential.

Reconstruction cue: Uniform tiny scaling can have tiny determinant and condition number one.

Source and navigation
Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification
University course development

Computational geometry often decides whether points are left or right of a directed line, whether three points are collinear, or whether a point lies inside a circle. These decisions reduce to determinant signs. For points in 2D, the signed area determinant classifies orientation. If its exact value is near zero, floating-point rounding can change the sign and make neighboring algorithms disagree, creating flipped triangles or invalid topology. Robust predicates evaluate a fast approximate determinant with an error bound; if the sign is certain they stop, and if uncertain they recompute with higher precision. This adaptive strategy spends extra work only near degeneracy. It does not make constructed intersection coordinates exact, but it protects discrete branching decisions that must be globally consistent in triangulation, mesh repair, and ray-edge intersection.

Appendix.title: Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics
Appendix.Content: Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Optimization chooses parameters to minimize an objective while satisfying constraints. Gradient descent steps opposite the gradient; Newton’s method also uses curvature, while quasi-Newton methods estimate curvature from gradient changes. Constraints may be enforced by parameterization, penalty terms, projection, or constrained solvers. In inverse kinematics, the parameters are joint angles and the objective measures distance between an end effector and its target. Forward kinematics maps angles to a hand or foot position; its Jacobian maps small joint changes to small endpoint changes. A damped least-squares step solves a stabilized linear system to reduce target error without exploding near singular poses. Joint limits, collisions, and multiple valid solutions make initialization and constraints important. The same framework applies to fitting cameras, deforming meshes, or matching image observations.
Phase 9–10 development

An optimization problem specifies an objective, variables, and equality or inequality constraints before an algorithm is selected. A gradient step uses first-order information; Newton and quasi-Newton steps add curvature, while line searches or trust regions control how far a local model is trusted. For nonlinear least squares, Gauss-Newton approximates curvature from the residual Jacobian and Levenberg-Marquardt damps the resulting system. Lagrange multipliers and KKT conditions describe constrained stationary points under their regularity assumptions. These local conditions do not by themselves prove global optimality.

Appendix.title: Light spectra and radiometry
Appendix.Content: Light spectra and radiometry
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Light models distinguish wave propagation, photon energy and geometrical rays. Radiometry describes physical flux/radiance/irradiance; photometry adds standardized visual weighting. RGB requires an interpretation and cannot identify a unique spectrum.
Prerequisites
No formal graph prerequisite. Begin with the stated units and model; this is an independent-series foundation.

Source and navigation
Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map
University course development

Radiometry distinguishes total radiant flux in watts, irradiance in watts per square metre, radiant intensity in watts per steradian, and radiance in watts per square metre per steradian measured with projected source area. A spectrum distributes the energy over wavelength; a three-channel RGB value is a measurement in a chosen color system and does not uniquely identify that spectrum. Solid angle measures directional extent rather than physical area. Consequently an area-light sample requires the projected-area and inverse-square Jacobian when expressed as a directional sample. Free-space radiance remains constant along an unobstructed ray, while irradiance from a point-like source changes with geometry. Photometry instead applies standardized visual weighting: luminous flux uses lumens, illuminance lux, and luminous intensity candela. These distinctions prevent treating brightness, exposure, flux and radiance as interchangeable scalar labels.

Appendix.title: Sampling aliasing and reconstruction
Appendix.Content: Sampling aliasing and reconstruction
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Uniform samples identify frequencies only modulo sample rate and corresponding real-signal equivalences. Strictly band-limited ideal reconstruction needs non-overlapping spectral replicas; exact-Nyquist phase is a boundary hazard. Prefilter before decimation.
Phase 9–10 development

Signal aliasing occurs when distinct signal frequencies produce the same sampled values; reconstruction then cannot recover which signal generated the samples without additional assumptions. Stratification, low-discrepancy sequences, and blue-noise point sets describe where samples are placed, not a guarantee that the signal is band-limited or that an estimator is unbiased. Each strategy still needs a valid support, probability weight, and reconstruction filter.
Prerequisites

Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map
University course development

Sampling records measurements of a continuous signal on a discrete grid. Frequencies that differ by integer multiples of the sampling rate can produce the same samples, so the sampled values alone cannot identify which original signal was present. For ideal band-limited reconstruction, the signal must be restricted below half the sampling rate; equality at the limiting frequency needs additional phase and endpoint conditions. A real pixel also integrates light over area and exposure time, making its measurement a filtered sample. Prefiltering attenuates frequencies that would alias, while reconstruction estimates a continuous signal from the stored samples. Ideal sinc reconstruction has infinite support; practical filters trade computation, sharpness, ringing and residual aliasing. More samples reduce integration error only when their placement and weights match the intended pixel or path-space measure.

Appendix.title: GPU vertex specification
Appendix.Content: GPU vertex specification
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A GPU vertex-input specification explains how bytes in one or more buffers become per-vertex shader inputs. A buffer object owns bytes; a vertex array object records their interpretation: enabled attributes, component count and type, normalization, stride, byte offset, and the buffer binding used for fetch. Stride is the number of bytes between successive vertices; offset is the first component’s byte position. For vertex i, the address is base + offset + i × stride. For interleaved records containing position (3 floats), normal (3), and UV (2), the stride is 8 × 4 = 32 bytes and the UV offset is 24 bytes. Modern binding APIs separate attribute format from the buffer binding; older pointer-style calls can capture the buffer bound at setup time. A wrong stride may still address valid memory, so the symptom is often plausible but scrambled geometry. The contract must agree with CPU packing, shader input types, and the API’s state-capture rules.

Appendix.title: Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation
Appendix.Content: Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

After a vertex is transformed, its clip-space coordinate is . Clip primitives against the view volume before perspective division; under the conventional OpenGL clip convention the inequalities are . A crossing edge is split by interpolating its homogeneous endpoints, which preserves the projective line and avoids dividing by a small or negative too early. Only surviving points are divided by to enter normalized device coordinates. Attributes then need perspective-correct interpolation: screen-space barycentric weights interpolate and , and the fragment value is their ratio. For a triangle with weights , . Direct linear interpolation in screen space is correct only for affine quantities or equal depth; otherwise textures warp. Clip-space depth conventions and the near/far interval vary by API and projection setup, so the inequalities must match the active pipeline.

Phase 11 camera development

Clipping and perspective-correct interpolation preserve projective geometry, while texture filtering asks how much surface area maps to a pixel. Neighboring camera rays approximate the image-to-surface footprint. At grazing angles one pixel can cover a long, thin region; a center-only texel lookup may alias detail even when attributes interpolate correctly. Use footprint estimates to select mip levels or anisotropic filters, while respecting visibility edges where derivatives jump. Ray differentials aid sampling but do not replace clipping or multisample coverage. Source basis: PBRT differential-ray texture filtering. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.
Worked clip-plane trace beside the shader explanation

For clip endpoints and , the right-plane intersection uses homogeneous edge parameter ; interpolating the already divided endpoints would use . The worked trace and pipeline figure also explain negative fourth components, the zero-divisor limit and declared depth conventions. This is used by the shader-stage teaching before program compilation and linking are discussed.
Executable raster-state continuation

The project now carries two complementary CPU witnesses. tools/labs/raster_reference_lab.cpp owns edge coverage, barycentrics, perspective-correct interpolation and depth ordering. tools/labs/raster_pipeline_state_lab.cpp continues the same pipeline through a homogeneous clip-plane intersection, an explicit four-sample coverage mask, stencil compare/pass update and premultiplied source-over blending.

That separation is deliberate: clipping happens in homogeneous coordinates before divide-by-; sample ownership happens after screen mapping; stencil/depth are stateful per-fragment/sample decisions; blending combines a surviving source with an existing destination. Treating all of them as “rasterization” without preserving these boundaries makes debugging nearly impossible.

Appendix.title: Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
Appendix.Content: Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Automatic differentiation evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the operations in a program. Each operation has a local derivative rule; composing the rules gives the derivative of the complete computation without symbolically expanding it or approximating it by finite differences. Forward mode propagates a tangent perturbation and computes a Jacobian-vector product (JVP), useful when there are few inputs. Reverse mode propagates sensitivities from outputs back to inputs and computes a vector-Jacobian product (VJP), making gradients of one scalar loss with respect to millions of parameters practical. Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation through a neural network’s computation graph. It does not remove numerical problems: nondifferentiable operations require conventions, saturated activations can yield tiny gradients, and an incorrect graph or reduction yields an incorrect gradient. Gradients are local sensitivity information, not proof of a global optimum. Finite differences remain a useful small-scale check, but cancellation and step-size tradeoffs make them a poor training method.
Phase 9–10 development

Forward mode propagates an input tangent through local derivatives and computes a Jacobian-vector product. Reverse mode propagates an output sensitivity backward and computes a vector-Jacobian product. These are chain-rule evaluations on the operation graph, distinct from finite differences, which perturb inputs and can suffer cancellation. The reverse pass requires a valid reverse-topological order and storage that remains alive until propagation finishes. Differentiating a converged solution uses an implicit equation and its local Jacobian; it is not automatically the same as differentiating every solver iteration.

Appendix.title: Learned image features and CNNs
Appendix.Content: Learned image features and CNNs
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A convolutional neural network (CNN) learns filters that detect useful image patterns from data. A convolution layer applies the same small kernel at many image locations, so a feature such as an edge can be recognized wherever it appears. Early layers often respond to local contrast or texture; later layers combine these responses into task-specific patterns. Stride and pooling reduce spatial resolution, trading detail for computation and larger receptive fields. Training adjusts filter values by gradient descent using backpropagation and labeled or self-supervised objectives. Weight sharing gives translation equivariance: shifting an input shifts the feature map, but does not guarantee full translation invariance or robustness to scale, viewpoint, lighting, or distribution change. Padding and stride determine border behavior and output size; too much downsampling can erase small objects. A learned feature is a representation useful for a training objective, not a human-interpretable semantic guarantee. Performance depends on data coverage, augmentation, architecture, optimization, and honest held-out evaluation.

Appendix.title: Attention and visual transformers
Appendix.Content: Attention and visual transformers
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Self-attention lets each token build a context-dependent mixture of other tokens. A learned linear map produces queries , keys , and values ; scaled dot products compare each query with all keys, softmax converts scores to weights, and those weights combine values. Multiple heads learn different relationships, while positional information tells the model where patches or words came from. Vision transformers split an image into patches, embed them as tokens, and process the sequence with attention and feed-forward blocks. Unlike a small convolution, global attention can relate distant regions in one layer, but its pairwise score matrix grows roughly as the square of token count. Patch size trades spatial detail for compute; positional encodings and training data affect transfer. Attention weights are a mechanism for mixing information, not an explanation of causal importance. A transformer still needs a task objective, data, optimization, and validation, and can fail under distribution shift or poor spatial grounding.

Appendix.title: Contrastive vision and image-language alignment
Appendix.Content: Contrastive vision and image-language alignment
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Contrastive image-language learning trains an image encoder and a text encoder to place matching descriptions near their images in a shared feature space. For a batch of paired examples, cosine similarities between normalized embeddings form a score matrix; a temperature scales the scores, and an InfoNCE-style cross-entropy treats the matching pair as the positive while other batch items act as negatives. The objective makes retrieval and zero-shot label comparison possible by encoding class names as text. It learns statistical alignment, not a guarantee that every phrase is grounded in the pixels. Batch composition, duplicate or semantically similar negatives, captions, and web-data biases all shape the representation. A model may associate a prompt with correlated context rather than the requested object, and similarity scores are not calibrated probabilities. Evaluation must distinguish retrieval, classification, localization, and reasoning rather than treating one score as general visual understanding.

Appendix.title: Latent-variable models and generative flows
Appendix.Content: Latent-variable models and generative flows
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Generative models describe how data could be produced, often by first sampling a latent variable and mapping it to an observation . A variational autoencoder (VAE) learns an encoder distribution and decoder ; its evidence lower bound balances reconstruction likelihood against a KL penalty that keeps the latent distribution tractable. A generative adversarial network (GAN) trains a generator against a discriminator, creating a game that can produce sharp samples but may be unstable or collapse to limited modes. Normalizing flows use invertible transformations so the data density can be computed with a change-of-variables Jacobian determinant. These methods solve different tradeoffs among likelihood, sample quality, latent structure, and optimization stability. Their assumptions matter: a VAE’s posterior family may be too simple, a GAN score is not a calibrated density, and a flow’s invertibility constrains architecture. Generated samples are not evidence that the model has learned the true causal process.

Appendix.title: Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR
Appendix.Content: Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Reservoir sampling keeps a compact candidate for a weighted distribution without storing every sample. When candidate has target weight , maintain a running weight sum and replace the stored candidate with probability proportional to ; the reservoir records enough normalization information to estimate the desired integral without bias under stated assumptions. ReSTIR reuses candidates across pixels and frames, which is valuable when direct lighting has many possible lights or paths but only a few can be evaluated per pixel. Reuse requires correcting for the source and target distributions, accounting for visibility changes, and managing temporal history. If weights or normalization are wrong, the image may be biased; stale reuse causes trails or light leaks when geometry or illumination moves. The method reduces expensive samples rather than making sampling free. It depends on a valid estimator, careful normalization, and an understanding of whether correlated reused samples preserve the intended expectation.

Appendix.title: Collision barriers and continuous detection
Appendix.Content: Collision barriers and continuous detection
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

A collision barrier turns a geometric safety condition into an optimization energy that rises sharply as bodies approach contact. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) combines barrier terms for vertex-face and edge-edge separations with a time-step formulation that prevents interpenetration while a deformable object moves. Continuous collision detection (CCD) asks whether two moving primitives touch at any time during a step, not only at its endpoints; a pair can cross and separate between discrete samples. Robust CCD therefore needs conservative root bounds and careful handling of near-degenerate geometry. The barrier does not replace a correct collision set: missing pairs, invalid orientations, or a nonconservative CCD test can still allow tunneling. Very stiff barriers also make optimization ill-conditioned and require line search or step restrictions. IPC’s guarantees depend on assumptions about the initial configuration, collision constraints, and numerical tolerances. The core distinction is discrete overlap testing versus continuous-in-time contact prevention.

Appendix.title: Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields
Appendix.source: Concepts/Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields.md
Appendix.Content: Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation seeks vertex positions that change as little as possible from a preferred local rigid transform. For each vertex neighborhood, fit a rotation to the deformed edge vectors, then minimize residuals between transformed rest edges and current edges. Alternating between local rotations and a global position solve makes a nonlinear shape-editing problem tractable, but the result depends on constraints, initialization, mesh quality, and rotation fitting. Instant Meshes uses direction or orientation fields over a surface to guide a quad-dominant remeshing; field singularities encode where a globally consistent direction cannot exist. A mesh’s half-edge connectivity, boundary structure, and orientation determine valid neighborhoods and field transport. Poor triangles, seams, boundary conditions, or inconsistent orientation can create artifacts. ARAP is a local preservation objective, not exact rigidity of the whole shape; a direction field guides topology but does not uniquely determine a good mesh without sizing and feature constraints.

End-to-end disk event stepping and randomized supervision — November 12, 2026

An additional stand-alone C++20 laboratory at tools/labs/disk_event_pipeline_lab.cpp now connects continuous disk collision discovery to a complete fixed-duration state update. It repeatedly finds the earliest encounter among all unordered disk pairs, advances all positions to the event, groups approximately simultaneous events, freezes each incoming restitution target, runs 32 accumulated projected normal-impulse sweeps, and re-queries the remaining interval. Nine fixed scenes exercise collision timing against a static body, two-body elastic energy/momentum, symmetric simultaneous contacts, separating motion, initial overlap rejection, event budget failure, chained events, ideal inelastic response, and duplicate stable-ID / zero-duration validation.

Discovered defect and correction: the first nine scenes passed, but a separately constructed deterministic 10,000-case unequal-mass isolated-pair experiment failed at trial 937. A valid impact had advanced two centres to a near-tangent configuration whose squared distance was a tiny amount below the squared combined radius; the original squared-distance tolerance rejected it as a deep overlap. The published correction computes the linear centre gap and uses a finite-precision length tolerance scaled to world-coordinate magnitude. After this correction, all 10,000 seeded cases passed under GCC and Clang and sanitizer tests. No claim is made that this tolerance is globally robust for arbitrary very large/very small coordinate ratios.

The successful randomized experiment has been retained as independently executable tools/labs/disk_event_property_lab.cpp. For each isolated impact it checks exactly one event, Newton’s restitution equation, linear momentum conservation and non-increasing kinetic energy. Both newly published source files were re-fetched from GitHub and their Git blob hashes matched the locally compiled files: event pipeline e69b18ba580329db14ef0bde18811e6737790084 and property test caa2fffdfe32048e6580887ad868eda36278700f. The shared workflow is configured to run both on GitHub but its hosted execution has not yet been confirmed. The contact narrative and README now link both sources and explain the numeric trace.

Remaining boundary: this is not a production Kairo world step; all-pairs event search is quadratic per rescan, contact detection is constant-velocity disk-only, friction/rotation and resting contacts are excluded, and thrown exceptions can leave the scene partially advanced.
