Appendix.title: Gaussian covariance projection and footprint
Appendix.Content: Gaussian covariance projection and footprint

A 3D Gaussian does not project to screen by simply projecting its center and keeping the same radius. Perspective is locally nonlinear, so the usual rasterization approximation linearizes the camera projection at the Gaussian center and propagates the 3D covariance through that local Jacobian.
Let camera-space point be
with pinhole projection
The Jacobian with respect to is
If the 3D covariance in camera coordinates is , first-order covariance propagation gives
This equation has useful invariants. If is positive semidefinite, is also positive semidefinite because for any screen vector ,
Symmetry should also be preserved numerically up to rounding.
World covariance to camera covariance
If a Gaussian covariance is stored in world coordinates and the camera’s linear world-to-camera transform is , then
For a rigid camera rotation, is orthogonal. For a similarity transform containing scale , covariance scales by as well as rotating. Forgetting that square is a common alignment bug.

Many splat systems parameterize a positive covariance from scale and rotation rather than storing an arbitrary symmetric matrix. Whatever parameterization is used, the runtime should preserve positive-semidefinite structure instead of allowing an unconstrained matrix to become an invalid ellipse.
Ellipse footprint

A symmetric 2×2 projected covariance has eigenvalues . The square roots are standard deviations along the principal screen-space axes. A conservative raster footprint can bound a chosen multiple of those standard deviations.
Adding a low-pass variance floor can stabilize subpixel Gaussians, but it changes the effective footprint. That is a quality/stability trade-off and should be measured, especially temporally.
Executable witness
tools/labs/gaussian_projection_reference_lab.cpp:

ListItem.Content: • finite-differences the pinhole projection and checks the analytic Jacobian;
• computes ;
• checks projected symmetry and PSD eigenvalues;
• verifies that doubling focal length scales covariance eigenvalues by four;
• includes low-order spherical-harmonic and compositing checks.

Appendix.Content: This is an independent CPU reference layer. It does not prove the current Metal/CUDA/Vulkan Gaussian implementation.
Related: Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting, Captured-world similarity alignment, Rendering history validity.
Conic inversion, tile duplication and depth order
Projection produces a 2D covariance, but a splat rasterizer normally consumes its inverse as a conic. For
the inverse is

For a pixel displacement , the Mahalanobis exponent uses . A conservative screen radius can be built from the largest eigenvalue of ; the resulting box determines which tiles receive a duplicate splat record. Those records must then be grouped by tile and ordered front-to-back before alpha compositing.

tools/labs/gaussian_tile_conic_lab.cpp now verifies the 2D inverse, positive conic evaluation, eigenvalue footprint bound, conservative tile duplication, stable tile/depth ordering, and the front-to-back transmittance identity. GPU radix sorting and exact ellipse-tile rejection remain separate native-performance layers.

Appendix.title: Gaussian alpha compositing and order
Appendix.Content: Gaussian alpha compositing and order
A splat rasterizer typically evaluates an opacity contribution for each projected Gaussian and composites visible contributors in depth order. Front-to-back compositing keeps a running transmittance
and for layer with opacity ,
After all layers, accumulated opacity is

Opacity accumulation is commutative under this formula, but color is generally not because earlier colors receive larger transmittance weights. Therefore sorting or another order-correct method is part of the image definition, not just an optimization.
Early termination

When becomes small, later layers can contribute at most a small amount if color values are bounded. An early-out threshold is therefore an approximation with a measurable error bound. The threshold should not be mixed into the layer before deciding whether that layer contributes; candidate-transmittance and post-accumulation stopping can differ by one visible contributor.
Numerical stability

Large numbers of tiny alpha values can accumulate rounding error. Clamping alpha should follow a stated kernel/model rule rather than hide negative or greater-than-one values produced by an earlier bug.
Sorting precision also matters. If depth keys quantize several splats to the same value, the tie policy should be deterministic if reproducible images are required.
Executable witness
tools/labs/gaussian_projection_reference_lab.cpp composites two colored layers in both orders. It proves equal final opacity but different color, making the ordering dependency observable.
Related: Gaussian covariance projection and footprint, Sampling support and missing strata.

Appendix.title: Captured-world similarity alignment
Appendix.Content: Captured-world similarity alignment

Two reconstructions of the same scene can disagree by a similarity transform even when both are internally consistent. A similarity transform Sim(3) contains rotation , translation and a uniform scale :
Rigid SE(3) alignment is the special case .

This distinction matters when combining monocular/COLMAP-style reconstruction, device tracking, LiDAR geometry, Gaussian scenes or engine coordinates. A translation/rotation-only fit can look approximately correct near the alignment origin while scale error grows with distance.
Covariance transformation
A covariance represents second-order spread around the transformed mean. Translation does not affect covariance. Under the linear part ,
That factor is required because variance has squared units.
Estimation

With corresponding point sets, similarity alignment can be estimated by centering the data, solving for rotation from cross-covariance, recovering scale from the centered energies, then translation from the transformed centroids. Robust systems must additionally handle outliers, degenerate configurations and coordinate-convention mistakes.

A good alignment report should include more than one mean error. Inspect residual distributions, spatial pattern, held-out correspondences and downstream image/depth consequences. A low training-set residual does not prove the transform generalizes.
Engine boundary

The alignment should be represented as one explicit typed transform with declared source and destination frames. Applying scale separately to positions while forgetting camera translations, covariance, velocity or distance thresholds creates a mixed-coordinate system.
Related: Gaussian covariance projection and footprint, Coordinate frames and change of basis, Conditioning and singularity.

Appendix.title: Clustered lighting depth slicing
Appendix.Content: Clustered lighting depth slicing

Clustered lighting partitions the camera frustum into three-dimensional cells and assigns lights to the cells they can influence. A fragment then tests only the lights attached to its cell rather than every light in the scene.

The screen dimensions are naturally tiled in x and y. Depth needs more care because perspective scenes can span orders of magnitude. Uniform linear z slices often waste many clusters far from the camera or give poor resolution near it.
A common logarithmic mapping for positive camera-space depth between near and far is
then
clamped to .
Equal multiplicative depth ratios occupy equal widths in log space. With and , the decades 1→10 and 10→100 span the same number of ideal log slices.
Light assignment

Depth slicing alone does not make a clustered renderer. For each point/spot light, determine a conservative cluster range from its influence volume. Then append the light ID to every overlapping cluster.
The GPU implementation usually has two allocation problems:

ListItem.Content: 1. count how many light references each cluster needs;
2. prefix-scan those counts to obtain compact non-overlapping list offsets;
3. fill the light-index array.

Appendix.Content: Atomic append alternatives exist, but they require overflow policy and contention measurement.
False positives versus false negatives

A conservative cluster test may include a light that ultimately contributes nothing to a fragment. That costs shading work but preserves correctness. A false negative drops illumination and is a correctness bug.
Cluster bounds therefore need to match the exact camera projection/depth convention, including reversed-Z if hardware depth is used to derive z.
Executable reference

tools/labs/realtime_rendering_reference_lab.cpp validates the logarithmic slice mapping, near/far clamping, monotonicity and equal-decade behavior. It does not yet implement full 3D light-volume/cluster intersection or GPU compaction.
Related: Prefix scan and stream compaction, Reversed-Z depth contracts.

Appendix.title: Temporal history validation and reprojection
Appendix.Content: Temporal history validation and reprojection

Temporal rendering reuses information from earlier frames, but the old sample is useful only when it still estimates the same current surface and the same target quantity. Reprojection therefore proposes a correspondence; validation decides whether to trust it.
Under one common screen-space convention, a motion vector stores
so the history lookup is
Other engines store the opposite sign. The important requirement is that the convention is stated once and tested by projecting the same point in current and previous camera transforms.
Validation signals
A history sample should be rejected when evidence says the reprojected location belongs to a different target. Useful signals include:

ListItem.Content: • out-of-bounds previous UV;
• camera-cut/history-generation mismatch;
• depth disagreement;
• normal disagreement;
• object/material/primitive identity mismatch;
• invalid velocity;
• resize or projection change;
• estimator/material/lighting changes that invalidate the accumulated quantity.

Appendix.Content: Depth thresholds should be scale-aware. A fixed absolute depth epsilon that works at one metre may be useless at one kilometre.
Disocclusion

Disocclusion is the classic temporal failure. A foreground object moves away and reveals background. The motion vector can point to a valid previous pixel, but that pixel represented the foreground. Bounds checks succeed while semantics fail. Depth/ID/normal validation is therefore about surface correspondence, not memory safety.
Accumulation and clamping

Once history is accepted, a temporal filter blends current and historical estimates. A high history weight reduces noise but increases lag and ghosting. Neighborhood clipping, variance clipping, reactive masks and confidence weighting are ways to constrain history when local evidence changes.
Those techniques should be tested on controlled sequences: static scene, camera pan, hard cut, moving foreground revealing background, emissive change, thin geometry and high-frequency texture.
Executable reference

tools/labs/realtime_rendering_reference_lab.cpp defines an explicit history predicate using bounds, history generation, object identity, relative depth and normal agreement. Tests cover a stable sample, camera cut, disocclusion, depth jump and off-screen reprojection. It also verifies the declared motion-vector sign and that invalid history contributes zero weight.
This is a CPU semantic oracle. It does not yet implement TAA neighborhood clipping, jitter, full screen reprojection or GPU parity.
Related: Rendering history validity, Reversed-Z depth contracts.

Appendix.title: Shadow filtering PCF and variance bounds
Appendix.source: Concepts/Shadow filtering PCF and variance bounds.md
Appendix.Content: Shadow filtering: PCF and variance bounds
A shadow map stores visibility information from a light-space camera. At shading time the receiver is projected into shadow-map coordinates and compared against stored depth.
The raw binary comparison is discontinuous. Filtering changes the estimator, and different methods filter different mathematical quantities.
Percentage-closer filtering
PCF performs several depth comparisons and averages the binary visibility results:
where is a declared bias under the shadow-map depth convention.
Filtering depths first and comparing once is not equivalent to averaging comparisons.
Bias is not a free visual knob. Constant/slope/normal-offset policies trade acne against detached shadows. The correct sign also depends on depth convention.
Variance shadow maps
VSM stores moments such as
Variance is
For receiver depth , a one-sided Chebyshev/Cantelli-style bound commonly used by VSM gives a maximum probability estimate of being on the visible side:

The moment representation can be filtered efficiently, but the probabilistic bound can cause light bleeding. Minimum variance clamps and light-bleeding reduction modify behavior and should be treated as approximations.
Executable reference

tools/labs/realtime_rendering_reference_lab.cpp computes a 3×3 PCF fraction on a hand-checkable map and checks that the VSM upper bound stays in [0,1] and decreases as a receiver moves farther beyond the mean blocker depth.
This does not prove cascade selection, perspective aliasing control, receiver-plane bias, EVSM, GPU sampling state or production shadow quality.
Related: Reversed-Z depth contracts, Sampling support and missing strata.

Appendix.title: Expectation, covariance, and dependence
Appendix.Content: Expectation, covariance, and dependence
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Expectation is the probability-weighted average of a random quantity, and variance is the expected squared deviation from that average. Covariance measures how two centered quantities vary together; correlation scales it to a unitless linear-association measure. For a random vector, the covariance matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because every directional quadratic form equals a variance. Zero covariance does not usually imply independence, except under special joint Gaussian conditions. Conditional expectation and total-variance identities decompose uncertainty into within-group spread and variation between group means. These moments drive Monte Carlo error analysis, Gaussian geometry, and linear uncertainty propagation. An empirical covariance depends on sample convention and denominator; Bessel correction concerns unbiased population-variance estimation under IID sampling, not a universal change to descriptive covariance.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Probability spaces, events, and conditioning
• Random variables and probability laws

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: • Common probability distributions and their assumptions
• Confidence intervals and sequential evidence
• Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

Appendix.title: Prefix scan and stream compaction
Appendix.Content: Prefix scan and stream compaction
A prefix scan turns local counts into globally consistent offsets. For an exclusive sum scan of input ,
If each element says how many output records it will emit, is the first output slot owned by element . This converts a race-prone global append into deterministic non-overlapping regions.
For Boolean compaction, let predicate . Scan to obtain offsets. Every active element with writes itself to output[scan[i]]. The final output count is scan[n-1] + b[n-1].
Parallel structure
The naive parallel scan that repeatedly doubles an offset performs work. A work-efficient tree scan performs an up-sweep/reduction followed by a down-sweep and uses work with depth.
On a GPU, a practical large-array scan normally has several levels:

ListItem.Content: 1. scan each workgroup block into local output;
2. record each block total;
3. scan the block totals;
4. add each scanned block offset back into that block’s local results.

Appendix.Content: Every phase has a dependency. Dispatching all phases without establishing visibility/order is not a valid scan merely because each shader is individually correct.
Shared-memory bank conflicts and subgroup width affect performance, while workgroup barriers only synchronize participating invocations in that workgroup.
Stream compaction as an allocation proof

Compaction is useful beyond filtering visible objects. It appears in GPU-driven draw generation, BVH construction, particle survival, tiled light lists, Gaussian tile duplication and sparse work queues.
The scan proves that each surviving producer owns a distinct range before any scatter writes occur.
Evidence boundary

The current repository has CPU-side scan/compaction reasoning in the canonical volumes but does not yet claim a native Vulkan/Metal scan kernel benchmark. The next hardware proof should compare a scalar CPU oracle, a workgroup implementation, multi-workgroup hierarchy, adversarial non-power-of-two sizes, and captured GPU timing.
Primary background: NVIDIA GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, “Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) with CUDA.”
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions.
Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, BVH build traversal and workload selection.

Appendix.title: Interpretation contract
Appendix.Content: Interpretation contract
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism
The width, layout, type, and conventions that turn an otherwise ambiguous bit pattern into data.

For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83. A contract must state width, signedness, field positions, byte order, allowed values, and any padding policy. Reinterpretation changes meaning; conversion may change the stored bits.
Prerequisites

• Bit significance — LSB means least significant bit, normally position 0 with weight 1.

Appendix.title: Quantization and compressed weights
Appendix.Content: Quantization and compressed weights
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism
Low-precision values and packed model weights reuse field-width, mask, shift, and bandwidth trade-offs.

Quantization maps a larger numeric domain to a smaller discrete set, usually with information loss. Packing stores those discrete codes compactly; dequantization reconstructs approximations. Bit packing alone is lossless for valid codes, whereas quantization changes represented precision.

M006 develops affine scales and zero points, local group calibration, offset-coded INT4, one-bit row centroids, metadata overhead and error metrics. Packing preserves discrete codes; quantization deliberately loses information. See the worked five-value group in the continuous story.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Bit packing — Packing places several constrained values into a carrier.

• Arithmetic policies — A policy states the intended response to an unrepresentable answer: wrap modulo a base, report checked failure, widen storage, clamp to an endpoint, or grow arbitrary precision.

Definition and mechanism

SSAA increases spatial observations; MSAA principally adds coverage-related sampling under its shading conventions. TAA reuses aligned temporal observations. Nonlinear shading makes pre-/post-filtering noncommutative, so coarse rates need appropriate input/output policies.
Phase 9–10 development

Antialiasing combines a sampling pattern with a reconstruction or integration footprint so unresolved variation contributes with controlled error. More samples can reduce Monte Carlo variance, while better placement can reduce structured error; these are different effects. Adaptive allocation based on observed samples changes the sampling procedure and can affect uncertainty estimates. Spatial sample allocation should remain distinct from importance sampling over path or event space.

Phase 11 camera development

Reprojection predicts where a prior sample lands under camera and object motion. Depth agreement tests whether the same visible surface likely occupies that location, but cannot prove stored color remains valid after lighting, exposure, material, or sampling changes. Combine projected position, depth tolerance, and disocclusion checks; reduce history weight when confidence is low. Monocular reconstruction has arbitrary global scale, so metric depth thresholds require an external scale or consistent units. Reprojection success is geometric evidence, not a photometric guarantee. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.
Neighborhood clipping and deterministic jitter witness
tools/labs/realtime_effects_reference_lab.cpp now extends history validity into two mechanisms that directly affect temporal stability.

The first is deterministic subpixel jitter generated from Halton bases 2 and 3. The sample lies inside one pixel but changes frame to frame, allowing temporal accumulation to observe different subpixel locations. A jitter sequence must be owned by the camera/projection history contract: if the current and previous transforms disagree about whether jitter is included, the motion vector and reprojection become inconsistent.

The second is neighborhood clipping. A reprojected history value can be geometrically valid yet photometrically stale after disocclusion or fast shading change. The smallest CPU oracle clamps the history sample into the current 3×3 neighborhood min/max interval before blending. Production TAA often uses variance-guided bounds, color-space transforms, reactive masks and velocity-dependent weighting, but the invariant remains: history should not inject values unsupported by the current local evidence.

The laboratory checks known first Halton points, uniqueness over an initial sequence, bright/dark history rejection and preservation of an in-range history value. It remains a semantic oracle rather than a complete production TAA implementation.

Appendix.title: Perceptual metrics and display calibration
Appendix.Content: Perceptual metrics and display calibration
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: XR01
Definition and mechanism

MSE/PSNR describe numerical differences under a declared domain; SSIM adds structural comparison. Gaze weighting is an engineering proxy, not validated human truth. Perceptual models require display/viewing/version settings and evidence for intended artifact/task conditions.
Prerequisites

• Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.

Definition and mechanism

Psychophysics estimates responses under defined stimuli/tasks. 2AFC chance, lapse, curve and criterion determine a threshold; sensitivity and response bias differ. Nonsignificance is not equivalence, and simulated images cannot independently establish human thresholds.

Appendix.title: Foveated rendering and uncertainty
Appendix.Content: Foveated rendering and uncertainty
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: XR01
Definition and mechanism

Foveation allocates work by a declared visual/gaze model; FFR, DFR and VRS change different mechanisms. Display-time uncertainty and gaze-landing tails affect safe allocation. Post-filtering a full reference is a proxy, not saved original rendering work.

Appendix.title: Stereoacuity and binocular foveation
Appendix.Content: Stereoacuity and binocular foveation
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: XR01
Definition and mechanism

Stereoacuity measures a disparity task, not every component of visual quality. Peripheral blur and eye-asymmetric dominance findings have stimulus/observer limits. Per-eye monocular metrics alone do not prove stable binocular perception.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Optical focus and binocular conflict — Optical image formation determines the direction/focus assumptions used by geometry and binocular analysis.
• Psychophysics and threshold inference — A perceptual conclusion requires a defined task and inference procedure.
• Visual acuity and eccentricity — Peripheral allocation uses a specified task-dependent angular sensitivity model.

Appendix.Content: Research validity and ablation
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: XR01
Definition and mechanism

Ablation isolates a method component; reference choice, confounds and uncertainty limit interpretation. External validity concerns conditions beyond the experiment. Software replication and perceptual replication need different evidence, while historical surveys cannot certify current novelty.

Cell.Content: Supplied topic, expanded mechanism and narrative node
SCALARS AS ELEMENTS OF A NUMBER FIELD — Field laws make nonzero division and vector scaling meaningful; a floating type is only an approximation. Scalars fields and real-number models

REAL NUMBERS AND THE PROPERTIES GRAPHICS RELIES ON — Order, intervals and completeness justify real geometry; bounded machine values are not the complete number line. Scalars fields and real-number models

COMPLEX NUMBERS AND TWO-DIMENSIONAL ROTATION INTUITION — Unit complex multiplication rotates a plane; conjugation reverses it, and magnitude drift adds unwanted scale. Complex numbers and planar rotations
VECTORS AS GEOMETRIC DISPLACEMENTS — Free displacement survives translation of its starting point; location and movement are different roles. Vectors coordinates and affine points
VECTORS AS COORDINATE TUPLES — An ordered tuple gives components, but neither its basis nor physical role follows from storage shape. Vectors coordinates and affine points

THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN A VECTOR AND ITS COORDINATES — One physical vector has different coordinates in different bases; distinguish passive description from active motion. Vectors coordinates and affine points
VECTOR SPACES AND THEIR AXIOMS — Closure and vector-space laws enable consistent combinations; unit directions are a constrained non-example. Vector spaces subspaces and span
SUBSPACES — A nonempty subset closed under arbitrary two-vector combinations is a subspace; shifted planes need affine language. Vector spaces subspaces and span
LINEAR COMBINATIONS — Arbitrary coefficients generate movements, not necessarily averages; negative weights are valid. Vector spaces subspaces and span
SPAN — The span is the smallest subspace containing generators; redundant inputs do not enlarge it. Vector spaces subspaces and span
LINEAR INDEPENDENCE — A zero combination must have only zero coefficients for independence; near dependence is a numerical question. Basis coordinates and dimension
BASIS VECTORS — Spanning ensures reachability and independence ensures uniqueness; both are necessary for a basis. Basis coordinates and dimension
DIMENSION OF A VECTOR SPACE — Dimension counts basis elements over the selected field; a plane stored in three components still has dimension two. Basis coordinates and dimension
COORDINATE REPRESENTATION RELATIVE TO A BASIS — Coordinates weight an ordered basis; reconstruct the physical arrow before interpreting the tuple. Basis coordinates and dimension
CHANGING BASIS CONCEPTUALLY — Changing coordinates solves the new basis relation; near-parallel basis axes amplify coefficient uncertainty. Basis coordinates and dimension
STANDARD BASIS IN — The two standard unit axes reconstruct every planar coordinate; visual up/right conventions remain separate. Basis coordinates and dimension
STANDARD BASIS IN — Three standard unit axes reconstruct spatial coordinates; no universal camera forward direction follows. Basis coordinates and dimension
VECTOR ADDITION FROM THE PARALLELOGRAM RULE — Head-to-tail and parallelogram movement yield componentwise addition in a common basis. Vectors coordinates and affine points
SCALAR MULTIPLICATION OF VECTORS — Scalar scaling stretches and may reverse direction; velocity times elapsed time yields displacement with correct units. Vectors coordinates and affine points

VECTOR SUBTRACTION AS DISPLACEMENT DIFFERENCE — Subtraction adds the opposite vector; ordered point difference produces the displacement from one location to another. Vectors coordinates and affine points
AFFINE POINTS VERSUS FREE VECTORS — Affine points have no intrinsic zero; point differences and translations are valid without choosing an origin. Vectors coordinates and affine points

POSITION VECTORS AND WHY POINTS ARE NOT MATHEMATICALLY VECTORS — A position vector is point minus chosen origin; changing the origin cancels only in appropriate differences. Vectors coordinates and affine points
DIRECTION VECTORS — Direction answers which way and must be nonzero; translation does not affect it. Vectors coordinates and affine points
DISPLACEMENT VECTORS — Displacement records change in position and may validly be zero; units and frame must match. Vectors coordinates and affine points
UNIT VECTORS — Unit vectors retain direction but remove magnitude; the zero vector cannot satisfy this promise. Vectors coordinates and affine points
EUCLIDEAN VECTOR MAGNITUDE — Pythagoras yields Euclidean length only in orthonormal coordinates; a slanted basis needs its metric. Norms lengths and induced distances
SQUARED MAGNITUDE AND WHY GRAPHICS OFTEN AVOIDS SQUARE ROOTS — Squared length avoids some square roots in comparisons but is neither a norm nor a metric. Norms lengths and induced distances
NORMALIZING A VECTOR — Divide a nonzero vector by its length to normalize; this operation is nonlinear. Unit directions and safe normalization
ZERO-VECTOR NORMALIZATION AND ROBUST HANDLING — Reject zero/non-finite inputs and scale before squaring; application noise thresholds are a separate policy. Unit directions and safe normalization
L1 NORM — The first norm sums absolute coordinates; its unit ball is a coordinate-dependent diamond. Norms lengths and induced distances
L2 NORM — The second norm is Euclidean; Cauchy–Schwarz proves its triangle inequality. Norms lengths and induced distances
L-INFINITY NORM — The infinity norm is the maximum absolute component; its unit ball is a coordinate-dependent box. Norms lengths and induced distances
DISTANCE INDUCED BY A NORM — A norm induces a metric by measuring point difference; different norms can choose different nearest points. Norms lengths and induced distances
DOT PRODUCT ALGEBRAIC DEFINITION — The real-coordinate dot sums component products under an orthonormal metric assumption. Dot products and orthogonality
DOT PRODUCT GEOMETRIC INTERPRETATION — Dot measures magnitude-weighted alignment; it equals cosine only for unit inputs. Dot products and orthogonality
DERIVING THE COSINE-ANGLE RELATION FOR THE DOT PRODUCT — Compare an expanded squared difference with the cosine rule to derive the angle relation. Dot products and orthogonality
ORTHOGONAL VECTORS — Orthogonality is zero inner product; zero has no angle, and numerical tests need scale-aware criteria. Dot products and orthogonality
VECTOR PROJECTION ONTO ANOTHER VECTOR — Require the along-axis remainder to be orthogonal to derive the target squared-length denominator. Projection rejection and scalar components
VECTOR REJECTION FROM ANOTHER VECTOR — Rejection removes the projected component and enables tangent-plane movement. Projection rejection and scalar components
SCALAR PROJECTION — Signed scalar projection is length along a target direction, not the coefficient multiplying the target vector. Projection rejection and scalar components
GRAM MATRIX CONCEPT — Pairwise basis dots form a Gram metric; coordinates measure physical lengths through this matrix. Gram matrices and coordinate metrics
Cross product definition in — Reconstructed enrichment: perpendicular oriented-area vector definition precedes the supplied determinant derivation. Cross products and oriented area
CROSS PRODUCT DETERMINANT DERIVATION — Signed coordinate-plane minors yield the cross formula; direct expansion verifies perpendicularity. Cross products and oriented area
CROSS PRODUCT GEOMETRIC MEANING — Cross produces an area normal, not merely an arbitrary perpendicular direction. Cross products and oriented area
CROSS-PRODUCT MAGNITUDE AND PARALLELOGRAM AREA — Cross magnitude equals base times height; triangle area is half the parallelogram area. Cross products and oriented area
CROSS-PRODUCT ORIENTATION AND THE RIGHT-HAND RULE — Input order and a chosen positive orientation fix the cross sign; mirrored transforms add a determinant sign. Coordinate handedness and orientation

WHY THE CROSS PRODUCT IS SPECIAL TO THREE DIMENSIONS — Ordinary graphics cross identifies bivectors with vectors in three dimensions; higher dimensions need qualifications. Coordinate handedness and orientation
SCALAR TRIPLE PRODUCT — Dotting an oriented area with a third movement produces a signed scalar volume. Triple products and signed volume
TRIPLE PRODUCT AS SIGNED VOLUME — Triple product is parallelepiped volume; a four-point tetrahedron has one sixth of its absolute value. Triple products and signed volume
VECTOR TRIPLE-PRODUCT IDENTITY — Expand a nested cross into dot-weighted vectors; cross grouping is not associative. Triple products and signed volume
ANGLES BETWEEN VECTORS — Nonzero finite directions define an unsigned angle in the interval from zero to pi. Robust vector angles
ROBUST ANGLE COMPUTATION WITH atan2 — Scale first and use atan2 of cross length and dot; a signed angle additionally needs an oriented plane. Robust vector angles
REFLECTION OF A DIRECTION ACROSS A NORMAL — Reverse the normal component to reflect across a plane; unit-normal and general-normal formulas differ. Reflection refraction and shading directions
REFRACTION GEOMETRY FROM SNELL’S LAW — Snell scales the tangent component; a negative transmitted squared cosine indicates total internal reflection. Reflection refraction and shading directions
HALF-VECTOR CONSTRUCTION IN SHADING — Normalize the sum of unit outward light/view directions; opposite inputs have no unique half-vector. Reflection refraction and shading directions
TANGENT VECTORS ON A SURFACE — Surface derivatives or triangle edges span tangent movement; texture tangents may retain physical stretch. Surface tangents normals and bitangents
NORMAL VECTORS ON A SURFACE — Geometric normals measure perpendicularity; shading normals can differ and need their own contract. Surface tangents normals and bitangents
BITANGENT VECTORS — Solve edge/UV equations for a second tangent; degenerate UVs and mirrored-island signs need explicit handling. Surface tangents normals and bitangents
ORTHONORMAL BASES — Unit perpendicular axes give an identity Gram matrix and simple dot-based reconstruction. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
CONSTRUCTING AN ORTHONORMAL BASIS FROM ONE DIRECTION — A least-aligned helper yields a nondegenerate frame from one direction, but does not ensure continuity. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
GRAM-SCHMIDT ORTHOGONALIZATION — Repeated projection removal preserves span while producing perpendicular axes for independent generators. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
MODIFIED GRAM-SCHMIDT AND NUMERICAL STABILITY — Measuring updated residuals changes rounding behavior; reorthogonalization cannot repair uncertain input rank. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
HANDEDNESS OF COORDINATE BASES — Triple-product sign classifies an ordered basis relative to chosen orientation, not memory layout. Coordinate handedness and orientation
RIGHT-HANDED COORDINATE SYSTEMS — Positive frame orientation is preserved by proper rotations and cyclic axis permutations. Coordinate handedness and orientation
LEFT-HANDED COORDINATE SYSTEMS — A reflected frame has opposite orientation while preserving Euclidean distances; API conventions need separate statements. Coordinate handedness and orientation
ORIENTATION TESTS IN 2D USING SIGNED AREA — Signed doubled triangle area supplies a two-dimensional orientation predicate with a documented axis convention. Coordinate handedness and orientation
ORIENTATION TESTS IN 3D USING TRIPLE PRODUCTS — Four-point triple products decide plane side and coplanarity under an explicit ordering convention. Coordinate handedness and orientation
BARYCENTRIC COORDINATES AS AFFINE WEIGHTS — Triangle weights sum to one for affine meaning; nonnegative weights identify the convex interior. Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

DERIVING BARYCENTRIC COORDINATES FOR A TRIANGLE — Edge Gram solves or signed area ratios recover weights; degeneracy and off-plane residuals remain separate checks. Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

INTERPOLATING ATTRIBUTES WITH BARYCENTRIC COORDINATES — The same affine weights interpolate attributes; nonlinear encoding and unit length require additional policies. Barycentric coordinates and interpolation
AFFINE COMBINATIONS VERSUS LINEAR COMBINATIONS — Only sum-one weights preserve point translation; sum-zero weights describe a displacement. Convex combinations and convex hulls
CONVEX COMBINATIONS — Nonnegative affine weights produce convex mixtures; extrapolation is affine but not convex. Convex combinations and convex hulls
CONVEX SETS — A convex set contains every line segment between its members; a boundary need not be convex. Convex combinations and convex hulls
CONVEX HULL INTUITION — A convex hull is all finite convex mixtures and may fill source concavities or holes. Convex combinations and convex hulls
MINKOWSKI SUM INTUITION — Pairwise set-coordinate addition represents sweeps and expansions; symmetric robot dilation is a special case. Minkowski sums and support mappings
MINKOWSKI DIFFERENCE INTUITION — Collision difference means A plus reflected B here, not set subtraction; overlap is origin membership. Minkowski sums and support mappings
SUPPORT FUNCTIONS OF CONVEX SHAPES — Support scalar and support point differ; opposite-direction support queries construct difference extrema on demand. Minkowski sums and support mappings

HOMOGENEOUS COORDINATES AS PROJECTIVE REPRESENTATIVES — Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence; finite representatives divide by their final coordinate. Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

POINTS AND DIRECTIONS THROUGH HOMOGENEOUS — Homogeneous one distinguishes points from zero-tagged directions under affine translation; zero tuple is invalid projectively. Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

NORMALIZED DEVICE-COORDINATE INTUITION AS A VECTOR-SPACE MAPPING — NDC standardizes device-coordinate ranges, not length; perspective division is nonlinear and follows clipping. Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
DUAL VECTORS AND COVECTORS — Covectors are linear scalar measurement rules; a metric hides their distinction from ordinary vectors. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms

WHY SURFACE NORMALS TRANSFORM DIFFERENTLY FROM POSITIONS — Preserve the normal’s pairing with transformed tangents to derive inverse transpose; singular cases need policy. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms
LINEAR FUNCTIONALS — A linear functional distributes across weighted vector sums; its kernel contains movements it measures as zero. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms
EXTERIOR-PRODUCT INTUITION — Exterior algebra retains areas and volumes without requiring a vector-valued cross in every dimension. Exterior products and geometric algebra
WEDGE PRODUCT AS ORIENTED AREA CONCEPT — Antisymmetric bilinear wedges encode oriented area; dependent generators have zero wedge. Exterior products and geometric algebra
GEOMETRIC-ALGEBRA MOTIVATION FOR GRAPHICS — The geometric product combines dot and wedge; plane elements connect to complex-like rotation structure. Exterior products and geometric algebra
FLOATING-POINT VECTOR STORAGE IN C++ — Floating storage has bounded precision and target layout; trivial copying does not certify external representation. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
VEC2 DATA STRUCTURE DESIGN — A two-component value type needs initialization, safe access and explicit semantic roles. Vector value types and component access
VEC3 DATA STRUCTURE DESIGN — Three-component storage supports spatial operations but is not automatically a point, normal or unit direction. Vector value types and component access
VEC4 DATA STRUCTURE DESIGN — Four-component storage can serve distinct roles; homogeneous coordinates and quaternions require separate contracts. Vector value types and component access
OPERATOR OVERLOADS FOR VECTOR ARITHMETIC — Overloads should express unambiguous vector arithmetic; name dot, cross and componentwise multiplication. Vector value types and component access
SWIZZLES AND COMPONENT ACCESS — Read swizzles reorder components; writable swizzles need temporary-copy and duplicate-destination policies. Vector value types and component access
ALIGNMENT OF VECTOR TYPES — Measure alignment, size and stride; greater alignment may add padding and is not a performance guarantee. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
PACKED VERSUS ALIGNED VEC3 REPRESENTATIONS — Compact storage and aligned compute types can coexist with explicit conversion at boundaries. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
SIMD IMPLEMENTATION OF VECTOR ARITHMETIC — SIMD within one vector differs from SIMD across objects; layouts, reductions and FMA affect throughput and results. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
APPROXIMATE VECTOR EQUALITY — Exact, componentwise, distance, angular and ULP comparisons answer different questions; closeness is not transitive. Vector tolerances and finite-state diagnostics
DEBUGGING NaN VECTORS — Catch the first invalid input or operation using finite checks; NaN propagation can silently skip decisions. Vector tolerances and finite-state diagnostics
VECTOR INVARIANTS IN ENGINE APIs — Validated wrappers establish finite/unit promises and operations must preserve or explicitly drop them. Coordinate-space types and validated invariants

DISTINGUISHING WORLD-SPACE AND LOCAL-SPACE VECTOR TYPES — Space-tagged points, vectors and transforms reject broad frame mistakes; dynamic local-frame identity remains a separate issue. Coordinate-space types and validated invariants

Reconstructing a Production-Ready Vec3 Library from First Principles — Reconstruct the scalar library from the mathematics, then verify contracts with edge cases and seeded properties. Inline capstone and tests

Cell.Content: Light spectra and radiometry and Reflectance and rendering equation: spectra/receptor response, units, BRDF and transport assumptions.
Retinal encoding and receptive fields: anatomy, receptors, phototransduction, center-surround and cortical processing.
Visual angle and calibrated rays and Visual acuity and eccentricity: angular units, local/average PPD, eccentricity, MAR conventions.
Optical focus and binocular conflict and PSF OTF and MTF: refraction, focus, diffraction, distortion and contrast transfer.
Contrast sensitivity adaptation and masking, Eye movements and display-time gaze, Psychophysics and threshold inference: task, timing and detection models.
Continuous signals and discrete samples: domains, timestamps, sampling versus quantization and error assumptions.
Fourier analysis and spectral phase: basis projection, DFT/FFT, phase, bins, leakage and amplitude conventions.
Sampling aliasing and reconstruction and Spatiotemporal sampling and retinal motion: spectral replicas, sinc, prefiltering, moving-pattern frequency.
Convolution and filter footprints and Multiscale texture filtering: kernels, separability, reconstruction, ringing, footprints and pyramids.

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Translation units and linking — Source → preprocessing → semantic compilation → object/BMI → link. A declaration can permit compilation while an absent implementation fails linking; BMI is not object code.
Declarations and definitions — Every definition is a declaration, not conversely. extern int x declares; int x=0 defines. Forward class is incomplete; fixed-underlying opaque enum is complete.
One Definition Rule — Multiple translation units must describe coherent entities. Header guards are per-TU; ordinary external definitions and inline/template exceptions have different constraints.
Scopes and name lookup — Scope belongs to a name; qualified lookup selects a context; hiding changes lookup without deleting the hidden object. ADL adds associated candidates.
Storage duration and object lifetime — Automatic/static/thread/dynamic classify storage. A block-scope static outlives the block; a local pointer and its dynamic pointee have distinct durations.

Object construction and storage reuse — Sufficient aligned storage and completed initialization establish an ordinary object lifetime. destroy_at can end the object while the byte buffer remains; casts do not construct arbitrary objects.

Object identity and generation handles — Equal values need not be one object, and reused addresses host different occupants. A slot/generation needs live-registry validation, not merely a non-sentinel index.
Fixed-width integer types — sizeof(char)=1 C++ byte; CHAR_BIT≥8. int has minimum capacity, not a universal32-bit width. Exact/least/fast and size_t express different requirements.

Scoped enums and validated domains — Scoped enumerators and no implicit integer conversion reduce accidents. Explicit underlying width does not validate received codes; states and combinable flags need separate designs.

Aggregate initialization — C++20/23 aggregate criteria are not the older user-provided-constructor rule. Designators follow member declaration order. Braces may select initializer-list or ordinary constructors instead.
Class access and invariants — struct defaults members and bases public; class defaults them private. Both are class types. Record/invariant intent is convention, not a syntactic capability limit.

Standard-layout and trivial copyability — Alignment creates internal/tail padding. Traits do not imply array traversal, packing, serialization or GPU compatibility. Named x/y/z require explicit indexing or actual array storage.

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
References and aliases — Binding establishes an alias; assignment acts on the referent. A reference-to-pointer can reseat that pointer, unlike a reference to its pointee.

Reference binding and converted temporaries — Type/category select the referent. const int& can track the original; const double& can bind a converted snapshot. Arrays keep extent through array references; bit-fields require special handling.

Temporary lifetime extension and Move casts and forwarding references — Direct local binding can extend a temporary, not transitive function-return aliases. Braces/parentheses/new exceptions matter; move is a cast, and deduced T&& forwarding collapses references.

Value categories and materialization — lvalue/xvalue identify, prvalue produces; glvalue and rvalue overlap at xvalue. A named T&& is an lvalue in ordinary use. decltype(name) differs from decltype((name)).
Pointer arithmetic and provenance — A pointer is an access path, not ownership. Null/object/one-past/invalid states differ; dereference requires live, aligned, type-accessible in-range storage.
Null pointers and optional access — nullptr distinguishes pointer absence from integer zero. Typed null deletion is valid; bare delete nullptr is ill-formed. Non-null does not prove lifetime.

Named members versus array elements — Array-relative positions zero through N may be formed; only zero through N-1 dereferenced. Same-array subtraction must fit ptrdiff_t. Adjacent members do not authorize array indexing.

Pointer arithmetic and provenance — A pointer’s storage relationship is not manufactured by a plausible integer. Specified round trips do not resurrect occupants or authorize arbitrary arithmetic; P3407 is discussion, not C++23 law.

Borrow invalidation and logical identity — Vector reallocation can dangle a borrow; swap assignment can leave a live slot with a different logical owner. Valid handles do not certify previous component references.

Deferred captures and borrowed views — Reference members, spans, string views and captured this pointers require referent lifetime. Copying a view does not own its buffer; an owning capture supplies a different contract.

Const qualification and shallow constness and Auto decltype and reference collapsing — Read-only access is not global immutability. Top-level const is often dropped by value deduction; actual const objects cannot be made writable by casts.

Multilevel pointer qualification — Separate pointer and pointee qualification. int** to const int** would enable unsafe injection; intermediate const blocks it. Const span descriptors do not imply const elements.

Ref-qualified accessors — const member functions restrict the object path; &/&& constrain caller category. Persistent getters can borrow; both mutable and const temporary getters need value/deleted policies.

Logical constness and mutable caches — Eligible mutable members permit representation changes under const access. Cache/source invariants require invalidation and synchronization; return protected snapshots. Mutable closures are not automatically thread-safe.

Cell.Content: Parameter passing and sink contracts — Argument expressions initialize separate value-parameter objects. Lvalue/xvalue/prvalue routes differ; a sink retains/transforms a value, and copied pointer members still alias.

References and aliases — Mutable/const/rvalue reference parameters borrow with different access and consumption contracts. Aliased source/destination references can change a sequential update’s result.

Parameter passing and sink contracts — Pointer parameters copy pointer values; T*& or pointer-output protocols can reseat caller state. Null optionality must be documented; array parameters adjust to pointers without extent enforcement.

Return values and copy elision — Result objects can be constructed directly; NRVO is optional while appropriate same-type prvalue initialization requires no intermediate transfer. Eligible local/parameter return expressions implicitly move in C++23.

Ref-qualified accessors and Temporary lifetime extension — Reference/view results retain owner lifetime/invalidation obligations. Temporary getters require policies for const rvalues too; decltype(auto) can return a reference through parentheses.

Constructors and invariant establishment — Members/bases initialize before the body. Initializers establish state; body assignments replace it. Constructor failure and factory error results are different protocols.

Default and value initialization — Default, zero, aggregate and value initialization differ. First-declaration defaulting is not an empty user-provided body; braces do not universally initialize every scalar.
Member order and delegating constructors — Declaration order governs members regardless of colon-list spelling. Provider-before-dependent order establishes correct construction/reverse cleanup.
Member order and delegating constructors — Delegation centralizes a target initialization path, then runs its own body. The target is the sole initializer; cycles are ill-formed.

Destruction and partial construction — Destructor body precedes reverse subobject cleanup; failed ordinary construction destroys completed subobjects. Delegating-target completion changes the whole-object cleanup case.

Copy semantics and resource identity — New-object copying follows members’ semantic operations; equal-sign initialization is not assignment. Pointer/reference copies preserve associations rather than clone referents.
Assignment and exception guarantees — Existing-object replacement must handle old ownership, self-aliasing and failure. Prepare before commit; reference/const members can delete generated assignment.

Copy semantics and resource identity — Deep/shallow are contract choices, not good/bad labels. Pixel values may duplicate, handles identify, graph clones remap; copy-on-write adds mutation/lifetime/synchronization costs.

Move operations and moved-from states — New-object moves can take resources and repair source state; scalar/inline members need not become cheaper. Ordinary constructors alone do not suppress implicit move generation.
Move operations and moved-from states — Move assignment also handles the destination’s former resource and self-move. Allocator policy can prevent constant-time adoption.
Move casts and forwarding references — move changes category, not ownership itself; const remains const. Explicit local-return moves can inhibit NRVO; move_if_noexcept selects a transfer access path.

Move operations and moved-from states — Source lifetime continues after moving. Valid-but-unspecified is not destroyed or undefined; operation preconditions still apply. A custom empty source needs an explicit maintained invariant.
Return values and copy elision — Immovable types can use guaranteed direct result construction; a named-local fallback still needs usable operations. Accessible destruction remains required.
Rules of Three Five and Zero — Destructor/copy constructor/copy assignment are coordinated raw-owner decisions; copying may instead be deleted. It is a design heuristic, not a compiler mandate.

Special member generation and traits — Five adds both moves. User-declared versus user-provided matters; a defaulted destructor suppresses dedicated implicit moves, while move-constructible traits can still classify copying as viable.

Rules of Three Five and Zero — Compose tested member owners rather than repeat transfer/release logic. Zero does not forbid ordinary constructors or prove cross-member invariants; Relocation versus move remains a versioned research bridge.

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
RAII and resource handles — Bind matched acquisition/release responsibility to a live owner; scope exit handles early return and unwinding. External asynchronous use can require deferred reclamation.
RAII and resource handles — Each fully acquired resource must immediately enter an owner; completed subobjects clean up if construction fails. CPU ownership does not alone establish GPU completion.
Ownership and non-owning views — Ownership means responsibility for ending use/lifetime; a borrow provides access without extending lifetime.
Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — unique_ptr is a move-only exclusive owner; get() borrows while release() transfers responsibility.
Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — A custom deleter pairs a native handle with its actual release protocol; deleter state/type can affect representation and conversion safety.
Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — shared_ptr copies join a control block’s strong ownership group; object and control-block lifetimes may differ.
Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — Reference-count operations have costs; control-block coordination does not synchronize arbitrary pointee operations.
Weak observation and ownership cycles — A weak edge avoids extending object lifetime; lock() safely attempts to obtain a temporary strong owner and can break cycles.
Weak observation and ownership cycles — enable_shared_from_this joins an existing owner group; never build an independent shared_ptr control block from this.

Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Allocation functions acquire raw storage; new-expressions combine allocation and initialization. Size, alignment, construction, failure cleanup and deallocation must match.
Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Arrays require correct count-aware construction/destruction and matching new[]/delete[]; containers usually own this protocol more safely.
Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Placement construction/construct_at begins an object lifetime in adequate pre-existing storage; it does not allocate that storage.

Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Explicit destruction ends an occupant’s lifetime, not necessarily storage. Reuse, transparent replacement and laundering have distinct conditions.

Cell.Content: Reason the concept appears in the request-to-backend narrative
A command record can hold overlapping alternatives but not several simultaneously active objects.
Raw union active-member and lifetime rules; trivial union assignment in tested C++20 lab.
A request must carry its active alternative rather than guess an interpretation from bytes.
std::variant, get_if, holds_alternative and visit, replacement and exceptional empty state; executable request-state checks.
An editor should depend on the backend’s promised operations, not the native implementation.
Base/derived interface contract contrasted with composition and closed alternatives.
A derived object contains a base subobject with its own identity and layout constraints.
Static versus dynamic object view; no invented vptr byte layout.
A base reference must call the selected backend’s implementation.
Virtual dispatch with observable CountingBackend result in the lab.
Indirection has implementation and performance consequences, but no mandated vtable layout.
Implementation-model explanation, devirtualization caveat and proposed measurement controls.
A backend contract needs operations without constructing the incomplete base.
Pure virtual operation and abstract interface; concrete derived override.
An owner typed as base must destroy the concrete derived object correctly.
Virtual destructor through std::unique_ptr<Backend>; derived-destruction assertion.
Copying a derived object into a base value can erase its specialized identity.
MeshObject / NamedObject slicing contrasted with a base reference; tested.
A backend can implement multiple independent interfaces, creating distinct base views.
Multiple inheritance, ambiguity and subobject-adjustment explanation.
A diamond may duplicate a common base unless virtual inheritance shares it.
Diamond with two paths through a virtual Root; identical subobject address test.
Upcasting to a public base is different from a downcast that assumes an actual derived object.
static_cast guarantees and the conditions it does not dynamically test.
A diagnostic needs to ask whether the runtime backend really has a concrete type.
dynamic_cast success and failed pointer cast tested; RTTI and design cautions.
Byte reinterpretation must not masquerade as object construction or safe aliasing.
reinterpret_cast limitations; byte views and bit_cast alternatives.
Removing const qualification is not the same as making a const object writable.
Operators should communicate a domain operation and preserve invariants.
Resource handles versus durations and inappropriate hidden side effects.
A handle’s equality includes its generation, not merely a reused slot.
Defaulted operator== derived from <=> and two identity assertions.
Identifiers need meaningful ordering; NaN can make floating comparison unordered.
Strong integer ordering, partial floating ordering and strict-weak-order concerns.
Overload selection is a compile-time decision based on arguments and conversions.
Integer/double overload calls tested; ambiguity and conversion cautions.
Virtual implementation selection and default-argument binding happen at different times.
Base default 2 with derived body produces 20; derived default 7 produces 70; tested.

M012 — Parts 181–200: typed asset requests, deferred callbacks and transactional publication

Cell.Content: Why the renderer story requires it and where the evidence sits
A raw integer is not automatically a meaningful byte count; the chapter contrasts implicit construction with deliberate unit conversion.
explicit ByteCount(std::size_t) prevents mistaken copy-initialization; compile-time checks verify the conversion restriction, not range validity.
explicit operator std::size_t() requires deliberate extraction; contextual conversions and overload effects are explained.
A synchronous C-style progress callback receives a function pointer plus borrowed context; the lab checks the invocation.
A Reporter member pointer requires a particular live instance; the lab calls the member through an object.
The copyable callable wrapper hides target type, not allocation/copy/lifetime cost; the lab checks an owning target and empty invocation.
AddBytes::operator() carries state for a progress update; pointer-member lifetime remains a borrow.
The closure object combines an operation with stored or referenced captured state; no concrete closure byte layout is claimed.
Snapshot and shared-owner captures show the difference between copied scalar state and an owned lifetime.
190 · Lambda capture by reference and lifetime hazards
A reference capture reads later mutations only while its referent lives; invalid async scene callback is explained but not executed.
The deliberately injected failure after resource creation unwinds a private local owner; typed result conversion occurs at the public boundary.
Resource destructor and move operations express non-escaping exception promises; compile-time traits connect to vector insertion guarantees.
193 · Strong, basic, and no-throw exception guarantees
Prepare privately, publish once, compare stored state and native-handle counts after failure; guarantee is limited to stated observable state.
194 · Error codes versus exceptions in engine code
Empty input and operational failure map to typed UploadError; exception categories remain an implementation detail within the bounded example.
The lab’s verify is active under NDEBUG; external input checks and internal invariant failures use distinct policies.
Invalid lifetime, out-of-bounds, aliasing and data-race examples are explained, never deliberately run as undefined behavior.
A raw file cannot be safely interpreted as a typed struct merely by pointer cast; object type-access and lifetime conditions are explicit.
IEEE binary32 bit_cast is tested under platform assertions; a separate little-endian serializer establishes portable file bytes.
199 · Trivial, trivially copyable, and standard-layout properties
WireHeader traits are checked without falsely asserting its raw storage is a six-byte file layout; differing type categories are explained.
200 · Designing a resource-owning C++ type from blank memory to safe API
Resource develops empty/owning/moved-from states, matching release, deleted copy, noexcept move and a device-outlives-owner contract; AssetStore adds a failure-atomic publication boundary.

M013 — Parts 201–216: generic asset preparation with constrained APIs

Provenance: authored reconstruction of the exact original M013 part titles from the integrated 180-chunk / 3,000-part contract, not a received M013 source transcript. Cell.Content: Why it becomes necessary, with directly inspectable witness
One asset_bytes operation handles multiple supported asset types; T is deduced from actual mesh and texture calls.
AssetDepot<T, Capacity> represents independent statically typed storage for mesh and shader records.
Capacity and texture Channels are compile-time values affecting type identity, storage and byte-size policy.
A complete AssetTraits<Mesh> specialization supplies mesh-specific byte-size behavior.
AssetTraits<Texture<Channels>> supplies one rule for the family of supported channel counts.
const T& and Args&& follow distinct deduction rules; callers need not manually name every deduced type.
All four &/&& combinations are derived, with lvalue and rvalue assertions in the lab.
The function-template Args&&... preserves incoming lvalues and rvalues across a generic API boundary.
std::forward<Args>(args)... selects the intended copy or move constructor for Mesh; both paths are tested.
total_bytes(const T&... assets) accepts a heterogeneous, compile-time-checked group, including an empty pack.
A built-in comma fold performs checked left-to-right byte accumulation; 12+48+15=75 and zero-argument cases tested.
HasByteSize uses std::void_t, decltype and declval to detect a valid trait expression without a hard error in its substitution context.
Named Uploadable accepts mesh and supported textures but not an unknown asset; tested with static_assert.
Compound requirements check the label’s conversion and exact byte-size result type, but do not execute runtime validation.
AssetDepot::emplace requires std::constructible_from<T, Args&&...>; invalid integer-to-mesh construction rejected at compile time.
route has a generic fallback and a Uploadable-constrained overload; correct static routing tested for supported and unknown types.

What was checked: compile-time admission/rejection; lvalue copying versus rvalue transfer; capacity rejection without state change; failed shader construction without publication; unused slot reuse; traits for 3/4 channels; numerical overflow rejection; batch sum and empty-pack behavior; and preferred constrained overload selection. What was not checked: KairoMath/Matrix.cppm, KairoECS/SparseSet.cppm or other live external repository code; C++ module build; GPU execution; multithreaded asset lifetime, cancellation, driver synchronization, full exception fault injection, or comparative performance.

M014 — Parts 217–230: one tile planner and its compile-time policy decisions

Status and provenance: authored reconstruction grounded in the original integrated curriculum and confirmed language references. Not a received M014 lesson transcript. Cell.Content: An internal pixel format and empty validation policy need compile-time properties; std::is_empty_v and std::is_base_of_v are checked in the lab and semantic limitations are explained.
PixelTraits<Format> inherits std::integral_constant<std::size_t,Channels>, giving static channel counts for supported formats.
Known RGBA versus RGB format selects whether a prepared plan has alpha; both variants are tested.
checked_product performs safe size multiplication both in static_assert and using runtime inputs; overflow is rejected before multiplication.
inline constexpr tile definition and precomputed Morton table are constant-expression objects, distinct from mutable diagnostics.
make_tile_definition requires a valid compile-time tile configuration, and make_morton_table builds the lookup table during constant evaluation.
constinit std::uint32_t g_plans_recorded=0 guarantees suitable static initialization but remains mutable and not thread-safe; the single-threaded count is checked.
A sixteen-entry table spreads four coordinate bits; morton4(3,5)=39 is derived and compile-time/runtime tested.
A concrete CRTP recorder and a std::function<void(const TilePlan&)> target each receive the same plan under different static/runtime contracts; neither is benchmarked.
RecorderBase<CountingRecorder>::record calls record_impl via a derived cast; the derived-object precondition and nonvirtual semantics are explained and tested.
TilePlanner<Format,BudgetPolicy,Recorder> composes budget validation and recording; both 64-byte bounded and stateless no-budget variants are exercised.
VerifyPayloadTag and MetadataOnlyTag select overloads that verify real bytes or deliberately produce only a manifest; invalid length is rejected in verified mode.
A holder deriving from an empty policy is measured beside an ordinary empty-policy member; observed sizes are toolchain-specific, not promised.
A policy member eligible for overlap is used in TilePlanner and an isolated holder; local sizeof results and MSVC portability differences are documented.

M015 — Parts 231–250: growing the asset registry without losing identities

Cell.Content: Where the problem forces its use; evidence
A bounded asset depot begins growing; the lab distinguishes live elements from reserved storage and checks contiguous values.
Derive the geometric relocation sum and amortized append cost; the lab observes capacity 2→4 on its local implementation, not a standard-prescribed factor.
Growth invalidates old element pointers/iterators; the lab checks the growth event without accessing stale addresses.
reserve(2) does not create elements; resize(5) constructs new ones with the tested default int values.
