M001 - Parts 1-20

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Physical and logical binary states: a device maps ranges of a physical measurement to 0/1; thresholds and noise margins let imperfect signals represent stable logical values. Storage retains state, while combinational logic calculates from present inputs.
Positional notation: bit at position contributes . independent bits provide patterns, whose unsigned values run from 0 through .
Binary conversion by Euclidean division: , . Save , repeat on , and reverse the saved sequence. For 13, remainders 1,0,1,1 give 1101. Handle zero explicitly.
Weighted decoding sums set-bit weights. Horner decoding repeatedly uses from left to right. Reading 1101 yields 1,3,6,13, confirming the same value.
Hexadecimal has 16 digits; four bits make one nibble and one hex digit. 1010 is A, 1101 is D, so 10101101 is AD.
Octal has eight digits and groups three bits. Left-pad 10101101 to 010 101 101, giving octal 255. Leading zero in a C++ integer literal requests octal.
Byte and octet: octet means eight bits; C++ byte width is CHAR_BIT. Machine word describes a processing convention, not a fixed unit. Exact format widths need explicit types.
Bit mask: a pattern selects owned positions. A low-width mask is because subtracting one from a power of two fills all lower positions with ones.
Bitwise AND filters: , . AD & 07 = 05. Compare the result with zero for any selected flag, or with the full mask for all selected flags.
Bitwise OR sets: , . AD \| 40 = ED. Repeating the same set operation has no further effect.
Bitwise XOR toggles: , . AD ^ 08 = A5; toggling again restores AD. XOR of two states marks differing positions.
Bitwise NOT inverts all positions at a stated width. Eight-bit NOT(0F)=F0; promoted int-width NOT has more positions. State width before interpreting its value.

Shift operations relocate bits. Logical right shift zero-fills; arithmetic right shift sign-fills. Left shift zero-fills low positions; discard behavior and numeric meaning depend on width and language rules.

For nonnegative unsigned arithmetic, left shift by resembles multiplication by and right shift floor division. Truncation changes the exact answer; signed division toward zero differs from arithmetic right shift for negative odd values.
Bit field extraction normalizes with right shift and isolates with a low mask: (AD >> 4) & 03 = 2. Mask-only gives 0x20, still at its original significance.
Insertion clears the destination mask, shifts the valid new value, then ORs it into the cleared word. Preserve outside-mask bits. Replacing quality 2 with 1 in AD produces 9D.
Bit packing combines disjoint, range-checked fields. OR contributions 05,08,20,00,80 to obtain AD. Packing saves payload bytes but introduces extraction and update work.
Unpacking reverses the declared schema. For LSB-first bits use byte and offset . Check the requested count, source capacity, and unused padding before indexing.
Boolean algebra defines false/true operations by truth tables. Logical versus bitwise operators differ in result domain; built-in logical AND/OR also skip unnecessary operands.
De Morgan's laws swap AND and OR when negation crosses the operator. Enumerate four inputs to prove both identities; keep a fixed width for the bitwise versions.

Appendix.Content: M002 - Parts 21-40

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Unsigned -bit range is . Distinguish state count 256 from maximum eight-bit value 255.
Signed magnitude uses one sign bit and magnitude bits. It has two zeros and requires sign-aware magnitude arithmetic. Eight-bit −5 is 10000101.
One's complement encodes negatives by bit inversion. −5 is 11111010. All ones is negative zero; addition returns a final carry to the low end as end-around carry.
Two's complement uses the negative residue and signed top-bit weight . Decode AD as 173−256=−83. The same adder supports positive and negative residues.
Negation follows . The first term is the width-limited complement, so −13 is NOT(00001101)+1=11110011.
Negating zero gives all ones plus one, leaving low bits zero. Two’s complement has exactly one zero and assigns every pattern a distinct signed integer.
Minimum signed value follows the asymmetric range . For int minimum, same-type negation, abs, or division by −1 cannot represent the positive result. Narrow storage may promote first.
Unsigned modular arithmetic retains residues modulo . 250+10 becomes 4 when narrowed to eight bits; on the usual host the original byte addition expression is int 260.
Signed integer overflow is Undefined behavior at the operation type’s width. Check bounds before evaluating, or use a type proved large enough. Evaluating overflow and checking afterward is too late.

Unsigned 0−1 wraps to maximum; going below signed minimum is signed overflow. A size_t loop condition i>=0 never becomes false. Prefer reverse iteration or a decrement-before-index pattern with a correct termination guard.

Carry and borrow move arithmetic information between digit positions. Four-bit 13+7 gives low 4 with carry 1. Unsigned carry differs from signed range failure. Borrow conventions depend on architecture.
Half adder: sum=A XOR B, carry=A AND B. Full adder adds carry-in; sum is three-way parity and carry is the majority of three inputs. A majority function is true when at least two inputs are true.
Ripple-carry addition chains full adders. Worst-case circuit delay grows with width; fixed-width software addition remains constant work. Generate/propagate terms permit parallel carry networks.
Subtraction through addition uses . Binary 6502-style SBC instead includes C: , so C=1 means no borrow.
Shift-and-add multiplication sums one shifted multiplicand for every set multiplier bit. 13×11=13+26+104=143. Both the shifting partial value and accumulator must hold the required wider range.
Binary long division shifts dividend bits into a partial remainder, then compares and conditionally subtracts the divisor. Check and . For 13/3, Q=4,R=1. Zero division and int-min/−1 are invalid.
Saturating arithmetic clamps a widened answer to endpoints: 250+20 becomes 255. Signed saturation is not associative, so evaluation order matters. Do not prematurely clamp an HDR intermediate.

Fixed-width integer types define exact widths when available. Least and fast families promise at least the width, with different goals. size_t is for sizes, ptrdiff_t for differences; plain char signedness varies.

Integral promotion occurs first; Usual arithmetic conversions then select a common type. Track stored type, promoted type, operation type, and destination conversion separately. ~uint8_t{0} is usually int −1.

Mixed signedness can convert negative operands to large unsigned values. Use consistent semantic types or std::cmp_* helpers; valid indexing still requires nonnegative and less-than-size conditions. std::in_range checks conversion representability.

Appendix.Content: Notation and validity

is carrier width, a bit position, field width, offset, and a 0/1 digit. , , , and mean AND, OR, XOR, and NOT; integer vectors require a stated width. and denote shifts. Modulo records a residue; floor rounds downward. A bijection pairs every element of one set with exactly one element of the other. An invariant is a property that must remain true across steps. An ALU is an arithmetic and logic unit.

Keep number semantics separate from executable C++ operators. A word-level formula assumes a fixed unsigned carrier; C++ built-in operators act after promotion. For C++23, signed right shift rounds toward negative infinity. Claims about signed overflowing addition remain subject to undefined behavior.
Why these dependencies matter

Representation supplies the weights needed for masks. Boolean operators supply the gates needed for adders. Masks and shifts supply the field operations needed for compact data. Finite width supplies the modular model needed for two’s complement. Promotions and conversions determine the domain in which C++ actually performs each operation. See Dependency Map and each concept’s prerequisites before reconstructing a later mechanism.
M003 - Parts 41-60

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Endianness orders significance bytes at increasing addresses. It does not change the integer value or reverse bits inside each octet. Separate significance, address traversal, and intra-byte packing order.

Little endian puts the least-significant byte first: 0x12345678 produces 78 56 34 12. Extract byte i by unsigned right shift by 8i, then narrow to eight bits; reconstruct by shifting each byte into its significance position.
Big endian puts the most-significant byte first: 12 34 56 78. Read left-to-right with value←256×value+byte: M001 Horner decoding in base 256.

Byte swapping and network order: swapping reverses octet significance; host/network conversion is a no-op when orders already match. Classic Internet fields often use big endian, but each protocol defines its own contract. Serialization fixes widths/order and validates lengths without native padding.

Alignment and padding: alignment A restricts starting addresses to multiples of A. C++ alignof reports the requirement; alignas requests a supported stronger alignment. Align-up needs nonzero A and overflow checks; an aligned numeric offset is not automatically a live pointer.

Internal and tail padding: internal padding precedes a member to meet its alignment. Under 1/4/1 member alignments, byte–uint32–byte uses offsets 0/4/8, with three internal padding bytes. ABI and object layout determines actual offsets.

Tail padding rounds complete-object size for aligned array stride. The same example ends at byte nine and rounds to size 12; the next object’s four-aligned member remains aligned. Never infer sizeof solely by summing payload sizes.

Field reordering and AoS versus SoA: order by decreasing alignment can reduce holes. A 1/8/1/4 example commonly shrinks 24→16 bytes. Measure sizeof/alignof/offsetof; ABI compatibility and hot/cold access patterns can outweigh smaller size. AoS stores complete records; SoA has one array per field.

Packed structures and misaligned access: packing extensions can remove holes but weaken member alignment. They do not define endianness, versions, or lifetime. A packed native object differs from a specified wire format.

Misalignment can cross cache-line/page boundaries, slow access, or fault depending on instruction/platform. C++ access still needs a suitably aligned live object. Reconstruct bytes or copy representation into an existing aligned trivially copyable object; copying alone does not normalize endianness.

Pointer arithmetic and provenance: address is a location identifier; a C++ pointer is a constrained typed access path. Within an array, p+i advances i×sizeof(T) bytes; one-past can be formed but not dereferenced. Numeric addresses alone do not establish access rights.

Addresses and virtual memory translates process-visible addresses to physical addresses. A contiguous vector buffer can span scattered frames. Virtual and physical contiguity distinguishes address-space adjacency from backing placement.

Process isolation and page permissions: each address space has its own mapping context. VA 0x400000 can map to frame 27 in A and frame 913 in B. Shared mappings may select the same frame; read/write/execute/user permissions constrain access.

Pages and page offsets: a virtual page is an address block; a frame is corresponding physical storage. For P=2^k, VPN=floor(VA/P), offset=VA mod P. The 4-KiB example uses k=12; actual page size depends on platform/configuration, not universally 4096.

Page tables and MMU: entries supply frame identity, permissions, and state; MMU is the translation/protection mechanism. The TLB caches translations, not data. A miss may resolve through page-table walking without a page fault.

Page faults and demand paging: OS intervention is needed under current mapping state. Valid demand loading/zero-fill may install a frame and retry; Copy-on-write may copy on first write. Unmapped/forbidden access may fail. A fault does not necessarily imply disk I/O.

Call stack and stack frames: calls conventionally use LIFO frames for return state, registers, spills, and some locals. Downward growth is a convention; not every local has a stack slot. Returning a dead-local pointer violates Storage duration and object lifetime, even if bytes remain.

Dynamic allocation and heap subdivides OS regions into variable-lifetime blocks. Allocator fragmentation distinguishes slack within allocated blocks (37 requested in a 48-byte class leaves 11) from separated free holes unable to satisfy one request. Allocation cost differs from access latency.

Static storage and initialization: namespace/static objects have program-duration storage. Initialized writable data commonly uses data-like regions; zero-initialized storage uses BSS-like zero-fill without literal executable zero payload. Dynamic initialization and cross-unit ordering need later treatment.

Read-only data and code: text commonly contains instructions, read-only regions constants. Writable-or-executable policy limits writable executable mappings. Modifying a string literal is undefined behavior; const automatic objects are not forced into read-only segments. Segment names/layout are implementation choices.

Appendix.Content: Bridges and distinctions that must not be omitted

ListItem.Content: • ASLR randomizes mapping locations; a textbook process diagram is not a layout guarantee.

• Thread storage duration exists alongside automatic, static, and dynamic duration; thread-local storage is not simply the call stack. Storage duration governs available storage; lifetime governs the live object within it.

Appendix.Content: Clarifications: the layout examples assume stated ABI rules; reordering may break a published ABI. Bounds and lifetime remain necessary even with valid mappings/alignment. Wording cross-checked against the C++ draft alignment, storage duration, and endianness sections.
M004 - Parts 61-76

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
IEEE-754 floating point: finite nonuniform representation plus explicitly specified rounding/special-value behavior; formats do not make every C++ float binary32.
Binary32: 1/8/23 stored fields, 24-bit normal precision and bias 127; 1.0 has word 3F800000.
Binary64: 1/11/52 stored fields, 53-bit normal precision and bias 1023; more precision is distinct from more exponent range.
Signed zero: floating sign is separate from magnitude; signbit sees negative zero whereas x<0 does not.
Exponent bias: normal stored exponent E=e+B; E=130 decodes to e=3 for binary32; classify reserved fields first.
Significand and hidden bit: normal leading binary 1 is implicit; 23 fraction bits plus it give 24 significant bits.
Floating-point encoding and decoding: 10.625=1.010101₂×2³ gives S=0,E=130,F=2A0000, word 412A0000.
Floating-point encoding and decoding: C1540000 has S=1,E=130,F=540000; reconstruct −1.65625×8=−13.25.
Signed zero: 00000000 and 80000000 compare numerically equal but have distinct representations/reciprocals.
Floating-point infinities: all-one exponent with zero fraction; distinct from maximum finite and dependent on sign/rounding in overflow.
NaNs and payloads: all-one exponent with nonzero fraction; unordered comparisons, quiet/signaling distinction, payload preservation caveats.
Subnormals and gradual underflow: E=0 uses no hidden one; binary32 x=(-1)^S F×2^-149, filling the normal-to-zero gap.
Machine epsilon: spacing above 1, 2^-23 for binary32, not min(), denorm_min(), or a universal tolerance.
ULP and representable spacing: normal binade spacing is 2^(e-23) for binary32; 1 has different immediate lower/upper gaps.
Rounding to nearest ties to even: choose nearest neighbor; exact halfway picks even retained significand; guard/round/sticky summarize discarded bits.
Directed rounding modes: upward, downward and toward-zero are signed directions; runtime environment changes must be checked and restored.

Appendix.Content: The continuous chapter contains these definitions and essential traces directly. Numerical reproductions establish supplied-formula behavior, not current repository implementation; see Supplementary/Sources and Code Anchors.
M005 - Parts 77-88

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Terminating fractions and dyadic rationals: a reduced fraction terminates in binary iff its denominator is a power of two; 0.1f stores 13421773/2^27, not 1/10.
Floating-point addition and absorption: align exponents, preserve guard/round/sticky, normalize and round; 2^24+1 is a nearest-even tie that stores 2^24.
Cancellation and loss of significance: nearly equal operands expose prior error relative to a small difference; sensitivity factor .
Sterbenz lemma: nearby nonnegative stored floats satisfying x/2≤y≤2x have an exact representable difference under suitable gradual-underflow rules; input uncertainty remains.
Floating-point exception flags: max×2 overflows; min-normal/2 is exact subnormal, while min-subnormal/2 rounds to zero with tiny/inexact behavior in the tested environment.
Absolute and relative error: absolute discrepancy carries units; relative discrepancy divides by nonzero reference magnitude. Distinguish forward/backward error and stability from conditioning.
Numerical tolerance policies: separate absolute and relative tolerances; validate them and non-finite inputs. Numeric exact equality is not representation equality.
Numerical tolerance policies: a global epsilon mixes units, scales, algorithmic error and conditioning; approximate closeness is nontransitive.
Fused multiply-add: one-rounding fl(ab+c) differs from fl(fl(ab)+c); the (1+2-23)2 witness yields 2^-46 rather than zero.
Floating-point reassociation: (a+b)+c and a+(b+c) can differ; naive, compensated and fixed pairwise reductions have different contracts.
Floating-point reassociation: distributive graphs differ: with a=1e10,b=1+2^-23,c=-1, factored result 1192.0928955078125 versus unfused expanded 1024.

Numerical reproducibility: precision, ordering, FMA, environment and compiler/math-library settings matter. Atomicity does not fix global order; capped TSDF updates are mathematically history-dependent.

Appendix.Content: All essential explanations and traces are in the continuous chapter. Repository findings remain supplied-source claims; no live engine experiment is implied. ## M006 - Parts 89-100

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Fixed-point representation: a signed raw integer I at scale S represents I/S; F=16 gives step 2^-16 and raw 212992 for 3.25.
Fixed-point range and resolution: require 2^-F≤requested step and M·2F≤2(N-1)-1. A 32-bit domain ±1e6 with step≤0.001 permits F=10 or 11.
Fixed-point rescaling: multiply at scale S², then round/divide by S; division uses A·S/B. Prove intermediate width, handle negative ties and zero divisors, and check destination range.

Arithmetic policies remain necessary for fixed point. Nearest unclipped absolute error≤1/(2S); near-zero relative error can be large. Controlled integer arithmetic can improve repeatability, not make every operation associative.

Affine quantization and zero point maps finite values to codes and reconstructs s(q-z). Groupwise scales cost metadata; source-shaped offset INT4 codes [1,5,8,11,15] pack to 51 B8 0F. One-bit row centroids are not automatically ±1.
UNORM and SNORM: UNORM8 reconstructs q/255; SNORM8 clamps q/127 at −1. Quantized normal components can require safe renormalization; sRGB is a separate interpretation.
Binary16 uses 1/5/10 fields, bias15, 11 normal precision bits, maximum65504, normal minimum2^-14, subnormal minimum2^-24. Word3E00 encodes1.5.

Bfloat16 uses1/8/7 fields, bias127, 8 normal precision bits; it trades detail for wide exponent range. Nearest-even conversion must classify NaNs instead of discarding their low payload into infinity.

Bit casting and representation transfers suitable initialized object representation; numeric cast converts a value. Eligibility does not solve byte order, arbitrary valid representations, alignment or mapped-object lifetime.

Binary format contracts declare widths/order/representation/version; Checked binary parsing validates products, subtracted bounds, exact lengths and resource limits. Magic/version are not integrity or authenticity.

Checksums CRCs and hashes summarize specified content. Additive sums miss byte reordering; CRC requires named parameters; a cryptographic digest needs a trusted reference, MAC or signature for an adversarial trust claim.

Memory dump interpretation decodes by offset/schema/byte order. The 2×3 demonstration has a28-byte header and24-byte binary32 payload; identical bytes have different meanings under integer, float or character interpretations.

Appendix.Content: Remaining evidence requirements: cache associativity and TLB effects require hardware/profile evidence; genuine SIMD acceleration and vectorization claims require disassembly and target ISA; actual Kairo/Maveb code claims require reading their current revisions; work stealing, high-contention lock-free code and GPU deferred destruction are not implemented by this representative lab. The original book/caption source review queue remains unchanged. The table maps coverage, not proven reader mastery or universal performance.
Phase 5 algorithms and data-structure workload contracts — Parts 401–500

Original contract: the exact original titles below come from the 3,000-part curriculum appended to the supplied integrated 180-chunk plan. The chunk boundaries are M025 401–410, M026 411–430, M027 431–445, M028 446–467, M029 468–486 and M030 487–500. The content is new authored reconstruction, not a newly received original lesson transcript, and the original parts act as coverage atoms rather than as isolated teaching pages.

Continuous teaching: From ADTs to arrays, hashing, trees and DSU connects to From graphs to paths, sorting, scans and caches. The Phase 5 C++20 lab checks selected rings, linear probing with tombstones, Bloom, DSU/MST, graph paths/DAGs, scans, Morton keys, LRU, DP and reproducible randomized properties. Trees such as AVL/red-black/B+ and GPU parallel scans remain conceptual until their own implementations are tested.

Phase 9-10 worked-trace navigation

Phase 8 - From constraints to a stable SVD contract
Follow one small rank-deficient fit through its geometry, answer, and checks. This supplements the Phase 8 story.
Let

The first row observes with gain three. The second row has zero coefficients, so it cannot produce the requested measurement five. The rank is one, the column space is the horizontal axis, and lies outside it. The null space is the vertical axis: changing is invisible to the map.

The SVD is already diagonal: , . The pseudoinverse is . Therefore . Every has the same residual ; is its minimum-norm choice. This trace separately answers consistency, rank, nullity, residual, and the pseudoinverse policy.

For truncation, . Here the input already has rank one, so the approximation is exact. If instead , then keeping only the first singular direction gives , spectral error , and Frobenius error . The norm names state which reconstruction discrepancy is being reported.

Now use centered planar samples . Their sample covariance with divisor is . The first component follows the horizontal line; the zero second eigenvalue says the observed samples have no vertical spread. Add small measurement noise and that zero becomes small, making the rank or PCA cutoff a scale-aware modeling decision.

An SVD routine should return dimensions and status, not just three arrays. Check relative to a declared input scale; check and separately, with identity sizes matching full/thin conventions; verify descending nonnegative singular values; enforce a maximum iteration count and surface nonconvergence. Passing these checks establishes those measured properties at the tested scale; it does not certify every singular value or guarantee an accurate solution for an ill-conditioned application.
Phase 7 - The moving-panel tracebook
Use active right-handed rotations, column vectors, radians in code, and the declared illustrative minus-Z projection with near 1, far 10 and NDC depth .
One local point reaches a screen-relative description
Let local scale be , orientation a positive-Z quarter turn, translation , and point . The camera sits at world with identity orientation.

Cell.Content: Scaling occurs in the declared local axes.
Right-hand positive Z maps X toward Y.
Camera is five units above the world plane and looks along .
Finite nonzero divisor; this point is within the selected clip volume.

Appendix.Content: Reconstructing local coordinates undoes translation, then rotation, then scale. Applying the inverse orientation with a guessed untranslated offset would mix frames. The same row-major scalar array could implement every operation if logical access and upload conventions remain correct.
The tangent and normal take different paths

Take local tangent and local normal . Scale then rotate gives . Reciprocal-scale then rotate gives . Their dot is . Normalizing for shading changes its length, not the perpendicularity. Neither vector receives translation. A mirrored model additionally needs an explicit winding/orientation policy.
Diagnose interpolation using a quarter point

Interpolate identity to a positive-Z orientation. At , ideal SLERP gives a turn. NLERP normalizes coefficients , yielding about . The midpoint alone would not expose this speed difference. With endpoints and , sign-aligning first avoids a zero midpoint and preserves the common orientation.
A parent edit invalidates only actual dependencies

For car → door → mirror, editing the door’s local transform makes door-local and door-world caches stale, along with mirror-world and derived inverse/normal caches. Mirror-local and car caches remain valid. Reparenting the mirror changes its world dependency even if its local coefficients remain identical. Preserving world pose during reparenting instead requires solving the new local map and checking whether the result still fits the allowed TRS representation.
Phase 6 - The robot panel tracebook
This cumulative trace extends the self-contained Phase 6 volume. The numbers are illustrative laboratory inputs, not observations from a real robot or renderer.
One physical object through six representations
Start with metre-valued workcell points , , and sensor point .

Div.Content: Point differences, not new point locations.
Oriented area vector in square metres.
Finite unit front normal; triangle area is .
Sum is one and all weights are positive.
Affine temperature model, not an asserted physical heat solution.

Appendix.Content: Move a point above the panel. The area normal dotted with is , yielding tetrahedron volume . Swap and both signs reverse; ordinary area and volume do not.
A mirror changes orientation, not all measurements

Mirror horizontal coordinates with . New first edge is and second edge remains . Their cross becomes . All edge lengths and all original pairwise dot products remain unchanged. The Gram matrix cannot tell us that the orientation flipped.

The ordinary transformed normal direction is still . The cross-derived oriented normal gains the additional factor . This is why a mesh pipeline needs a consistent front-face and mirror policy rather than one generic “transform vector” call.
Nonuniform scaling exposes a hidden normal bug

For tangent and normal , double only the horizontal scale. Tangent becomes . A naively transformed normal gives dot , not zero. The inverse-transpose normal gives dot zero. Normalize the latter only after deriving its correct direction.
A frame can be valid without being continuous

With normal , a least-aligned horizontal helper produces tangent and bitangent . All axes are unit and perpendicular, and the frame is positive. Perturb the normal through a helper-selection tie: a different helper can become preferred abruptly. Correct axes do not establish smooth frame evolution. Animated systems must decide whether continuity or a texture reference is required.
Perspective-correct attribute trace

For two projected endpoints with , equal screen weights produce reciprocal-weight denominator . Surface weights become and . If endpoint attributes are and , affine surface interpolation at that screen location gives , not the naive .
The first lost quantity can precede every formula

Store intended horizontal coordinates and in binary32. Near that scale, one unit is below the local representable spacing, so both can round to the same value. Subtraction then yields zero. Promoting those already-rounded values to binary64 does not recover their difference. Retain a wider global representation or subtract in an appropriately local frame before narrowing.
Collision difference without an explicit shape

Take intervals and . In positive direction, the difference support is . In negative direction, choose . The origin lies between them, consistent with overlap. For , , the extrema are , both negative; the intervals do not overlap. A full higher-dimensional collision algorithm must manage its simplex and stopping policies separately.
What the executed lab actually demonstrates

The inline scalar program checks the panel weights, area, frame, projection, rejection, reflection, finite-state rejection, huge/tiny scaled normalization, angles, transmission and total internal reflection. It also runs 2,000 deterministic moderate-range cases for decomposition, orthogonality, projection idempotence, reflected length and cross antisymmetry/perpendicularity. None of these tests certify all floating-point inputs, performance, a robust orientation implementation, or human understanding.
XR - From geometry to sample loss and evidence
The complete explanations and code remain in the independent XR story.
Use this table to follow the quantities from one step to the next:

Cell.Content: Average and local density differ under the planar projection.
Alternating zero/one; take even samples; obtain all zeros
Decimation can turn a pattern into a misleading constant.
This declared alternating sequence gives its intended mean. The filter is not an ideal universal cutoff.
DFT bins 7 and 29 give one-sided amplitudes 0.3 and 0.1
The stated amplitude normalization separates the two components.
Gains 0.951850 and 0.291213 at 0.05 and 0.25 cycles per pixel
Higher-frequency contrast is reduced more strongly.
Encoded 0.5 instead decodes to 0.214041. The arithmetic domain matters.
Change allocation with the same true-gaze metric
This is one toy-model result, not a human threshold or saved GPU work.
The formula matches the selected criterion for the illustrative parameters.

Appendix.Content: Frame history can be clean and wrong
Follow a moving character:

ListItem.Content: 1. The previous frame sees the character at a pixel.
2. The character moves, exposing the background.
3. Incorrect reprojection brings the old character color into that background.
4. Accumulation reduces random noise but retains a ghost.

Appendix.Content: A depth or identity mismatch can justify rejecting that history.
A gaze-region change creates a second problem. An old peripheral sample may belong to the correct surface but lack the detail required now.
Lower MSE or lower variance alone does not establish that the reused information is correct.
An allocation claim and a runtime claim are different
Normalize the original frame time to one:
Only the second component benefits. If its work becomes 70% cheaper:
The speedup is:
The calculation assumes additive, non-overlapping costs. A real GPU may have overlap, bandwidth limits, occupancy changes, or synchronization costs.
A post-filtered full reference does not establish that any original shading work was skipped.
C++ - Value-transfer and cleanup board traces
Essential code and traces remain inline in the payload journey and the event laboratory.

Cell.Content: Both members completed; complete Whole did not. No destructor-body -3 event.
Destructor body precedes reverse member cleanup.
Delegating target completes, delegating body throws
Complete target established object; cleanup invokes its destructor then member destruction.

Appendix.Content: Positive IDs mean construction/body entry, negatives mean destruction. The fixed recorder does not allocate from destructors. Exception traces establish the tested lifetime rules, not a policy for every subsystem’s error handling.
Assignment failure versus successful ownership transfer

Start A with byte7 and B with byte9 in separate buffers. Prepare B=A with an injected allocation failure: B still holds byte9 at the same live buffer, A still byte7, and allocation count is unchanged. Move-construct C from A: C owns byte7, A is documented empty. Copy-construct from empty A: new owner is empty without traversing a null range. Move-assign C into B: B’s byte9 allocation is released, B takes byte7, C becomes empty. Self-move B through its alias preserves its value under this particular owner’s contract. Reset B to empty and end scope: live allocation count0.
The aliased update does not behave like two copies

For destination+=source; source*=0.5, starting with distinct source4/destination4 gives destination8/source2. If both parameters designate one float, its state is4→8→4. The second statement sees the first statement’s write. Passing scalar values instead creates independent parameter values; no caller mutation is implied.
Observation is not a mandatory NRVO count

On the recorded Clang C++23 build, the named Probe return observed zero moves ordinarily and one with optional elision disabled. The immovable same-type prvalue result remained valid in both. This differentiates language-required direct construction from a compiler-selected named-local elision. Do not substitute these observed counts for a timing or allocation benchmark.

The essential explanation remains inline in the borrow story. This deeper board exercise separates the targets of three paths. Assume a vector with three live Slot objects, enough capacity, and assignments that do not end the destination Slot lifetime.

Direct alias versus converted snapshot

Start count=10, bind const int& live=count and const double& snapshot=count. The first referent is count; the second is a new converted double containing10.0. After count=50, live observes50 and snapshot observes10.0. At the end of their enclosing scope the extended double temporary dies; no separate double was owned by count.
A function call does not renew the deadline

Construct temporary string → bind call parameter → return that same path → bind caller’s receiving reference → complete full-expression → destroy temporary. The receiver’s longer lifetime is irrelevant. Contrast direct local binding, which specifies extension, with returning std::string by value, which establishes an owning result. The complete rule is in Temporary lifetime extension, not “references make temporaries live longer.”

Source3/cache-empty → Get holds mutex, computes9, copies9, unlocks → Set holds mutex, replaces source with4, clears cache, unlocks → Get computes16 and copies it under mutex. The earlier returned9 remains a valid independent snapshot. If Get had exposed a reference, clearing the optional could end that referenced integer’s lifetime. Locking only while obtaining the reference does not protect its later use.

Appendix.Content: Input and conventions
Schema, from least to most significant position:
Appendix.Code: bits 0-2 mode | bit 3 visible | bits 4-5 quality | bit 6 locked | bit 7 dirty
Appendix.Content: Input: {mode=5, visible=1, quality=2, locked=0, dirty=1}. Field zero occupies the least-significant available bits.
State-by-state trace
Base interpretations:
Quality extraction:
LSB-first bit-array packing of [1,0,1,1,0,1,0,1] accumulates 01, 05, 0D, 2D, then AD; unpacking index 5 computes (0xAD >> 5) & 1 = 1.
Result and invariant checks

ListItem.Content: • Every field round-trips to its input value.
• The five fields occupy eight non-overlapping bits exactly.
• Changing quality to 3 clears 0x30, writes 0x30, and yields 0xBD; all non-quality bits remain unchanged.

Appendix.Content: Boundary or failure trace

OR-only replacement fails when a new value needs to clear an old 1. For example, replacing quality 3 with 1 via word | (1 << 4) leaves the old high field bit set and still decodes as 3. Clear-before-OR produces the intended 1.

Use eight-bit result storage. C is the ninth unsigned bit, V reports signed two’s-complement range failure, N copies result bit 7, and Z tests whether the low result byte is zero.
State-by-state trace
Case 1 - signed overflow without carry:
Appendix.Code:
01111111 unsigned 127, signed 127 + 00000001 unsigned 1, signed 1 ---------- 10000000 unsigned 128, signed -128
C=0: no ninth bit; unsigned 128 fits V=1: signed mathematical 128 does not fit [-128,127] N=1: result high bit is set Z=0: result is nonzero

C=1: unsigned mathematical 256 needs a ninth bit V=0: signed mathematical result is valid zero N=0: low result high bit is clear Z=1: low result byte is zero

Result and invariant checks

ListItem.Content: • C and V are independent; neither can replace the other.
• N reports the stored sign bit, not whether a signed overflow occurred.
• An eight-bit emulator must retain a wider temporary long enough to compute C, then mask the architectural result.

Appendix.Content: Boundary or failure trace

10000000 represents -128. Complement-plus-one returns 10000000 because mathematical +128 cannot fit. At the fixed-bit residue level the pattern is stable; evaluating same-type signed negation in C++ overflows and is undefined.
Reconstructing each state change
Decimal to binary and back

For 173, successive quotient/remainder pairs are (86,1), (43,0), (21,1), (10,1), (5,0), (2,1), (1,0), (0,1). The remainders are low bits first, so reverse them to get 10101101. Horner accumulators while reading this result are 1,2,5,10,21,43,86,173. This checks both directions without assuming that the displayed order equals array order.
Replacing a field while preserving neighbors
Replace quality 2 with 1 in AD:
Appendix.Code: field width w=2, offset s=4 low mask L=03; positioned mask M=30 eight-bit NOT(M)=CF clear: AD & CF = 8D encode new value: (01 & 03) << 4 = 10 write: 8D | 10 = 9D read back: (9D >> 4) & 03 = 01 outside field: AD & CF = 9D & CF = 8D
Appendix.Content: The last equality proves preservation rather than only checking the new field value.
Multiplication by selected partial products
Multiply 13 by 11. Start result=0, partial=13, multiplier=11. A low multiplier bit of 1 includes the partial product; shift the multiplier right and the widened partial left between stages.
Check 13×11=143. The widened partial is essential: if it were retained in a narrow original operand, shifts could lose bits before the accumulator sees them.
Division by shifting the remainder

Divide binary 1101 (13) by 3, reading dividend bits from most to least significant. At each stage append the next bit to the partial remainder, compare with 3, subtract if possible, and append the quotient decision.
Quotient 4 and remainder 1 satisfy 13=4×3+1, with 0≤1<3.
C++ expression types and a safe index
For uint8_t a=250,b=10 on the host used here:

ListItem.Content: 1. Stored operands are eight-bit unsigned values.
2. Integral promotion converts each to int because int represents 0–255.
3. Addition executes as int arithmetic, producing int 260.
4. auto keeps int 260; explicit conversion to uint8_t stores residue 4.

Appendix.Content: For int index=−1 and unsigned size=10, an ordinary mixed-sign comparison may convert −1 to a large unsigned value. std::cmp_less(-1,10u) correctly returns true mathematically, but that alone does not authorize indexing. The valid condition is index>=0 && std::cmp_less(index,size).
Binary subtraction and incoming borrow

Take A=5, B=3. With carry C=1, compute 5+NOT₈(3)+1=5+252+1=258: result=2, carry-out=1 (no borrow). With C=0, compute 257: result=1, since an incoming borrow subtracts one extra. For A=3,B=5,C=1, exact unsigned difference is −2: low result=254, carry-out=0 (borrow). This is the binary SBC convention, independent of any repository implementation claim.
M003 - Bytes to physical memory
A matching and mismatching endian decode
Bytes are hexadecimal. Reading LE bytes as BE produces 78563412; no intra-octet bit reversal occurs. A schema version=1, count=0x12345678, payloadSize=9, written U8/U32-LE/U64-LE, yields:
Field offsets are 0/1/5, length 13. A typical native record places fields at 0/4/8, size 16. Packing may resemble the schema length but does not define its byte order or version contract.
Struct layout and an aligned array
Assume member size/alignment pairs 1/1, 8/8, 2/2, 4/4.
Holes are seven plus two bytes; payload 15, size 24. Reordering id/color/layer/flags gives 0-7/8-11/12-13/14 plus one tail byte: size 16. Verify on the target ABI.
A 1/4/1 record ends at nine but has size 12. At base 0x1000, next object starts 0x100C and its integer at 0x1010. A fictitious stride nine would put that integer at 0x100D, breaking alignment.
Page translation with an unchanged offset
Assume 4-KiB pages and an allowed resident mapping.
Appendix.Code: VA 0x12345ABC P 0x1000 = 4096 VPN = VA / P 0x12345 offset = VA % P 0xABC mapping VPN 0x12345 -> PFN 0x987 frame start 0x987000 PA = start + offset 0x987ABC
Appendix.Content: Process B may map the same VPN to another PFN; adjacent virtual pages may map distant frames. These are address-space mappings, not endian conversions.

Four bytes starting at offset FFE occupy FFE/FFF in page one and 000/001 in page two. A valid first mapping does not prove the second readable. Four bytes at cache-line offset 62 similarly span two 64-byte lines.
One member load, separated by mechanism
Assume active at offset zero, IEEE-754 32-bit float at offset four, object VA 0x12345000, valid alignment, and 4-KiB pages.

ListItem.Content: 1. Member offset produces VA 0x12345004.
2. Split into VPN 0x12345 and offset 004.
3. TLB/page-table lookup supplies allowed PFN 0x5A7.
4. PA=0x5A7004; cache/memory supplies bytes.
5. With stated little-endian float representation, 00 00 80 3F corresponds to bits 3F800000 and float 1.0; IEEE-754 floating point develops why later.

Appendix.Content: A TLB miss can walk valid tables without OS faulting. A nonresident valid page can fault, acquire backing, and resume. A forbidden access may fail. Real processors overlap this conceptual sequence.
Ownership and lifetime, not geography

A local vector object commonly occupies a frame; elements occupy its separate dynamic buffer. A copied span points to elements, not vector metadata. Returning that span after destroying the vector dangles it; reallocation can also invalidate views. Keeping an owner alive is necessary but not always sufficient.

Static locals retain storage across calls; automatic const locals need not use read-only mappings; string literals have static storage and must not be modified. Old numeric addresses or remaining bytes do not extend lifetime.
Fault recovery and copy-on-write

Two mappings share frame F read-only. For a permitted private COW write, OS allocates F2, copies F, changes the writer’s mapping to F2 with write permission, and restarts. Not every protection violation is repairable.

Diagnosis: absurd decoded value→byte order; second array element misaligned→stride/tail padding; released vector span→lifetime; first-touch latency→fault/commitment; allocation fails amid holes→fragmentation; published file lost after crash→publication versus durability.

Pedagogy and substantive corrections

The triangular workcell panel anchors a connected story: movement → coordinates → reachability and basis → measurement → decomposition → area/orientation → surfaces and optics → affine interpolation → convex collision → projective representation → dual measurements → implementation contracts.

The rewrite puts questions and ordinary meanings before terminology, defines symbols close to their equations, retains worked intermediate states, and keeps independent code examples and the runnable capstone inline. All mathematical prose uses dollar-delimited LaTeX. The token-efficiency skill constrained inspection output, not explanation depth. The Playwright skill guides local math rendering without changing Obsidian configuration.

Important clarifications include: coordinate Euclidean length assumes an orthonormal metric; squared distance is not itself a metric; a small dimensional determinant is not a universal conditioning test; zero direction is not a normalization fallback; off-plane Gram barycentrics represent a projection; projective equivalence does not license arbitrary clip-representative rescaling; a direction vector and projective point at infinity retain different information; normal/covector and cross-derived area transformations differ by determinant scaling; support functions require stated attainment assumptions; unsafe adjacent-member indexing is not rescued by apparent contiguity; NaNs must be constructed rather than obtained by reading indeterminate memory.

Corrections and modeling contracts

The planar display’s average PPD must not be labeled its central local density. The expanded notes derive the projection derivative: FOV47.658899degrees, average40.286285PPD, center37.936213PPD for W0.53m/D0.60m/N1920. Spectral amplitude reporting distinguishes interior one-sided amplitudes from normalized complex magnitudes; DC/Nyquist are not doubled. Balanced difference-of-Gaussian constant cancellation requires gain/normalization conditions.

Exact-Nyquist phase is a boundary hazard; post-filtering cannot generally undo alias ambiguity. A fixed display refresh rate is not a universal perceptual cutoff. Motion-vector units/direction and jitter need contracts; TAA is not exposure integration. Temporal variance benefits require stationarity, independent noise and valid alignment. Psychometric correctness differs from generic detection, curve parameters differ from a selected threshold, and nonsignificance is not equivalence. A simulated foveation filter that computes a full reference first does not prove saved shading work or human invisibility.

Appendix.Content: Corrections and explicit implementation contracts

ListItem.Content: 1. Fixed conversion rejects non-finite input before rounding/casting. The supplied range checks alone do not reject NaN.

2. Fixed multiplication/division use proved int64 intermediates and checked destination narrowing. Negative nearest-even rescaling uses unsigned magnitudes and quotient/remainder; it never negates INT64_MIN or adds a potentially overflowing positive half-scale.

3. C++23 signed shifting is not described as universally undefined. Instead the lab uses scaled multiplication and an explicit rounding algorithm to avoid confusing modular shift behavior, floor, truncation and desired rescaling.

4. The source’s lrint quantizer follows the active rounding direction. The teaching quantizer declares nearest-even, validates finite samples/scales, and bounds the ratio before integer conversion. It is not represented as identical production behavior.
5. Offset code q+8 is distinguished from two’s-complement INT4. Half-step quantization bounds exclude clipping and finite-parameter/evaluation error.

6. Smaller groups trade adaptation for metadata, without a universal monotonic quality guarantee. Full-group asymptotic bits/sample are distinguished from exact ceiling-based storage for small/partial groups.
7. Binary16 loss scaling is not presented as a cure for already-large values; BF16 keeps exponent width but not every FP32 endpoint or precision property.
8. BF16/half NaNs are explicitly canonicalized in the toy converters; raw tensor words preserve bits without signaling-NaN arithmetic.
9. Parser bounds use subtraction after offset validation; shape products are checked before multiplication; exact length and a 4096-element resource cap precede allocation.
10. Zero-copy mapping requires representation, bounds, alignment, lifetime and permitted typed-access rules—not merely an offset divisible by four.
11. The dump helper rejects zero/excessive row width, advances by remaining bounded length and uses a local formatting stream.
12. Error metrics promote float operands before subtracting when evaluated in double. Scalar reconstruction error is not task-level accuracy.
13. CRC detection, cryptographic integrity, authenticity, schema validity, publication and durability remain separate contracts. No security primitive or production format migration was implemented.

Appendix.Content: Corrections and teaching decisions

ListItem.Content: 1. The binary subtraction operands are 1753/1024 and 1751/1024, giving 2^-9; the supplied difference/exponent was incorrect.
2. Numeric equality is not byte identity: signed zeros compare equal, while NaNs are unordered.
3. The cross-product example loses the +1 during binary32 input conversion near 1e8, before product rounding. Later promotion cannot recover it.
4. Distinct binary32 neighbors near 1e9 differ by 64; the source’s +32 example can round to the same input.
5. The existing validated, widened float comparator is reused. An unchecked generic tolerance formula is not labeled production-safe.
6. Gamma bounds retain algorithm, range, magnitude and conditioning assumptions. Exact nearby subtraction does not imply accurate original inputs.
7. Capped weighted recurrence is history-dependent even with exact representable arithmetic; this is separate from persistent-state narrowing.

8. The mixed-state laboratory fixture uses 0.5 and its next binary32 neighbor, staying within its normalized [-1,1] sample contract. An initial out-of-contract fixture threw during development; it was corrected before both final builds.

Appendix.Content: Merge corrections and explicit policies

ListItem.Content: 1. The source’s complement-key ULP distance special-cases equal zeros but retains two zero slots for cross-zero intervals. The finite-only teaching metric collapses signed zeros in its key, rejects NaN/infinity, and verifies negative-min-subnormal to positive-min-subnormal distance 2.

2. The supplied scalar tolerance formula rejects equal infinities but can also accept finite-versus-infinity and opposite infinities, via infinity ≤ infinity. These additional failure paths are reproduced. An alternative float-specific policy validates tolerances, handles non-finite values first, and widens finite comparisons. No production fix was made.
3. Tiny/subnormal does not by itself mean an underflow flag; distinguish exactly representable tiny values from tininess/inexactness conditions.
4. Raw-word quiet/signaling classification does not execute signaling-NaN arithmetic. Payload preservation through floating value transport/operations is not claimed.
5. Rounding demonstrations check mode-setting success and restore the initial mode, rather than forcing nearest as the cleanup action. The laboratory restores direction, not all status flags.
6. The matrix excerpt asserts before its fallback; do not describe identity return as the unconditional debug-build outcome.
7. ULP is given an explicit local/directional convention at powers of two; finite maximum’s upward neighbor infinity is not an ordinary finite gap.

Appendix.Content: Coordinate frames and change of basis

Definition and mechanism

A frame gives an origin and independent axes relative to another frame. Its matrix maps local coordinates to that parent description. Changing description uses the inverse destination frame followed by the source frame; active motion and passive coordinate change answer different questions.
Reconstruction cue: Coordinates from frame A to frame B use inverse(F_B) times F_A.

Appendix.title: Axial depth and Euclidean range
Appendix.Content: Axial depth and Euclidean range
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Axial depth measures distance along the camera’s forward axis; Euclidean range measures distance from the camera centre along the viewing ray. With a right-handed view frame looking along , positive axial depth is , while range is . They agree only on the optical axis. For a unit ray direction with , a range measurement converts to axial depth as . A range sensor and a perspective depth buffer may therefore encode different quantities. Applying a depth-buffer formula directly to a range image distorts reconstructed geometry away from the image centre. At view point , axial depth is while range is , a visible distinction off-axis.

Appendix.title: Hardware depth-buffer linearization
Appendix.Content: Hardware depth-buffer linearization
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Perspective projection maps axial distance nonlinearly into NDC depth. For a declared projection depth row , solve ; finite conventional, finite reversed, infinite reversed, and OpenGL-style conventions have different coefficients or NDC conversions. The depth sample must first be interpreted in the same range and direction used by the projection matrix. This is why a single generic formula without an API and projection contract is unsafe. Verify near and far endpoints, test round trips over a range of distances, and handle an infinite-far endpoint such as reversed depth explicitly. Near/far endpoint checks catch sign mistakes immediately; interior round trips then test scaling and finite precision.

Appendix.Content: Screen-space ray generation and mouse picking
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

A screen ray begins with a pixel location mapped through the viewport to NDC, then through inverse projection and camera pose into a world-space origin and direction. For perspective cameras, rays usually share the eye origin; orthographic rays have parallel directions but different origins across the image. Mouse picking must use the same high-DPI scaling, viewport offset, origin, and Y convention as rendering. Near and far unprojection can define a ray segment, but a point at infinity or an infinite far plane needs an explicit direction construction. Picking then intersects that ray with scene geometry or uses an object-ID buffer.

Appendix.title: Ray differentials and camera sampling measures
Appendix.source: Concepts/Ray differentials and camera sampling measures.md
Appendix.Content: Ray differentials and camera sampling measures
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

A camera sample selects a film location and usually a shutter time, then maps that sample to a weighted ray or path contribution. Ray differentials approximate how neighboring pixel samples change the generated ray; after intersection they estimate the surface footprint covered by a pixel and help choose a texture filter level. A sampling measure states which quantity is sampled and therefore which probability density belongs in a Monte Carlo estimator; area, solid angle, image-plane area, and discrete pixel measures are not interchangeable without a Jacobian. Example: two adjacent pixels generate rays whose intersection points span a large patch on a distant oblique surface, so filtering should average that footprint rather than use a single high-frequency texel. Differential rays are local first-order approximations and can fail at discontinuities or complex lens mappings; the weight and PDF must match the camera model and chosen measure.

Example: For a pinhole camera, offset the raster sample by one pixel in x and y, generate neighboring rays, and intersect them with a textured plane; the resulting parallelogram estimates the pixel footprint for texture filtering.

Assumptions: Differentials approximate nearby rays locally and are not exact at visibility or lens discontinuities.; Importance weights/PDFs are valid only when defined in the same measure as the estimator.
Prerequisites

• Visual angle and calibrated rays
• Lens optics and depth of field

A norm is nonnegative, definite, absolutely homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality. It induces distance by taking the norm of a point difference. Coordinate-defined first, second and infinity norms answer different geometric questions.
For , the three norms are , and . Squared length scales quadratically and is not itself a norm or induced metric.

Appendix.title: Forward and backward error
Appendix.Content: Forward and backward error
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

Forward error measures output discrepancy. Backward error measures how much the input must change for the computed output to be exact. Stability concerns algorithm errors; conditioning concerns problem sensitivity. Small backward error can coexist with large forward error.

Appendix.title: Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse
Appendix.Content: Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse

The exact SVD defines by reciprocating every positive singular value and transposing the orthogonal factors. minimizes residual first and Euclidean solution norm among minimizers second. A numerical cutoff instead produces : if it discards a positive singular value, it solves a retained-rank approximation and can increase the residual of the original system. The cutoff makes the treatment of weak directions explicit.
Use it when: rectangular or rank-deficient least squares needs a minimum-norm answer.

Developed in Phase 8: The exact pseudoinverse reciprocates every positive singular value, yielding the least-squares solution with minimum Euclidean norm. A practical cutoff defines a different, truncated operator: discarding even a positive singular value can increase the residual for the original system, so the tolerance and retained rank are part of the mathematical answer. the exact pseudoinverse · truncation and regularization
Prerequisites
Singular value decomposition, Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Matrix norms and numerical error.
Used by

Appendix.title: Matrix functions
Appendix.Content: Matrix functions

For diagonalizable matrices, a scalar function can be applied to eigenvalues in a usable eigenbasis. Matrix exponential models linear constant-coefficient dynamics; logarithm and square root require domain and branch choices. Stable algorithms such as scaling-and-squaring are distinct from the defining power series.
Use it when: integrating linear dynamics or interpolating structured transforms.

Developed in Phase 8: A matrix function applies scalar behavior to invariant directions when the decomposition permits it, but its definition and its stable algorithm are separate. The exponential solves a linear differential equation; logarithms and square roots require domain and branch choices, and powers range from repeated multiplication to fractional transforms. matrix functions · domains and branches

Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Matrix multiplication and composition order, Matrix norms and numerical error.

Appendix.title: Sparse and iterative solvers
Appendix.Content: Sparse and iterative solvers

Sparse storage avoids zeros when structure and scale justify its index overhead. Iterative methods replace a dense factorization with matrix-vector products and a convergence process. Conjugate gradient requires symmetric positive definiteness; preconditioning, residual criteria, and a maximum iteration count belong in the contract.
Use it when: large structured systems make dense storage or factorization impractical.

Developed in Phase 8: Sparse storage pays off when zeros and dimensions outweigh indexing overhead, while direct factorization can create fill that destroys sparsity. Iterative methods instead use matrix-vector products and stopping tests; conjugate gradient requires an SPD operator, and preconditioning, a maximum iteration count, and a true residual make convergence reviewable. storage and fill · direct versus iterative solving
Prerequisites
Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky, Matrix norms and numerical error.
Used by
Matrix factorization choices, Matrix storage indexing and strides.
Teaching path: sparse and iterative methods.

Appendix.title: ODE initial-value problems and stiffness
Appendix.Content: ODE initial-value problems and stiffness
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

An ordinary differential equation specifies a state’s rate of change as a function of state and time. An initial-value problem adds the starting state; together they define the trajectory when existence and uniqueness conditions hold. Numerical integration advances approximate states through finite time steps. Stability concerns whether numerical errors remain controlled under repeated updates, not just whether one step is accurate. A stiff system contains modes with very different time scales; explicit methods may require impractically small steps to remain stable even when the visible solution changes slowly. Implicit methods can enlarge the stable step region but require solving equations. Consistency, stability, and convergence are distinct properties. A simulator should choose its step and integrator based on the dynamics, not merely the display frame interval or apparent smoothness of one trajectory.

• Eigenvalues and eigenspaces
• Absolute and relative error

Appendix.title: Time integrators and symplectic updates
Appendix.Content: Time integrators and symplectic updates
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

A time integrator turns a differential equation into a discrete state update. Explicit Euler uses the current slope; midpoint and Runge–Kutta methods combine several slope evaluations to improve local accuracy; semi-implicit Euler updates velocity before position and can behave better for mechanical systems. Symplectic methods preserve the geometric structure of Hamiltonian dynamics, often keeping long-run energy error bounded rather than allowing systematic drift. No method is universally best: order, stability region, cost, conservation, and stiffness all matter. A higher formal order does not guarantee better behavior at an unsuitable step size or under discontinuous forces. Compare integrators on the same problem, step policy, and error target. Update order is part of the algorithm: changing it can change stability and physical behavior, not merely code style.
Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities
Appendix.Content: Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Implicit differentiation obtains how a solution changes when it is defined by an equation rather than an explicit formula. If a state satisfies F(y,θ)=0 and the Jacobian with respect to y is invertible, differentiating gives dy/dθ=−(∂F/∂y)⁻¹(∂F/∂θ). This can differentiate equilibrium states, constrained optima, and roots without unrolling every solver iteration. For a converged optimizer, differentiating stationarity and constraint conditions yields sensitivity equations, but active-set changes, nonunique solutions, singular Jacobians, and imperfect convergence complicate the result. Continuous sensitivity equations propagate derivatives alongside an ODE; adjoint methods can reduce cost when there are many parameters and few scalar outputs. These are modeling tools with assumptions, not a guarantee that every algorithmic branch is differentiable.
Prerequisites

• Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics
• ODE integration and stability

Appendix.title: Basis coordinates and dimension
Appendix.Content: Basis coordinates and dimension

Definition and mechanism

Phase 7 stores basis images as matrix columns and derives coordinate conversion . The endpoint bases and whether motion is active or passive determine the product; row-major storage does not. Reconstruction and active/passive example.

A basis is an ordered independent spanning set. Independence makes coordinates unique; spanning makes every vector reachable. Dimension counts basis elements over the chosen field, not stored components or bytes. A basis change alters coordinates without necessarily moving the physical vector.
, so its slanted-basis coordinates are . A plane inside three-dimensional coordinates still has dimension two.

Appendix.title: Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling
Appendix.Content: Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Sampling transforms convert simpler random inputs into a target law. Inverse-CDF sampling maps a uniform value through a quantile function; rejection sampling accepts proposal draws according to a bounded target-to-proposal ratio; importance sampling estimates an integral by dividing each sampled integrand by the actual proposal density. Each method requires correct support and endpoint handling. Importance sampling is unbiased when the proposal covers every contributing region and the weighted contribution is integrable; finite variance additionally requires the integral of f²/p to be finite. Rejection sampling needs a valid finite envelope. Discrete floating-point inputs can hit boundaries that have zero probability in an ideal continuous model. Report the density with its measure and use the same measure in the estimator. A proposal that misses target support cannot be repaired by a larger weight.
Prerequisites

• Probability density and change of measure
• Stateful pseudorandom generators and stream state

Appendix.title: Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp
Appendix.Content: Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

To normalize nonnegative weights, divide each by their sum; direct summation can overflow even when the normalized probabilities are representable. Scale by the largest weight before summing. For log weights , compute , where . Subtracting the maximum prevents exponential overflow, and the result can be used to form softmax probabilities. This assumes at least one finite, valid weight and requires an explicit policy for all-zero, negative, NaN, or infinite inputs. Underflow of very small normalized probabilities is a separate concern from overflow; do not silently equate zero after underflow with mathematically impossible. For log weights , subtracting keeps exponentials bounded while leaving the normalized probabilities unchanged.

Appendix.title: Confidence intervals and sequential evidence
Appendix.Content: Confidence intervals and sequential evidence
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A confidence interval is a procedure with repeated-sample coverage under stated assumptions; it is not a posterior probability assigned to a fixed parameter. A normal interval for a mean uses a known population standard deviation or an approximation justified by the central limit theorem. With unknown scale and IID normal observations, the Student t distribution accounts for estimating the standard deviation. Heavy tails, sample dependence, multiple comparisons, and optional stopping can invalidate simple textbook guarantees. Adaptive algorithms that stop when a fixed-sample interval looks narrow need sequentially valid methods or a separately justified stopping rule. Report the target, sampling unit, dependence structure, estimator bias, interval procedure, stopping policy, and independent-run count. A narrow interval around a biased estimator measures precision about its expectation, not correctness of the target.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Common probability distributions and their assumptions
• Expectation, covariance, and dependence
• Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance

Appendix.title: Position reconstruction from depth
Appendix.Content: Position reconstruction from depth
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Given a pixel and an axial depth value, reconstruct a view-space point by converting the pixel to NDC, forming its camera ray, and scaling that ray so its forward-axis component equals the measured depth. Alternatively, transform the corresponding homogeneous clip point through an inverse projection matrix and divide by its resulting homogeneous coordinate. To obtain world position, apply the inverse view transform. These routes must share the actual viewport, pixel-centre, NDC-depth, and projection conventions used to render the image. In large worlds, subtract camera-relative origins before reducing precision; converting an already-rounded coordinate cannot restore lost detail. In a camera-relative renderer, reconstruct near the camera origin before adding a large global offset.

Appendix.title: Camera gauge freedoms and observability
Appendix.Content: Camera gauge freedoms and observability
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

A gauge freedom is a coordinated change to unknown scene and camera parameters that leaves every measured image unchanged. In calibrated monocular structure from motion, translating and rotating the entire reconstruction changes only the chosen world frame, while a common scale change of points and camera translations preserves projections; absolute metric scale therefore needs an external reference. Observability asks which local parameter changes produce distinguishable measurements. Linearizing reprojection residuals gives a Jacobian; its weighted information tensor or matrix reveals weak parameter combinations through small eigenvalues after gauge directions are fixed. Example: adding more points to one planar, nearly fronto-parallel view may reduce pixel noise while focal length and distance remain strongly coupled. These conclusions assume a stated camera/scene model, correctly associated observations, and local linearization; the information matrix diagnoses local constraints, not global uniqueness. Report uncertainty only after fixing the gauge and specifying the observation noise model.

Example: A monocular map can be uniformly enlarged with all camera translations enlarged by the same factor and render the same images; a known baseline or measured object length fixes that scale gauge.

Assumptions: The gauge statement assumes calibrated monocular perspective cameras and no metric prior.; The information-matrix interpretation is local and depends on residual weighting and parameterization.
Prerequisites

• Coordinate frames and change of basis
• Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

Appendix.title: Interpolation versus approximation
Appendix.Content: Interpolation versus approximation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Interpolation reproduces every prescribed sample exactly, while approximation minimizes or controls an error criterion and may miss the observations. The distinction matters when data are noisy: a high-degree interpolant can fit measurement noise and oscillate between samples, while a lower-complexity approximation can better represent the underlying trend. In texture reconstruction, the samples themselves often define the represented signal, so interpolation is an appropriate reconstruction rule. In calibration, observations have uncertainty, so fitting a model may be more defensible. Neither method is automatically superior; choose based on the meaning of the data, the error measure, and whether evaluation stays within or extrapolates beyond the sampled domain.

Appendix.title: PCA and covariance eigensystems
Appendix.Content: PCA and covariance eigensystems

Center sample rows, then find the orthogonal directions of greatest variance. For centered , SVD gives directions in , scores in , and covariance eigenvalues . Units and feature scaling change the question; near-equal eigenvalues make individual axes unstable.
Use it when: describing point clouds, reducing dimensions, or estimating a best-fit plane.

Developed in Phase 8: PCA first centers observations so the covariance measures variation around the sample mean. The right singular vectors of centered data give principal directions, gives scores, and squared singular values scaled by sample count give covariance eigenvalues; feature units and small eigengaps affect interpretation. centering and principal axes · plane fits and eigengaps

Phase 9–10 development: For a random vector with finite second moments, covariance is . For every vector , , so covariance is positive semidefinite. Its eigenvectors give uncorrelated principal directions and the eigenvalues give variance along them. Whitening rescales nonzero-variance directions and needs a stated policy for zero or tiny eigenvalues. A Gaussian kernel used to model rendering footprints is a spatial distribution model, not automatically a statement about epistemic uncertainty.

Appendix.title: Polar decomposition
Appendix.Content: Polar decomposition

The right polar form separates an orthogonal factor from a positive-semidefinite stretch . The orthogonal factor may include reflection; singular matrices can make its completion nonunique. Symmetric stretch can include shear in the chosen coordinates.
Use it when: separating local rigid-like motion from symmetric deformation.

Developed in Phase 8: Polar decomposition factors a map into an orthogonal part and a positive-semidefinite stretch. The SVD constructs both left and right forms, separates reflection from a proper rotation, and gives the nearest orthogonal or special-orthogonal factor when the singular directions allow a unique choice; zero singular values leave completion freedom. left and right stretch · nearest proper rotation and ambiguity

Singular value decomposition, Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Determinants orientation and volume.
Used by

Appendix.title: Matrix factorization choices
Appendix.Content: Matrix factorization choices

Choose a solver from the matrix promises and task: pivoted LU for general square systems, Cholesky for SPD systems, QR for full-rank least squares, SVD or rank-revealing methods when weak directions matter, and iterative methods for suitable large sparse workloads. Reuse factors for repeated right-hand sides.
Use it when: choosing an algorithm before implementing or calling a numerical routine.

Developed in Phase 8: The factorization should follow the matrix structure and the requested result: LU handles general square systems, Cholesky exploits positive definiteness, QR fits full-rank least squares, and SVD handles uncertain rank and spectral questions. The comparison also weighs sparsity, reuse, memory, and whether an iterative tolerance is acceptable. factorization selection · the runnable LU example

Gaussian elimination and pivoting, LU factorization and reusable solves, Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky, QR factorization and least squares, Singular value decomposition, Sparse and iterative solvers.

Appendix.title: Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation
Appendix.source: Concepts/Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation.md
Appendix.Content: Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A Bézier curve blends control points with Bernstein basis weights. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one on , so the curve remains in the control points’ convex hull and reaches its first and last control points at the endpoints. De Casteljau’s repeated linear interpolation evaluates the curve using numerically straightforward convex combinations; the intermediate levels also reveal subdivision geometry. A cubic Bézier’s endpoint tangents depend on its first and last control-polygon edges, so moving a handle changes direction and scale. The convex-hull guarantee applies to the curve parameter interval; extrapolation outside it loses that containment property. Subdivide the curve before tessellation when screen-space curvature changes rapidly; parameter steps alone do not guarantee uniform pixel error.
Prerequisites

• Spline bases and curve evaluation

Appendix.title: Cubic Hermite interpolation
Appendix.Content: Cubic Hermite interpolation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A cubic Hermite segment is determined by endpoint values and endpoint tangent data. With normalized , its four basis polynomials blend the two endpoint positions and two tangents. Tangents are derivatives with respect to the parameter, so physical-time derivatives must be scaled by segment duration: a velocity in units per second is not interchangeable with a tangent per normalized parameter. Hermite curves are useful when a camera path or animation must pass through known positions while exposing direct control over its entry and exit directions. The endpoint constraints determine one cubic polynomial; continuity between adjacent segments still requires compatible endpoint tangents.

Appendix.title: Random variables and probability laws
Appendix.Content: Random variables and probability laws
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A random variable is a measurable mapping from outcomes to numerical values; its probability law describes how those values are distributed. Discrete laws assign probability mass to points, while continuous laws use densities relative to a chosen measure. A cumulative distribution function exists for either kind and records probability accumulated up to a threshold. Mixed distributions can contain both atoms and continuous parts. Density is not probability at an exact point, and it changes with coordinates according to a Jacobian. Expectation integrates a function against the law, whether the variable is represented by a PMF or PDF. These distinctions matter in sampling APIs: returned value, support, endpoint behavior, and reported density must refer to the same measure. A finite computer sampler approximates a continuous law with finitely many representable outputs.

Appendix.title: Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks
Appendix.Content: Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

The Jacobian is the matrix of first derivatives of a vector-valued function. It maps a small input displacement to a first-order output displacement, a forward sensitivity often called a pushforward or Jacobian-vector product. Gradients transform in the reverse direction by the transpose Jacobian, the pullback used in reverse-mode differentiation. These operations differ because vectors and covectors have different transformation rules. Jacobians compose by matrix multiplication and their determinants describe local volume changes. A Jacobian is local: it does not replace a nonlinear transformation globally. At singular points it can lose rank or become ill-conditioned, affecting inverse sensitivity, uncertainty propagation, and optimizer steps. State coordinate ordering and column-vector conventions before interpreting signs or multiplication order.
