Appendix.title: Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening
Appendix.Content: Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A multivariate Gaussian is determined by a mean vector and a symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance matrix. When the covariance is positive definite, its density is an elliptical bell whose principal directions are covariance eigenvectors. Cholesky factorization maps independent standard-normal samples into correlated samples; whitening applies an inverse factor to express observations in unit-variance coordinates. Singular covariance instead confines the distribution to a lower-dimensional affine subspace and has no ordinary density with respect to full-dimensional volume. Covariance transforms as AΣAᵀ under a linear map and approximately as JΣJᵀ through a nonlinear map near a reference point. These equations support sensor fusion and projected uncertainty, but a Gaussian rendering kernel is not automatically a normalized probability density or epistemic uncertainty model.

Appendix.title: Latin-hypercube sampling
Appendix.Content: Latin-hypercube sampling
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Latin-hypercube sampling divides each coordinate axis into equal strata and uses a permutation so every sample occupies one stratum per dimension. With randomized within-stratum positions and randomized permutations, each sample has uniform marginal coordinates; samples are dependent by design. This can improve coverage for some integrands at arbitrary sample counts, including counts that do not form a square grid. It does not guarantee lower variance for every function, and IID variance formulas cannot be applied without accounting for dependence. Test exact stratum coverage deterministically, then compare estimator error over repeated randomized trials for the intended integrand. For , each axis still receives five strata, avoiding the missing-cell bias of taking five cells from a grid.

Appendix.title: Off-axis stereo projection and disparity
Appendix.Content: Off-axis stereo projection and disparity
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Stereo cameras use two eye centres separated by a baseline, while each projection frustum is shifted so a chosen zero-parallax plane aligns in the images. Parallel eye orientations with asymmetric frusta avoid the vertical mismatch and discomfort often introduced by toe-in cameras. For rectified pinhole cameras, disparity is approximately , so inferred depth is under the calibration and rectification assumptions. Depth uncertainty grows roughly with for fixed pixel disparity error. Distinguish interpupillary distance from lens and display-centre spacing; the rendered baseline is an optical/comfort design decision. Use consistent pixel units for focal length, baseline, and disparity before computing metric depth.

Appendix.title: Omnidirectional camera projections
Appendix.Content: Omnidirectional camera projections
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Cubemaps, equirectangular panoramas, and fisheye lenses map unit directions onto different image domains. A cubemap selects one of six faces and projects two direction components; equirectangular coordinates map longitude and latitude to a rectangle; fisheye mappings use a radial function of angular distance. These parameterizations are not equal-area: uniform pixel sampling does not imply uniform solid-angle sampling. Choose the mapping that matches capture or rendering needs, define face orientation and seam rules, and measure reconstruction with angular error between unit vectors. Fisheye formulas also differ (equidistant, equisolid, orthographic, stereographic), so name the model before interpreting pixels. At the poles, longitude is undefined, so seam and pole handling need explicit sampling rules.

Appendix.title: Newton and quasi-Newton optimization
Appendix.Content: Newton and quasi-Newton optimization
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Newton’s method builds a local quadratic model of an objective from its gradient and Hessian, then solves for the model’s stationary point. Near a well-conditioned solution with suitable smoothness and curvature, it can converge faster than gradient descent. Away from that regime, the Hessian may be indefinite, poorly scaled, or a poor model over the proposed step. Line searches and trust regions control step acceptance. Quasi-Newton methods such as BFGS estimate curvature from successive parameter and gradient changes, avoiding repeated exact Hessian construction. Their guarantees depend on assumptions and update safeguards. Optimization should monitor objective change, gradient norm, step size, constraints, and numerical failures; a small step alone can indicate stagnation rather than success. The method’s result is a local solution unless global structure proves more.
Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt
Appendix.source: Concepts/Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt.md
Appendix.Content: Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Nonlinear least squares minimizes one half the squared norm of a residual vector. Its gradient and Hessian involve the residual Jacobian; the exact Hessian also contains second derivatives of each residual. Gauss–Newton drops those latter terms, producing a positive-semidefinite normal matrix and an efficient local step when residuals are small or the model is close to linear. Levenberg–Marquardt adds damping to control ill-conditioned or overly aggressive steps, blending Gauss–Newton with gradient descent. These algorithms are useful for camera calibration, bundle adjustment, and geometric fitting. Residual scaling, parameter units, rank deficiency, and gauge freedoms influence the solution. Normal equations can square the condition number, so QR or other structured solves may be safer. A small residual does not prove parameters are identifiable or physically correct.
Prerequisites

• Hessians and local curvature
• Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky

Appendix.title: Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise
Appendix.source: Concepts/Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise.md
Appendix.Content: Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Sampling quality concerns the arrangement of points across dimensions used by an estimator, not only each coordinate’s one-dimensional histogram. Stratification partitions a domain and allocates points across cells, reducing large gaps for suitable integrands. Quasi-Monte Carlo sequences such as Sobol aim for low discrepancy and often improve integration of smooth, structured functions, though their samples are dependent and error estimates differ from IID Monte Carlo. Blue-noise point sets suppress low-frequency clumping while retaining local separation; they are useful in image sampling and spatial placement but do not automatically minimize every integral’s variance. Scrambling, domain mapping, dimensional ordering, and discontinuities affect performance. Compare methods against a clear target function and measure. The supplied probability narrative introduces stratification and Sobol but not blue-noise constructions; that part is an explicit teaching addition, not a received source claim.

Appendix.title: Tensor-product interpolation
Appendix.Content: Tensor-product interpolation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Bilinear and trilinear interpolation apply one-dimensional linear weights independently along each coordinate axis. In a rectangular cell, each corner contributes the product of its axis weights; the weights are nonnegative and sum to one for coordinates inside the cell. This preserves the range of scalar corner values, but the interpolated surface can be twisted rather than planar, and derivatives may jump across cell boundaries. For a voxel field, trilinear interpolation provides a continuous in-cell estimate; differentiating it yields a local gradient, which need not have unit length even when samples approximate signed distance. Keep coordinates normalized to the cell and define behavior outside the sampled grid explicitly.

Appendix.title: Pointer arithmetic and provenance
Appendix.Content: Pointer arithmetic and provenance
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C008
Definition and mechanism

M008 adds null/object/one-past distinctions, same-array representable subtraction and round-trip limits. Provenance proposals are research, not adopted C++23 rules; byte inspection differs from arbitrary typed access.

A scalar member behaves as a one-element array for pointer arithmetic, not as an array containing adjacent sibling members. &x+1 can be a one-past pointer but cannot be dereferenced to access y. Actual array storage supports traversal; a span only views an already-valid range. Layout/size assertions do not authorize sibling traversal.

A pointer is a typed access path constrained by array bounds, alignment, and object lifetime, not merely an integer. Within an array, p+i advances i elements; one-past is permitted for traversal but not dereference. Byte views inspect representations; uintptr_t, when provided, is an integer conversion facility, not permission to access arbitrary storage.

Appendix.title: Derivative as a local linear map
Appendix.source: Concepts/Derivative as a local linear map.md
Appendix.Content: Derivative as a local linear map
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

The derivative measures first-order change. In one variable it is the limit of the difference quotient; in several variables it is the linear map that best predicts small output changes near a point. For a scalar function, this local model is the tangent line. For a vector-valued function, it is a matrix acting on an input perturbation. The derivative is local: its approximation error becomes small relative to the perturbation as the step shrinks, but the linear model need not remain accurate over a large region. This view unifies instantaneous velocity, gradients, Jacobians, and optimization directions. It also gives a practical check: compare a small finite perturbation with the derivative’s predicted change, while remembering that floating-point rounding and curvature limit how small or large the perturbation should be.

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

A geometric predicate decides a category from a sign, such as orientation. Near cancellation, ordinary floating arithmetic may not certify that sign. Adaptive arithmetic adds work only when justified error bounds leave uncertainty. Exact stored-input decisions cannot restore rounded-away physical information.
A triangle can have an accurately small area estimate yet an uncertified orientation sign. Declaring every small value zero changes topology instead of proving a decision.

Phase 11 camera development

Adaptive orientation and incircle predicates protect discrete sign decisions from floating-point error by refining arithmetic when an error bound cannot certify the result. Camera estimation has a different uncertainty: noisy pixels and weak observability can leave pose uncertain even when every sign is exact. Predicate robustness does not improve measurement accuracy, and a low reprojection residual does not guarantee every combinatorial decision was reliable. Keep layers distinct: use robust predicates for topology, uncertainty weights for image residuals, and Jacobian spectra for weak directions. Appendix.title: Rigid Contact - Persistent Manifolds and Solver Reconstruction
Appendix.source: Supplementary/Rigid Contact - Persistent Manifolds and Solver Reconstruction.md
Appendix.Content: Rigid contacts: from point velocity to a persistent contact manifold

BlockQuote.Content: Scope: original, independently reconstructed teaching for the existing engine collision-response narrative. The executable witnesses are rigid_contact_lab.cpp and persistent_contact_lab.cpp. These are 2D velocity-level CPU witnesses; they do not claim to be Kairo’s engine implementation, 3D production manifold generation, or continuous collision detection. Symbols and sign conventions below follow those two witnesses.

Appendix.Content: Why a contact is a constraint rather than a force chosen by eye

Imagine a box descending onto a static floor. The collision detector reports that the geometry is touching or overlapping, but it does not say which velocities are physically admissible. With body A as the floor and body B as the box, define the contact normal n to point from A toward B. At contact position p, the lever arms measured from each body’s centre of mass are r_A = p − x_A and r_B = p − x_B. For a planar rigid body, its point velocity is v(p) = v_com + ω × r, where planar scalar angular speed ω produces ω × (r_x,r_y) = (−ω r_y, ω r_x). This matters because an object rotating toward the floor can be closing at a corner even when the centre of mass is moving away.

The relative velocity of the two material points is u = (v_B + ω_B × r_B) − (v_A + ω_A × r_A). The normal component u_n = u · n tells us whether those two points are closing (u_n < 0) or separating (u_n > 0). For a non-penetrating unilateral contact without restitution, the desired post-solve condition is u_n ≥ 0, with a nonnegative accumulated contact impulse λ_n ≥ 0. Their complementarity condition is λ_n u_n = 0 at an exact solution: either the contact carries a positive separating-prevention impulse and reaches zero normal speed, or the bodies separate freely and the contact carries no impulse. Finite-iteration solvers only approximate this coupled condition.
Deriving effective inverse mass, rather than memorizing its denominator

The impulse on B is +λ n and the reaction on A is −λ n. Newton’s linear momentum law gives Δv_B = +λ m_B⁻¹ n and Δv_A = −λ m_A⁻¹ n. Angular impulse about the centre of mass gives Δω_B = +λ I_B⁻¹ (r_B × n) and Δω_A = −λ I_A⁻¹ (r_A × n), where the planar cross product of vectors is the scalar r_x n_y − r_y n_x. A rotation changes point velocity through Δω × r, and its projection onto n adds an angular term proportional to the squared lever arm.
Consequently the normal relative velocity changes by Δu_n = k_n λ, where

Here k_n is inverse effective mass in the contact direction, not mass itself. The same physical impulse changes normal speed less when the effective mass is large. The equation follows from the full point-velocity update; it is not valid to omit rotational terms whenever the contact is off-centre. A static body uses zero inverse mass and inertia, but two completely unresponsive bodies yield k_n = 0 and must not be divided by. The corresponding tangential value k_t is obtained by substituting the perpendicular unit tangent t = (−n_y, n_x) for n.
For a desired post-impact normal speed b, one unconstrained correction is Δλ = (b − u_n)/k_n. A real contact cannot pull the bodies together, so the accumulated normal multiplier is projected:

Apply only the difference, Δλ_n = λ_n^{new} − λ_n^{old}, to body velocities. Applying the whole accumulated value every iteration would add the same historical impulse repeatedly, making motion energy grow artificially. Conversely, resetting the accumulator on every sweep defeats the projected Gauss–Seidel interpretation and prevents reliable friction bounds.
Restitution is a contact-creation decision, not a new bounce each iteration

For an impact with pre-solve normal speed u_n^before < −v_threshold, the outgoing speed target in this simplified solver is b = −e u_n^before, with restitution coefficient e ∈ [0,1]. This target must be sampled before contact impulses change the velocity and then held fixed during the iteration. If a solver recomputes b from the current velocity at every visit, a persistent resting point can acquire artificial new bounce energy. The witness distinguishes a new impact from a persistent contact through an explicit newImpact argument; a production engine requires an actual contact-state machine and impact detection so the decision is not left to a careless caller.

For the central collision test, both bodies have mass 1 kg, A starts at 2 m/s, B at 0 m/s, and the normal is +x. Their relative closing speed is −2 m/s; with e=1 and k_n=2 kg⁻¹, we need Δλ_n = (2 − (−2))/2 = 2 kg·m/s. The resulting velocities are 0 m/s and 2 m/s. Linear momentum remains 2 kg·m/s, and the kinetic energy remains 2 joules. This equality is specific to the elastic, frictionless, central, idealized two-body case—not a conservation promise for frictional or inelastic impacts.
Why friction depends on the normal impulse

For the upward normal n=(0,1) the laboratory chooses the tangent t=(−1,0). The sliding box initially moves at +3 m/s in x, so its tangent-coordinate velocity is u_t = −3 m/s. The unconstrained tangent impulse is −u_t/k_t; here k_t=1 kg⁻¹, giving +3 kg·m/s. The normal collision supplies λ_n=2 kg·m/s. With coefficient μ=0.5, the Coulomb limit is μλ_n=1 kg·m/s, so the stored tangent impulse is +1, not −1. Multiplying +1 × (−1,0) produces an x-directed impulse of (−1,0), reducing the box’s x velocity from +3 to +2 m/s. The sign of the stored scalar is relative to the chosen tangent direction; it cannot be interpreted without that basis.

The projected update is λ_t^{new} = clamp(λ_t^{old} − u_t/k_t, −μλ_n, +μλ_n). This is a scalar tangent model for 2D; real 3D contact has a two-dimensional tangent plane and requires a disk-cone constraint or a chosen approximation. The witness applies a single coefficient and does not model static-versus-dynamic friction transition, anisotropy, rolling friction, torsional friction or compliant materials.
Why a manifold needs persistent identity and sequential sweeps

A wide box can contact a floor at two corners. Both rows modify the same centre-of-mass velocity and angular velocity. Solving one row therefore changes the velocity seen by the next row. A one-pass independent pair of impulses is not equivalent to solving their coupled system. The reference witness stores two world-space contact points, evaluates each row in sequence, and repeats sweeps. The residual normal speeds and angular velocity are checked after twenty sweeps. Its iteration result is deterministic for its fixed row order but should not be advertised as an order-independent exact solution.

On the next frame, a geometry matcher must identify whether each physical contact feature persisted. If the same feature, body pair, contact orientation, and compatible basis survive, previously accumulated impulses are useful initial guesses. Warm-start once by applying the cached impulses to the newly constructed pre-solve velocities before iteration. Never warm-start twice, and never reuse a tangential scalar after rotating the tangent basis without transforming it. A changed feature ID, reversed A/B order, altered normal, teleport, or discontinuous mass/inertia change may invalidate the cache. The witness includes a feature ID as data but does not implement feature matching; that is a separate production requirement.

Caches may also require dt-aware scaling when timestep changes, and a true contact solver must decide how speculative contacts and missed or sleeping frames are handled. Warm-starting can improve convergence, but it is not a substitute for manifold quality.
Contact identity: why matching by memory address or contact index is insufficient

The physical reaction at a point can be reused between frames only if the cache still refers to the same interacting surface features. When two faces touch, clipping may produce two manifold points whose array order changes as the bodies rotate. If we cache impulse #0 against array position #0, a later reordering can accidentally apply the left-corner impulse at the right corner, creating a torque that was never physically demanded. A robust narrow phase should assign each contact a stable feature pair, for example an incident vertex/edge identifier and reference face identifier, with deterministic canonicalization of body ordering. These identifiers are geometric facts maintained by collision generation, not sequential indices assigned by a container.

The executable contact-cache witness concentrates on the subsequent policy rather than inventing a complete polygon clipper. The Key holds canonical body IDs plus two feature identifiers. The map stores the previously accepted normal and tangent impulse, its local normal direction, the previous friction coefficient, timestep, and last-seen frame. The cache is valid only if the same key was seen on the immediately preceding frame, the normal has changed by no more than 15 degrees, and the new timestep is between half and twice the cached timestep. These are documented laboratory thresholds, not universally optimal thresholds or engine-wide facts. The code rejects reversed body order because reversing A and B changes the sign of the normal and impulse convention.

A tangent impulse is a vector in world space, although this 2D solver stores it as one scalar relative to a perpendicular tangent. When the normal rotates from n_old to n_new, the tangent axes t_old=(-n_old.y,n_old.x) and t_new=(-n_new.y,n_new.x) also rotate. The old physical friction impulse is P_t_old=λ_t_old t_old. The scalar along the new tangent is its dot projection:
$ \lambda{t,new}^{seed} = \frac{\Delta t_{new}}{\Delta t_{old}} \left(\lambda{t,old},\mathbf t_{old}\cdot\mathbf t_{new}\right). $

The normal cache receives the same heuristic timestep ratio, and the tangent is clamped to ± μ_new λ_n_new. With an old upward normal (0,1), the old tangent is (-1,0). If the normal turns 10 degrees, the tangent projection of a previous scalar impulse 0.5 is 0.5 cos(10°) ≈ 0.492404, while the world impulse direction has changed consistently. Reusing 0.5 unchanged would preserve the scalar but not the intended projection onto the new contact tangent. This linear projection is a warm-start heuristic, not an exact solution of the new contact constraint; the subsequent iterative solver must still correct its residual.

An edit to the friction coefficient clears only the tangential cached impulse in this experiment, retaining the normal impulse if all other validity rules pass. A material change in restitution, velocity discontinuity, teleport, substantial mass/inertia change, sleeping transition, or topology discontinuity may also require cache rejection in a production system and is not automatically detected by this small input type. Impulse scaling by timestep ratio is similarly a common starting heuristic, not an unconditional physical identity; the test exercises ratios 0.5, 1, and 4 and rejects the last. A caller must invoke begin_frame, use lookup to seed each new manifold row, warm-start those rows once, run velocity iterations, store each final impulse exactly once, and prune stale entries. Pruning at the wrong moment can erase still-needed contacts; storing duplicate feature keys silently makes iteration results depend on array ordering, so the witness rejects duplicates.

The implementation has a testable boundary: it assumes a reliable feature matcher has already produced identifiers, that contact validity has been established by the geometry system, and that stable body IDs are never prematurely recycled. A generation-counted body handle would be safer than an integer object index alone. The cache does not detect 3D tangent-frame rotation, it does not calculate a physically accurate contact point, and its ordered map is a reference implementation rather than a measured real-time allocation strategy. A production engine should benchmark a preallocated flat hash map or per-pair cache with explicit frame ownership and deterministic iteration requirements.
Velocity correction is not penetration correction

The equations above change velocities. They do not, by themselves, repair existing overlaps in positions. A production pipeline generally needs a distinct and carefully scoped policy: geometry generation and signed separation, speculative contact margins, split impulses or position-level stabilization, and consistent timestep handling. Naively adding a large position-error velocity bias can inject energy, make stacks jitter, or break restitution. This CPU witness intentionally has no position integrator, no Baumgarte term, no split impulse and no continuous collision detection. Therefore its passing tests cannot establish the correctness of CCD tunneling prevention or deep-overlap recovery.
From end-of-frame overlap to continuous time of impact

The contact solver described above only acts on contacts it has been given. A fast-moving disk can start to the left of a thin obstacle and finish to the right of it without overlapping at the end of a fixed simulation step. If collision detection samples positions only at the step boundary, it sees no collision, so even a mathematically perfect impulse solver cannot prevent tunneling. This is the reason continuous collision detection (CCD) is a separate geometric question: what is the first time, within the proposed integration interval, when the moving shapes touch?

For two disks with initial centres x_A and x_B, constant velocities v_A and v_B, and radii r_A, r_B, define the relative centre separation p = x_B - x_A, relative velocity v = v_B - v_A, and sum of radii R = r_A + r_B. Their separation at time t is p(t) = p + tv. They first touch when the squared centre distance equals the squared radius sum:
$ \lVert \mathbf p+t\mathbf v\rVert2=R2. $
Expanding the dot product gives the quadratic
$ at^2+bt+c=0,\qquad a=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v,\quad b=2\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf v,\quad c=\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf p-R^2. $

The meaning of the coefficients is crucial. c is the initial squared-distance gap: c<0 means the disks are already overlapping and this witness returns t=0, assigning overlap correction to a separate solver; c=0 means initial touching. If a=0, the relative geometry never moves during the interval. For initially separated disks, b≥0 means squared distance is not initially decreasing, so a collision cannot occur under these constant velocities. A discriminant D=b²−4ac<0 means the motion line misses the expanded-radius disk. D=0 gives a tangent or grazing touch, which counts as a contact in this laboratory.

The familiar quadratic expression (-b−sqrt(D))/(2a) can lose precision when nearly equal quantities are subtracted. The swept-disk CPU witness instead computes a stable intermediate q = -0.5(b − sqrt(D)) in its restricted b<0 branch, then evaluates the roots as t_near = c/q and t_far = q/a. Their product remains c/a, and the smaller root is tested against 0≤t≤Δt. The code uses std::fma in the discriminant to avoid one rounding step, but this is still finite-precision arithmetic; reliable collision detection across extreme dynamic ranges needs scale-aware error analysis or a more robust predicate policy.

Consider a disk of radius 1 m stationary at the origin and another radius-1 disk initially at x=10 m moving left at 100 m/s. Its centre must move 8 m before touching, so the time of impact is 0.08 s. At Δt=0.1 s, the moving disk would end at the origin and overlap if sampled; for an even faster moving disk it could end past the obstacle and be missed entirely. An analytical time-of-impact query reports the 0.08 s encounter regardless of the end position. During a simulation step, a practical engine can advance up to this impact, generate a contact normal, solve or schedule the event, and then advance the remaining time, with a bounded substep count and an explicit policy for simultaneous events and resting contacts.

The event’s collision normal is the normalized relative separation n(t) = (p+tv)/|p+tv|, pointing A to B. When initial centres coincide, there is no unique geometric normal; the witness uses a deterministic velocity-based fallback or +x if relative velocity is zero. This fallback is a test policy rather than a geometrically determined surface normal. The tests explicitly examine grazing touch, no-hit trajectories, hits outside the requested frame, existing overlap, coincident centres, invalid parameters, a high-dynamic-range trajectory, and Galilean invariance under equal velocity added to both bodies. The latter should not change relative motion or time of impact.

What this does not solve: disk CCD assumes translational linear motion throughout the interval and fixed radii. It does not include forces or acceleration changing the trajectory, rotation of polygons, concave meshes, vertex-edge events, general convex support functions, conservative advancement, broadphase swept bounds, contact island rescheduling, stable substep integration, or CCD after multiple impulses. It also does not prove the absence of false misses at all floating-point scales. These exclusions must be explicit when moving from a CPU analytic oracle to the engine’s full collision pipeline.
A complete impact event: geometry, first time, impulse and remaining interval

The earlier swept-disk query identifies an impact but does not evolve a scene. The independent disk event pipeline laboratory connects geometry, state integration, simultaneous constraints and the remainder of the frame. It does not claim to be Kairo’s actual world step. The model assumes fixed-radius, non-spinning disks, piecewise constant velocities, instantaneous frictionless impulses, and linear motion between impacts. There are no forces, torque, resting-contact stabilization, soft contacts or arbitrary polygons.

The entire algorithm follows from keeping one variable: remaining time. At each iteration, query all unordered disk pairs for their first collision in that remaining interval. If no pair collides, advance every position by its current velocity times the entire remaining interval. If collisions exist, find the earliest time, move all disks to that instant, collect other impacts at approximately the same time, freeze each event’s incoming normal velocity and restitution target, solve their normal impulses, then repeat the time-of-impact scan because the impulses have changed the future motion.

The numerical trace is visible in the first laboratory test. A radius-1 stationary disk is at x=0. Another radius-1 disk starts at x=10 with velocity −100 m/s, and the requested frame duration is 0.10 s. The moving disk must travel 8 m before the two surfaces meet, giving TOI=0.08 s. The world advances both disks through 0.08 s, then an elastic impulse against the infinite-mass disk reverses its incoming velocity to +100 m/s. The remaining time is 0.02 s, so its centre ends at x=4 m. An end-of-frame overlap test cannot reconstruct this physically meaningful trajectory by merely reversing the velocity at t=0.10 s.

For non-spinning disk collisions along the line of centres, the inverse effective mass is the sum of inverse masses, k = m_A⁻¹ + m_B⁻¹. With unit collision normal n pointing from A to B, relative normal speed u_n=(v_B−v_A)·n, and fixed impact target b=−e u_n_before, the solver’s unilateral accumulated impulse is
$ \lambda{next}=\max\left(0,\lambda{previous} +\frac{b-(\mathbf v_B-\mathbf v_A)\cdot\mathbf n} {m_A{-1}+m_B{-1}}\right). $

Only the difference Δλ = λ_next − λ_previous changes velocities. In a simultaneous batch, multiple contact rows may share a disk, so each row modifies the velocities seen by subsequent rows. The laboratory runs 32 sequential sweeps, freezing the original bounce target rather than repeatedly inventing a new restitution event. A symmetric three-disk scene tests two simultaneous impacts; another three-disk scene tests two impacts at different times in one frame.

The discovery procedure is O(n²) for each rescan because it checks every unordered pair, with no spatial acceleration. The same-time grouping threshold and near-touch geometry threshold are explicit finite-precision policies, not robust computational-geometry predicates. Grazing trajectories with zero closing normal speed are skipped. Deep initial overlaps are rejected rather than repaired. An event budget throws when exhausted, preventing an infinite event loop from masquerading as successful advancement. Importantly, a thrown exception can leave the input scene partly advanced: a production caller needs a rollback snapshot or transactional step if partial state mutation is unacceptable.

The nine deterministic tests exercise fast impacts, isolated elastic momentum and energy conservation, simultaneous row coupling, separating pairs, initial overlap rejection, event-budget exhaustion, chained events, ideal inelastic energy loss, and zero-duration/duplicate-ID validation. These tests establish a small analytic oracle, not a general proof of energy or convergence for arbitrary many-body simultaneous collisions, a guarantee against floating-point tunneling, support for rotating convex objects, or a persistent resting-contact engine. For an impact against an externally fixed body, momentum conservation of the two displayed disks alone is not the correct closed-system invariant; the stationary environment receives the reaction.
Reducing collision search without losing collisions: conservative swept bounds

The event-step laboratory above asks every pair of disks whether they will collide during the remaining time interval. With n bodies, this examines n(n−1)/2 unordered pairs after each event. For 1,000 disks, that is 499,500 expensive exact pair-time queries per scan—even if almost every disk is far away from the others. A broad phase exists to reject pairs that cannot possibly interact using a cheaper geometric test; it is not allowed to reject a true collision merely to be fast. This is why the central proof obligation is conservative coverage, not an attractive benchmark on one scene.

For a disk of radius r, initial centre p=(p_x,p_y), velocity v=(v_x,v_y) and remaining interval Δt, its centre under constant velocity travels along the segment from p to p+vΔt. Every possible disk position lies inside its swept axis-aligned rectangle. Its x bounds are min(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)−r and max(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)+r; y is analogous. The swept-broadphase reference lab conservatively rounds each boundary one representable floating-point value outward with std::nextafter. The exact continuous disk shape is a capsule around the segment, while its swept AABB is a larger rectangle: the rectangle admits extra pairs but must not discard any collision, provided the endpoints and bounds are correctly represented.

The algorithm sorts these rectangles by their minimum x coordinate, breaking ties by stable disk ID. As it visits each new rectangle, it removes from an active set any earlier rectangle whose maximum x lies strictly before the current minimum x. Every remaining active rectangle overlaps along x; the algorithm then compares their y intervals. Pairs that pass both checks are returned in deterministic lexicographically sorted index order, with a duplicate assertion. A true disk impact at time t∈[0,Δt] means the two disk regions intersect at that time; their swept AABBs must both contain the intersection point. Therefore their AABBs overlap in x and y and the pair must survive the broad-phase filtering. The reverse implication is false: AABBs may overlap even when the disks pass at different times or miss geometrically. The exact TOI narrow phase must therefore test every candidate before scheduling an event.

The laboratory compares its candidate set with an independent analytic disk TOI predicate, rather than comparing the broad phase against itself. Each true TOI pair must appear in the returned set. It tests a high-speed crossing, 100 stationary well-spaced disks with zero candidates, 200 seeded randomized scenes containing 35 disks each, and malformed identity/time inputs. The random scenes therefore examine up to 119,000 unordered pairs for conservative coverage, because each 35-disk scene contains 595 pairs. These are useful regression witnesses, not a proof against all finite-precision failures.

Sorting has O(n log n) comparison cost. Maintaining the simple active vector has potentially O(n²) scanning and removal cost when many broad AABBs overlap; the output itself can contain O(n²) candidate pairs in a dense scene. A scalable production version may use a better interval structure, broadphase BVH, grid, or incremental pair cache, and should benchmark temporally coherent motion rather than assuming this sample has production throughput. The original broadphase witness remains independently testable; the event stepper now has an optional swept-candidate mode alongside its exhaustive reference mode. Both generate candidate pairs for the current remaining interval, and the event stepper rebuilds candidates after each velocity-changing impact. A differential test source is committed to compare complete outcomes, but its successful GitHub-hosted execution remains unverified. This code-level integration is not yet native Kairo runtime integration or evidence of speedup.
How to reconstruct and verify the witness

Read the Row fields as a prepared contact Jacobian in compressed form: ra/rb are the lever arms, n/t are the constraint axes, kn/kt are scalar rows of the matrix J M⁻¹ Jᵀ. The method relative_velocity computes Jv, inverse_effective_mass computes a row’s inverse effective mass, solve_one projects impulse increments, and warm_start applies an already-owned cache once. make_row validates data and freezes the impact target. The six tests cover central momentum/energy, friction orientation, angular impulse, separating and static degeneracies, coupled two-contact iteration/next-frame cache, and nonfinite-input rejection.

Run strict compilation and execution, then run a sanitizer build. Expected output is persistent-contact witness: 6 suites PASS. This verifies only the tested cases on the compiling environment; the repository GitHub Actions workflow repeats strict and undefined-behavior checks, with remote status to be verified separately.

A reconstruction exercise is to add two bodies with unequal masses and an off-centre contact, compute kn by hand and compare every intermediate u_n, Δλ_n, Δv and Δω. A stronger follow-up exercise is to implement real feature matching, deliberately reverse normals between frames, and demonstrate that incorrectly reused cached tangential impulses generate artificial energy. Neither extension is presently claimed as implemented.
Verified boundary and research questions

The lab does not verify Kairo’s current renderer or physics engine, broadphase pair generation, narrowphase contact topology, 3D Jacobians, static/dynamic island management, precise multi-contact complementarity, numerical convergence across arbitrary scenes, determinism across compilers, robust CCD, or real-time performance. Before a research claim about stability or speed, define independent scene families, error metrics (maximum penetration, residual closing speed, drift, energy increase), iteration budgets, timestep families and order-randomization trials. Compare warm versus cold starts without changing geometry, feature matching or tolerances at the same time.

Navigation and first-use risks found by the live link inventory

The three books contained approximately 23 links into the old archival volumes at the inspected head: 1 from Mathematics, 11 from Graphics and 11 from Game Engine. The source targets still exist, so these are mostly legacy detours, not missing files. Nevertheless they violate the spirit of one reader-facing continuous destination per subject. Their replacement requires determining which in-book heading now owns each prerequisite; a blanket text substitution would break provenance and risk moving a reader to the wrong derivation. Until reconciled, the old link is supporting provenance rather than an instruction to start a fourth book.

A first-pass wiki-link regex reported spurious missing targets such as nodiscard, no_unique_address, GPU attributes and media paths. Those are often C++/shader syntax, escaped expressions, or images, not Obsidian page links. An audit tool must ignore fenced/inline source and distinguish image attachments from Markdown notes before treating these as missing content. Heading existence itself also proves only the presence of a title, not a coherent implementation.

The Engine source insertion is particularly large and now occupies roughly forty thousand lines before the original mid-engine renderer material. Graphics also contains an early full XR source block. These are high-priority reading-flow issues even though the mechanical content-preservation checks are green. Preserve original words, but use linking, carefully justified section placement and substantive bridge explanations to make the story follow a recurring engine problem rather than a pasted source queue.
Implementation-depth contract for every developed concept

A reader should be able to close the book and build the mechanism. Therefore a concept is not “done” until its first meaningful use provides: the forcing engineering problem; definitions of every symbol, convention and unit; the derivation and its assumptions; the concrete memory/state representation and ownership; the full algorithm and decision branches; a complete documented implementation or a clearly labeled API-specific implementation; a numerical trace with inspectable intermediate state; failure/degeneracy and alternatives; proof of invariants and bounded behavior; and reproducible positive, negative and metamorphic tests. The note itself must contain these, not just a heading, a pointer to a video, or a code file that the reader must discover elsewhere.

Witness categories must remain distinct. A CPU-only pedagogical model can prove logic, arithmetic and expected rejection cases. It cannot prove production GPU memory visibility or Apple/NVIDIA driver behavior. A reference engine test cannot establish the current Kairo integration unless the exact Kairo commit and reproducible build are inspected. A mathematically derived assumption is not an observed result; a video transcript’s claim is not verified code; the 3,000-part route map is an ownership assignment rather than 3,000 completed reconstructions.
Current development increment: logical render-graph compiler

The Game Engine volume now carries a full C++20 pass-graph compiler inline at the point where renderer intent becomes backend work. The independent laboratory is tools/labs/render_graph_contract_lab.cpp, source-synchronized through tools/check_continuous_code_sync.py. It builds a DAG from per-resource last-writer and reader-cohort state, records RAW/WAR/WAW hazards, handles imported history, topologically sorts with deterministic tie-breaking, and rejects duplicate resources, uninitialized transient reads, feedback and explicit cycles. The six-pass G-buffer/shadow/lighting/temporal/tone-map/present trace and negative cases make those semantics inspectable. GCC and Clang compiled/reran the reference locally with -O1 and -O2 -DNDEBUG, warnings-as-errors.

Boundary: This is a single-queue logical whole-resource compiler, not an implemented Vulkan or Metal render graph. It does not emit stage/access masks, image layout transitions, queue-family ownership, timeline waits, transient aliasing or device-loss recovery. Those remain first-class milestones, not implicit features of this passing laboratory. See the Vulkan synchronization specification for the separate memory-model obligations.

Appendix.title: Rendering history validity
Appendix.Content: Rendering history validity

A temporal renderer reuses information from earlier frames only if that information still estimates the same target quantity at the reprojected location. “Previous frame exists” is therefore not enough. History needs a validity contract.
A history sample may become invalid because of:

ListItem.Content: • camera cuts or projection changes;
• resize or dynamic-resolution changes;
• object transform discontinuities;
• newly visible or disoccluded surfaces;
• material or lighting changes;
• estimator changes such as sample pattern, exposure domain or denoiser configuration;
• resource reallocation or version replacement.

Appendix.Content: Reprojection is a hypothesis

Motion vectors or previous transforms propose a correspondence from current sample to previous sample. The renderer should test that hypothesis with available evidence such as depth, normal, object/material identity, velocity magnitude or neighborhood statistics.
A common failure is using a valid coordinate that points to the wrong surface. Bounds checking prevents memory errors, not temporal ghosting.
Versioned history

Treat history like a cache with a key. Relevant state changes advance a version or invalidate specific history resources. The render graph can then express that a temporal pass consumes history version N and produces version N+1.

This is also important for progressive path tracing. Accumulation belongs to a camera/scene/material/light/estimator state. If any target-defining state changes and old samples remain, the output converges to a mixture of different images.
Failure-oriented tests

Useful temporal tests include a hard camera cut, a moving foreground object revealing background, an emissive material changing abruptly, resize, FOV change, jitter-sequence restart, and an object whose ID remains but geometry changes. For each case, record which history samples should survive and why.

The existing render-graph witness proves logical resource dependencies, not temporal validity itself. Native renderer evidence should capture motion/depth/ID buffers and show the acceptance/rejection mask.
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#Let a renderer evolve without losing resource ownership.
Related: Temporal reprojection and history validation, Reversed-Z depth contracts.

Appendix.title: Sampling support and missing strata
Appendix.Content: Sampling support and missing strata

The support of a sampling distribution is the set of outcomes it can generate with nonzero probability. Importance sampling can change how often regions are visited, but it cannot estimate a nonzero contribution from a region that the estimator never samples unless another technique covers that region.
For an integral
an ordinary importance estimator using density is
This requires wherever contributes to the target integral, up to measure-zero exceptions.
If a region has nonzero integral but there, taking more samples from the existing support cannot repair the missing contribution. The estimator converges to the wrong target.
Stratification

Partition domain into strata . A correct stratified estimator accounts for each stratum’s measure/probability. If a 3×3 pixel partition has nine equal cells but the algorithm always samples only the first five and treats their mean as the full-pixel mean, it has changed the integration domain.
Randomly selecting strata with the appropriate selection probability can remain unbiased; permanently omitting fixed strata cannot.
MIS support

Multiple importance sampling can repair a weak proposal when another technique covers the missing region and the combined estimator uses compatible PDFs. The PDFs must include discrete technique/light selection probabilities as well as continuous densities.
Debugging
Visualize sample positions and build a support occupancy histogram. Many “mysterious bias” bugs become obvious when entire regions are empty.
For image-space algorithms, also test edges/corners of the reconstruction filter, not only the pixel center.
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#A missing region cannot be repaired by taking more samples there.
Related: Multiple importance sampling, Latin-hypercube sampling, Antialiasing and sample allocation.

Appendix.title: Reversed-Z depth contracts
Appendix.Content: Reversed-Z depth contracts

A depth buffer stores an ordering coordinate, not Euclidean distance. Reversed-Z changes the mapping so near geometry receives larger depth values and far geometry approaches zero. The precision advantage comes from combining the reciprocal structure of perspective depth with floating-point numbers whose representable values are denser near zero.
The entire renderer has to agree on the convention. Reversing only the projection matrix while keeping old clear/comparison assumptions creates a system that is internally contradictory.
Contract checklist
For a conventional zero-to-one API depth range, a common reversed-Z setup uses:

ListItem.Content: • near plane mapped near 1;
• far distance mapped toward 0;
• depth buffer cleared to 0;
• comparison set to GREATER or GREATER_EQUAL;
• hierarchical depth/occlusion reductions defined consistently with “larger is nearer”;
• screen-space reconstruction derived from the exact projection convention.

Appendix.Content: Infinite-far reversed projection can remove an explicit far-plane distance from the perspective matrix, but frustum/culling policy still needs a practical world-space bound when the application cannot process infinite geometry.
Why floating point helps

Perspective depth is approximately affine in . Conventional mapping spends many floating-point representable values near depth one, where far geometry is crowded. Reversed-Z places far geometry near zero, where floating-point exponent scaling gives much more useful relative spacing.
With integer/fixed-point depth, reversal alone does not create the same dramatic distribution advantage; the floating-point representation is part of the argument.
Reconstruction must use the actual matrix
Do not paste a “linearize depth” formula from another API. Different clip-space ranges, handedness, finite/infinite far planes and reversed mappings change the coefficients.
A robust reconstruction derives camera-space position from the same projection matrix or stores explicit projection parameters and tests known near/far points.
Occlusion and temporal systems

Hierarchical Z, SSAO, SSR, clustered depth slicing, picking and temporal rejection all consume depth meaning. Every reduction or comparison must be audited when the convention changes. A min-reduction hierarchy written for standard depth may need a max-reduction interpretation under reversed-Z.
Tests

Project known camera-space depths, confirm monotonic ordering, quantize them to the real depth format, reconstruct them, and measure relative world-space error over logarithmically spaced distances. Also test clear-value behavior with an empty frame and a near geometry sample.
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Give depth an explicit meaning.
Related: Hardware depth-buffer linearization, Rendering history validity.

Appendix.title: Probability spaces, events, and conditioning
Appendix.Content: Probability spaces, events, and conditioning
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A probability model consists of a sample space, a collection of measurable events, and a probability measure assigning values to those events. Conditional probability renormalizes the measure within an event of positive probability; Bayes’ theorem reverses conditioning by combining likelihood with prior probability. Independence is a factorization property, not a synonym for disjointness or zero correlation. Conditioning on a zero-probability event cannot use the ordinary ratio directly; continuous models need density-based or regular conditional formulations. This framework keeps possible outcomes separate from distributions placed on them and clarifies what information an experiment provides. A random model can describe a deterministic pseudorandom generator over a distribution of seeds, but one fixed seed produces a fixed sequence. State the event model and conditioning assumptions before interpreting probability as evidence.

Appendix.title: Common probability distributions and their assumptions
Appendix.source: Concepts/Common probability distributions and their assumptions.md
Appendix.Content: Common probability distributions and their assumptions
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Distribution families encode different experiment structures. Bernoulli models one binary trial; binomial counts independent trials with the same success probability; uniform assigns constant density or mass over a specified support; Gaussian models a bell-shaped law through mean and covariance; exponential describes memoryless waiting under a constant event rate; Poisson counts events in a fixed exposure under independent, stationary event assumptions. Their formulas are not interchangeable labels: each relies on support and sampling assumptions. Moments summarize center and spread but may fail to exist for heavy-tailed laws. Multivariate Gaussian models also require a symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance, with positive definiteness needed for an ordinary full-dimensional density. Identify the experiment, parameter meanings, and dependence structure before selecting a distribution. The same family can model measurement noise, a prior, or a sampling proposal, which are different roles.
Prerequisites

• Expectation, covariance, and dependence

Appendix.title: Online moments and Welford accumulation
Appendix.Content: Online moments and Welford accumulation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Online statistics update a mean and centered sum of squares as observations arrive, using constant storage. Welford’s recurrence computes a new mean from the old mean and one sample, then adds the product of deviations measured before and after that update. The centered form avoids severe cancellation in E[X²]−E[X]² for data with a large offset and small spread. Divide accumulated scatter by n for descriptive population-normalized variance or by n−1 for unbiased sample variance under IID finite-variance assumptions. The recurrence is numerically better behaved, not immune to overflow, count exhaustion, or all rounding error. Parallel workers can merge count, mean, and scatter summaries with a correction term for different means; merge order can change floating-point results.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Expectation, covariance, and dependence
• Accumulated rounding error

Appendix.title: Robust summaries and error metrics
Appendix.Content: Robust summaries and error metrics
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Histograms, quantiles, medians, and robust scales summarize different features of a finite dataset. Histogram bar area represents probability only when heights are divided by sample count and bin width. Quantile conventions differ across software, so report the interpolation rule. The median minimizes absolute deviation and resists some extreme observations; the mean minimizes squared deviation and is more sensitive to outliers. MAD and trimmed means provide other robustness choices with efficiency tradeoffs. MSE and RMSE emphasize large errors, MAE is less sensitive to them, and relative metrics can become unstable near zero. Aggregating per-scene scores differs from pooling every observation. Choose the metric from the scientific question, units, and failure cost, and report tail behavior when rare large errors matter.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Expectation, covariance, and dependence
• Absolute and relative error

Appendix.title: GPU workgroups and synchronization
Appendix.Content: GPU workgroups and synchronization

GPU execution has several scopes that must not be collapsed into the word “thread.” An invocation executes one logical shader instance. Invocations are grouped into workgroups for explicitly shared local memory and workgroup barriers. Hardware may execute smaller subgroup or SIMD groups inside a workgroup. Many workgroups make up a dispatch.

A workgroup barrier can coordinate invocations that participate in that workgroup. It cannot create a global barrier across arbitrary workgroups in the same dispatch. If an algorithm requires all blocks to finish phase A before any block begins phase B, use a mechanism that establishes that dependency: usually separate dispatches/commands with API synchronization, or a carefully designed device-wide primitive supported by the target model.
Execution barrier versus memory visibility

“Everyone reached the same point” and “everyone can now observe the required writes” are related but distinct contracts. APIs and shading languages expose memory scopes and semantics because a control barrier alone is not a universal cache flush.
The producer/consumer question is always:

ListItem.Content: • what operation produced the bytes?
• what later operation consumes them?
• which execution scopes must be ordered?
• which memory accesses must become visible?
• which resource/subresource is covered?

Appendix.Content: Subgroups

Subgroup collectives can exchange values and perform ballots, reductions and scans without workgroup shared memory. They are fast but require care around subgroup width, inactive lanes and portability. An algorithm that silently assumes 32 lanes can break on hardware using a different subgroup size.
Shared memory and bank conflicts

Workgroup memory is physically optimized for cooperation but has finite capacity and bank structure. Tiling can reduce global bandwidth, yet an unfortunate address pattern can serialize accesses through bank conflicts. Register pressure and shared-memory allocation also constrain occupancy, so increasing tile size is not free.
Evidence boundary

The canonical notes now distinguish CPU semantic models from native hardware evidence. A CPU prefix-scan or render-graph test can prove dependency logic but cannot prove Vulkan visibility, Metal hazard behavior, subgroup width or driver performance. Hardware claims require validation layers, GPU capture/counters, and device-specific results.
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Let many invocations cooperate without inventing a global clock.
Related: Prefix scan and stream compaction, Shader buffer ABI.

Appendix.title: BVH build traversal and workload selection
Appendix.source: Concepts/BVH build traversal and workload selection.md
Appendix.Content: BVH build, traversal, and workload selection
A bounding-volume hierarchy is a tree whose nodes bound groups of primitives. Its purpose is not to make intersection magically faster; it is to let a query prove that large groups cannot matter.
For an overlap query Q, traversal follows a simple implication:
if Q does not overlap node.bounds, then Q cannot overlap any primitive below that node.

That pruning claim is only correct when every child primitive is actually contained by every ancestor bound. Tree construction therefore owns an invariant: each internal bound is the union of its children, and each leaf bound contains the primitives assigned to the leaf.
Build choices

A median split sorts or partitions primitive centroids and divides them into similarly sized groups. It is simple and usually avoids catastrophically unbalanced trees, but equal primitive counts do not imply equal traversal cost.
Surface-area heuristic construction estimates expected query/ray work. In the common ray-tracing interpretation, a split cost has the form
where is parent surface area, are child areas, are primitive counts, is traversal cost and is primitive-intersection cost. Binned SAH approximates candidate split positions efficiently.

LBVH chooses hierarchy structure from Morton ordering. It can build quickly and map well to parallel hardware, but tree quality can be worse than a careful SAH build for some scenes. Which strategy wins depends on how often the scene rebuilds and how expensive later queries are.
Traversal representation
A production BVH must choose node layout as deliberately as split policy. Questions include:

ListItem.Content: • binary versus wider nodes;
• array indices versus pointers;
• parent links or stackless encodings;
• leaf primitive ranges;
• AoS versus SoA bounds;
• quantized bounds;
• traversal stack depth and overflow behavior;
• child ordering by query direction or distance.

Appendix.Content: For GPU traversal, divergence and memory coalescing can dominate the nominal tree complexity.
Dynamic scenes

Refitting recomputes ancestor bounds without changing topology. It is cheap when objects move modestly, but tree quality can decay. Rebuilding restores quality at higher cost. A useful dynamic policy measures a quality proxy and rebuilds when continued bad traversal is more expensive than reconstruction.
Dynamic AABB trees instead maintain a mutable hierarchy and often enlarge leaf bounds by a motion margin. The margin trades fewer reinserts for more false candidates.
Executable reference

tools/labs/spatial_index_lab.cpp builds a median-split BVH over deterministic random AABBs and compares 250 overlap queries against a brute-force oracle. Any missed or extra primitive is a test failure. The same laboratory also contains A* graph search with relaxation, reinsertion and unreachable-goal handling.
The witness does not claim SAH quality, LBVH construction, dynamic updates, SIMD traversal, ray packet behavior, navmesh construction, or KairoSpatial parity. Those remain separate evidence layers.
Related: AABB overlap and containment, Prefix scan and stream compaction, Field reordering and AoS versus SoA.
SAH, Morton and refit witness

tools/labs/bvh_sah_refit_lab.cpp advances the construction side beyond the earlier median-split query oracle. It computes prefix/suffix bounds for candidate partitions and minimizes the surface-area-weighted primitive cost, verifies that two separated three-object clusters split between the clusters, tests 3D Morton bit interleaving on a controlled monotone coordinate sweep, and refits a parent bound after one child moves.

This is enough to make the equations executable, but not enough to call the builder a production binned SAH or LBVH. A complete next layer needs fixed-bin accumulation, stable primitive partitioning, LBVH range/split construction from Morton prefixes, dynamic-tree rotations or reinsertion, and measured build-versus-query trade-offs on real workloads.

Appendix.title: Bit
Appendix.Content: Bit
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism
A two-state unit of information whose meaning depends on an interpretation contract.

A bit has two possible logical states. Eight independent bits have 2⁸ = 256 patterns because each position doubles the choices. A Boolean value is a truth value; a stored bit may instead be part of a number, instruction, or format field.

Appendix.title: Bit significance
Appendix.Content: Bit significance
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism
LSB/MSB describe mathematical weights, not byte order in memory.

LSB means least significant bit, normally position 0 with weight 1. MSB is the highest significant position; in an eight-bit unsigned value it has weight 128. A displayed leftmost bit, first packed array element, and first byte at an address are separate ordering choices.

Appendix.title: Offset-binary coding
Appendix.Content: Offset-binary coding
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism
A bias turns signed levels into unsigned codes. For the source-shaped INT4 convention c=q+8, -3 becomes nibble0101, not the two’s-complement nibble1101.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Unsigned modular arithmetic — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
• Interpretation contract — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism.
Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it.
Pending: Do not assume an INT4 label defines offset versus two’s-complement storage.
Source and navigation
Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map
Ordering and bias
Offset-binary represents signed values by adding a fixed bias before storing an unsigned code:

With an -bit field and the common midpoint bias , the smallest signed value maps near code zero and the largest maps near the all-ones code. Unlike two’s complement, the unsigned lexical order of codes then matches the numeric order of represented values. That property is useful in some exponent fields, ADC outputs, sortable binary formats and hardware interfaces.

The bias is part of the format contract. Decoding with the wrong bias shifts every value while still producing plausible numbers. The IEEE-754 exponent field is related but reserves all-zero and all-one exponent codes for subnormals/zero and infinities/NaNs, so it is not simply an unrestricted offset-binary integer.
Tests should check both endpoints, the code corresponding to numeric zero, monotonic ordering, and rejection or handling of reserved codes when the surrounding format defines them.

Appendix.title: Integrity and authenticity
Appendix.Content: Integrity and authenticity
Curriculum depth: Derived with executable primitive witnesses · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair
Integrity means detecting unauthorized or accidental modification relative to a trusted reference. Authenticity additionally answers who or what was authorized to create the message.
Hashing a file and storing the digest beside it protects against accidental corruption only when the digest itself is trusted. An attacker able to replace both can recompute the hash.
A message authentication code solves a different problem: parties share a secret key and compute a tag such as
Someone without the key should not be able to forge a valid tag for a modified message under the security assumptions of HMAC and the underlying hash.

A digital signature separates signing and verification keys and supports different trust models. The choice between MAC and signature is therefore architectural, not a matter of which API call is available.
HMAC construction
For hash block size , normalize key to one block, then compute
The inner and outer domains prevent the construction from being equivalent to a naive hash of key concatenated with message.
tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp checks HMAC-SHA256 against an RFC 4231 known-answer vector.
Key management is part of authenticity
A mathematically correct MAC does not help if:

ListItem.Content: • the key is embedded publicly in the executable;
• keys are reused across incompatible protocols without domain separation;
• a compromised key is never rotated;
• comparison leaks useful timing information in an adversarial environment;
• replayed old authenticated messages are accepted without nonce/counter/version policy.

Appendix.Content: Cryptographic primitives are building blocks, not complete protocols.
Production boundary

The educational implementations in this repository exist to make the bytes/rounds/contracts reconstructable. Production systems should use vetted cryptographic libraries and platform key-storage facilities rather than treating a teaching SHA/HMAC implementation as hardened security code.
Related: Checksums CRCs and hashes, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Shamir secret sharing.

Appendix.title: Bit casting and representation
Appendix.Content: Bit casting and representation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism

A same-size eligible bit_cast transfers representation, not numeric value. On the checked binary32 host, bit_cast(1.0f)=3F800000, whereas a numeric cast gives 1. Pointer punning is not an equivalent legal operation.

M006 separates representation copying, numeric conversion and endian coding. Eligibility does not validate arbitrary padding/target representations or establish a typed object in file-mapped bytes. Use initialized compatible scalars and explicit external encoding.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Fixed-width integer types — A same-size unsigned carrier holds the specified interchange representation.
• Interpretation contract — A bit transfer and a numeric conversion interpret the same carrier differently.
• IEEE-754 floating point — The format/arithmetic contract gives these bits their numerical domain.

Appendix.title: Integral promotion
Appendix.Content: Integral promotion
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Narrow integral operands promote to int when it represents their entire range, otherwise to unsigned int; the operator acts at that promoted width.

Narrow integer types become int if int represents every original value; otherwise they become unsigned int. Promotion happens before the operation, not only on assignment. On the usual host, uint8_t{250}+uint8_t{10} is int 260; converting afterward to uint8_t yields 4.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Fixed-width integer types — When supplied, std::uint32_t has exactly 32 bits; uint_least32_t has at least 32; uint_fast32_t is chosen for speed with at least 32.
• Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.

Appendix.title: Bit packing
Appendix.Content: Bit packing
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism
Multiple constrained values share a carrier word; extraction and mutation must preserve the declared schema.

Packing places several constrained values into a carrier. Input [1,0,1,1,0,1,0,1] packed LSB-first produces 0xAD. Unpacking needs the logical count because the final byte may contain unused bits. Define whether padding must be zero, ignored, or rejected.

Appendix.title: Undefined behavior
Appendix.Content: Undefined behavior
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Invalid shifts, out-of-bounds access, signed overflow, division by zero, and INT_MIN / -1 provide no valid C++ execution result; optimizers may assume they never occur.

The C++ language imposes no requirements on an execution that invokes undefined behavior. It is not an error value or a guaranteed trap. Signed overflow, division by zero, invalid shift counts, and out-of-bounds accesses are examples. Check preconditions before performing the operation.
Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Serialization
Appendix.Content: Serialization
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism

Serialization maps semantic fields to a specified byte sequence; decoding validates and reconstructs them. Width, order, version, bounds, and padding policy belong to that contract. A U8/U32-LE/U64-LE header occupies 13 bytes at offsets 0/1/5, independently of a native record’s possible 16-byte ABI layout. Packing removes some holes, not host dependencies. Publication and durability are subsequent operations.

M004 extension: a binary32 representation word such as 3F800000 can be serialized as little-endian bytes 00 00 80 3F. Raw-bit preservation retains signed-zero and NaN-payload differences; canonicalization deliberately merges them. Numeric equality does not imply byte identity. This is a format policy, not permission to change existing files.

M006 adds explicit schema/version/identity contracts, overflow-safe dimensions and resource limits, raw-word payload preservation, integrity coverage and a complete 52-byte demonstration. A native scalar writer is not automatically cross-endian stable.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Interpretation contract — Representation, type, and lifetime must identify what object exists.
• Fixed-width integer types — The representation width fixes byte count and valid shift range.
• Endianness — Byte order tells how digit significance maps to sequence positions.

Appendix.title: IEEE-754 floating point
Appendix.Content: IEEE-754 floating point
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

IEEE-754 specifies floating formats and behavior including representation classes, rounding directions and exception conditions. A finite bit pattern is interpreted through sign, exponent and significand rules, not as a two’s-complement integer.

Binary32 has 1/8/23 stored fields and 24-bit normal precision; binary64 has 1/11/52 fields and 53-bit normal precision. Word 412A0000 encodes 10.625 in binary32. Exponent-zero and all-one fields distinguish zero/subnormal and infinity/NaN. Normal spacing expands with exponent; nearest-even and directed modes choose representable results under explicit rules. These format names do not prove every C++ float/double has those representations.
M005 develops alignment, cancellation, FMA and accumulated error. Numeric equality is not representation identity, and moving rounding points can change the computed result.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Bit field — A field is a declared range with offset s and width w, not automatically a C++ language bit-field member.
• Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.

• Bfloat16 — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract.

Appendix.title: Storage duration and object lifetime
Appendix.Content: Storage duration and object lifetime
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C010
Definition and mechanism
Direct local reference binding can extend a temporary under specified rules; a returned parameter alias does not renew the deadline. A reference’s own lifetime does not prove the referent’s lifetime.

Construction and destruction can delimit an occupant while backing storage remains. The inline C++ lab uses construct_at/destroy_at in an alignas byte buffer and new/delete as the combined allocation/construction and destruction/release operations. The pointer object does not own or extend pointee life. Implicit object creation occurs only for specified operations and suitable types; a reinterpret_cast is not a universal construction operation.

Storage duration specifies how long storage is potentially available: automatic, static, thread, or dynamic. Object lifetime describes when a particular initialized object exists within it. Old bytes can remain after lifetime ends without authorizing access. const restricts mutation, not physical placement. Language categories do not dictate a universal segment map.

M010 reuses this separation for smart owners and arenas: a wrapper’s storage duration, the managed object’s lifetime, the ownership-group lifetime, and an external GPU-use interval may all end at different times. Placement construction reuses suitable live storage; object destruction alone does not return that storage to an allocator.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Interpretation contract — Representation, type, and lifetime must identify what object exists.

Definition and mechanism
Modular, checked, widened, saturated, and arbitrary-precision arithmetic define different outcomes when a mathematical result does not fit.

Appendix.title: One-bit centroid quantization
Appendix.Content: One-bit centroid quantization
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism
One sign label selects one of two row means. Row [-1,-3,2,4] reconstructs [-2,-2,3,3], with RMSE one. Two float32 centroids cost 64 additional bits per row.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Quantization and compressed weights — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.

Source and navigation

Reconstruction depth

One-bit centroid quantization does not merely store a sign. A group of source values is partitioned into two reconstruction levels, often centroids and , and each element stores one membership bit. Decoding is therefore

If the centroids are fixed to symmetric values such as , metadata becomes cheaper but the representation loses the ability to follow asymmetric distributions. If they are fitted per group, metadata cost increases but reconstruction error can fall.
The useful engineering quantity is total cost, not bits-per-weight in isolation:
Small groups adapt better but pay more metadata and may reduce SIMD efficiency. Large groups amortize metadata but force unrelated values to share two reconstruction levels.

A correct implementation tests deterministic centroid selection, empty-cluster handling, tie policy, bit packing order, group tails, finite decoded values, and error against a declared metric. For inference, the important next question is whether the binary code can participate directly in a dot-product kernel or must be expanded first; that determines whether compression actually saves bandwidth.

Appendix.title: Quantization error metrics
Appendix.Content: Quantization error metrics
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism

For N>0, RMSE is sqrt(sum squared discrepancies/N), MAE is mean absolute discrepancy, and max error is the largest observed magnitude. Promote float operands before subtraction when measuring in double.
