Appendix.title: Cache lines and memory bandwidth
Appendix.Content: Cache lines and memory bandwidth
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism
Packing can place more logical values in each transferred cache line, trading arithmetic for lower footprint and traffic.

A cache line is the block moved between cache levels; memory bandwidth is bytes transferred per unit time. With an illustrative 64-byte line, byte-per-bit data stores 64 logical bits, while packed data stores 512. Real line sizes and performance must be measured for the target.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Byte and octet — An octet is exactly eight bits.
• Addresses and virtual memory — An address names a storage location in an address space.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: • Field reordering and AoS versus SoA — depends on this concept; see its prerequisite explanation.

Appendix.Content: M003 development

A four-byte load at line offset 62 crosses two 64-byte lines; a page crossing also requires a second translation. Reordering 24→16-byte records reduces footprint, not necessarily measured traffic or speed. Field reordering and AoS versus SoA separates hot field arrays from full records; TLB caches translations rather than contents.

Appendix.title: Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags
Appendix.source: Concepts/Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags.md
Appendix.Content: Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
C reports unsigned carry, V signed-range failure, N the result’s sign bit, and Z an all-zero architectural result.

For eight-bit addition, C tests exact sum>255; V tests signed sum outside [−128,127]; N is result bit 7; Z tests low result==0. 7F+01 gives 0,1,1,0; FF+01 gives 1,0,0,1 in C,V,N,Z order. These are binary arithmetic flags, not decimal-mode behavior.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Two's complement — For raw unsigned value u in N bits, signed decoding is u when u<2ᴺ⁻¹, otherwise u−2ᴺ.
• Full adder — A full adder adds A, B, and carry-in.

Appendix.title: Huge pages and TLB reach
Appendix.Content: Huge pages and TLB reach
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

A larger page covers more bytes per translation. With T same-size cached entries, illustrative reach is T×P bytes. One GiB requires 262144 pages at 4 KiB versus 512 at 2 MiB. Larger pages trade flexibility, availability, fragmentation and fault granularity; the counts alone do not prove performance improvement.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • TLB — Larger pages change the amount of memory covered by cached translations.
• Allocator fragmentation — Coarser allocation granularity introduces space/availability trade-offs.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.
Recall and next depth
Calculate page counts without asserting a universal speedup.
Pending: Mixed page sizes, workloads, benchmarks and OS policy.
Source and navigation
C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reach, fragmentation, and measurement

TLB reach is approximately the number of cached translations multiplied by the page size. If a TLB can hold translations, switching from 4 KiB pages to 2 MiB huge pages can increase the bytes covered by those translations by a factor of 512.

That does not make huge pages universally faster. They can increase internal fragmentation, make allocation/compaction harder, change NUMA placement behavior and waste memory when only small portions of each huge page are touched. Transparent Huge Pages may also promote or split mappings asynchronously, so an application should not infer actual page size from its allocation API alone.

The right benchmark holds the useful computation fixed while varying working-set size and access stride, then observes TLB/page-walk counters where available. A speedup from huge pages should correlate with translation pressure rather than simply with a different allocator or cache footprint.
For engines, huge pages are most plausible for stable, large, densely accessed arenas—not as a default for every allocation.

Appendix.title: Mixed-precision state updates
Appendix.Content: Mixed-precision state updates
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

Finite binary32 promotes exactly to binary64, but lost bits are not recovered. Double update arithmetic followed by float persistent storage rounds each step. A three-sample mean near 0.5 distinguishes float from double state despite double intermediates.
Prerequisites

• Binary64 — A wider format can represent finite binary32 values exactly but not recover earlier loss.
• Rounding to nearest ties to even — Midpoint decisions determine separate/fused results and narrowed persistent state.

Appendix.title: Deterministic reduction tree
Appendix.Content: Deterministic reduction tree
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

A reduction fixes input order, partition and merge topology so scheduling cannot change the arithmetic grouping. Midpoint recursive splitting is one such tree. Different SIMD widths or partitions can otherwise change it.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Compensated and pairwise summation — A fixed pairwise topology specifies the additions a deterministic reduction performs.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: • Numerical reproducibility — uses this mechanism to establish its numerical contract.

Appendix.Content: Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the definition’s example and name the assumptions that make it valid.
Pending: Cross-platform identity also requires compatible operation semantics, precision, libraries and environment.
Source and navigation
M005 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth

Floating-point addition is not associative, so a parallel reduction can change low bits when thread count, work partition or scheduling changes. A deterministic reduction tree fixes grouping order independently of which worker finishes first.

For eight values, a balanced tree can always compute . The balanced tree can also reduce error growth compared with some highly unbalanced orders, although it is not equivalent to exact or compensated summation.

Determinism costs constraints: the implementation may need stable chunk boundaries, temporary partials and an ordered merge. On GPUs, subgroup width and dispatch shape can otherwise change the effective tree.

Tests should permute scheduling while preserving logical indices and require identical result bits for the deterministic path. A separate accuracy test should compare against a higher-precision or compensated reference; repeatability and numerical accuracy are related but distinct properties.

Appendix.title: Production manifests and transactional publication
Appendix.Content: Production manifests and transactional publication

A production manifest is a durable description of what should be built and published. It prevents a pipeline from depending on hidden editor state or on “whatever files happen to be in this directory.”

A useful manifest separates identity from location. A logical asset ID names the thing the project means. Source and output paths say where a particular revision is read and written. A cryptographic digest can identify exact content bytes. A schema version says how to interpret all fields.
Path safety

Normalize paths before planning any write. A production-safe policy normally rejects parent traversal, unexpected absolute paths, ambiguous separators, and paths that escape the declared project root after symlink resolution.
Lexical normalization alone cannot prove symlink safety. The filesystem must be queried at the point where real paths are resolved, and the resolved target must still lie inside the approved root.
Deterministic plans
The same manifest and tool versions should produce the same ordered build plan. Determinism makes logs diffable, cache keys stable and failures reproducible.
Planning should be side-effect free. A dry run should reveal every intended output, overwrite, deletion and dependency before publication begins.
Staging and commit
A safe publication sequence is:

ListItem.Content: 1. validate the whole request;
2. write derived outputs to staging names or directories;
3. validate staged bytes and metadata;
4. fsync or equivalent when durability is part of the promise;
5. publish with the platform’s proven atomic replacement mechanism;
6. update manifest/index state;
7. retain enough evidence to diagnose rollback or partial failure.

Appendix.Content: Atomicity and durability are separate. A rename can make a new name appear atomically yet still not guarantee survival across power loss unless the required data and directory metadata were persisted.
Idempotence

Repeating the same publication should either be a no-op or produce the same visible state. A pipeline that appends duplicate records, increments versions accidentally or rewrites unrelated timestamps on every run is harder to cache and reason about.
tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp models deterministic plan generation and idempotent publication in memory. It intentionally labels real filesystem durability as unproved.
Related: Atomic publication and durability, DCC adapters and engine publication.

Appendix.title: Discretization, truncation, and roundoff
Appendix.Content: Discretization, truncation, and roundoff
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Discretization replaces a continuous object or domain with a finite grid; truncation omits terms or limits an iterative expansion; roundoff comes from finite-precision arithmetic. They have different causes and respond to different changes. Refining a spatial grid may reduce discretization error while increasing computation. Adding more terms can reduce truncation error. Increasing precision or reformulating arithmetic can reduce roundoff, though a poor algorithm may still dominate. A signed-distance field sampled too coarsely can lose a thin feature entirely, while an ODE’s Euler step has a local truncation error even under exact arithmetic. An error budget should distinguish these mechanisms instead of calling every disagreement “numerical error.”
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Accumulated rounding error
• Taylor models and approximation error
• Numerical quadrature and error

• Numerical error budgets

Appendix.title: Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images
Appendix.source: Concepts/Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images.md
Appendix.Content: Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

A function is a rule that assigns exactly one output to every allowed input. Its domain states which inputs are valid; its codomain states the declared output set; its image is the subset actually reached. These sets affect whether an inverse exists and whether a formula is defined at a boundary. For example, squaring maps the real line into nonnegative outputs but is not one-to-one until its domain is restricted to nonnegative values. In a camera map, division by depth makes zero depth invalid, while a positive-forward convention further restricts visible points. Treating these as contracts makes composition safer: the output of one function must lie in the next function’s domain. A typed implementation can encode some, but not all, of these mathematical restrictions.

Appendix.title: Russian roulette path termination
Appendix.Content: Russian roulette path termination

Russian roulette reduces expected path length without deterministically deleting every long path. At a continuation point, choose a survival probability . If the path terminates, its future contribution is zero. If it survives, divide the surviving throughput by .
For a continuation contribution ,
Then
The compensation preserves the continuation expectation. It does not guarantee lower variance, and it does not undo bias from a separate hard bounce cap.
Choosing the survival probability

A common design bases on remaining throughput magnitude, usually after a minimum depth. But the exact scalar used—maximum channel, luminance-like measure, spectral bound—changes variance and path behavior. Clamp policies must be documented.
A very small creates rare, very large weights , which can increase variance dramatically. A too close to one saves little work. The point is an efficiency trade-off, not a ritual after N bounces.
Conditional probability matters

The compensation uses the probability of surviving at that decision, conditioned on the path state that reached it. If the probability changes per bounce, multiply the path throughput by the reciprocal of each actual survival probability encountered. Do not divide later by a generic average probability.
Executable reference

tools/labs/monte_carlo_transport_lab.cpp runs one million deterministic-seed roulette trials and verifies that the sample mean remains close to the un-terminated contribution after survival compensation.
That does not prove a complete renderer. It isolates the stochastic invariant so a path tracer can test roulette independently of geometry, BSDF and light-sampling bugs.
Read the connected derivation at Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#Follow one path without losing its probability.
Related: Multiple importance sampling, Reproducible numerical benchmarking.

Appendix.title: Tensor runtime layout and views
Appendix.Content: Tensor runtime layout and views

A tensor runtime does not begin with neural-network vocabulary. It begins with a byte-addressing contract. A tensor value needs an element type, a rank, a shape, a mapping from logical indices to storage offsets, and an ownership/lifetime rule for the backing storage. If any of those are implicit, later operations such as broadcasting, transposition, slicing, matrix multiplication, device transfer, or quantized kernels can silently disagree about what the same bytes mean.
For a contiguous row-major tensor with shape
the canonical stride of axis is
so an index addresses

Shape describes the logical domain while strides describe the storage map. A transposed or sliced view may have the same elements without being contiguous. A runtime that assumes offset = row × width + column for every two-dimensional tensor will eventually misread a view.

A rank-zero tensor is a scalar and has shape []; it is not the same object shape as a rank-one tensor of shape [1]. A zero-sized dimension is also meaningful: shape [4,0,8] has zero elements but still has rank three. These distinctions matter when importing external graph formats because shape information is part of the interface contract rather than decoration.
Broadcasting is an index transformation

Broadcasting does not physically duplicate the smaller tensor. Align the input and output shapes at the trailing axes. For every aligned axis, the input size must either equal the output size or equal one. If the input size is one, every output index on that axis maps to input index zero.

For a bias of shape [3] applied to a matrix [2,3], output coordinates across both rows map back to bias indices 0,1,2 repeatedly. This is why some runtimes can represent a broadcast axis with a zero stride: advancing the logical output coordinate does not advance the input address.
Views, aliases, and mutation

A view is cheap because it shares storage. That also means it shares lifetime and mutation hazards. A runtime must decide whether an operation accepts arbitrary strided inputs, requests a contiguous materialization, or dispatches to separate kernels. Reshape is metadata-only only when the requested logical order can be represented by the existing storage arrangement; otherwise it requires a copy.

The same question appears on the GPU. A kernel receiving shape and stride metadata can support arbitrary views, but the extra integer arithmetic and irregular memory access can cost more than making a compact copy. The correct choice is workload-dependent and should be measured.
Executable reconstruction

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp contains a standalone C++20 tensor representation with checked element counts, contiguous strides, multi-index addressing, and trailing-axis broadcasting. Its negative test rejects incompatible shapes rather than allowing an accidental indexing interpretation.

The witness is intentionally small enough to rebuild from memory. It does not claim to implement a production tensor allocator, autograd engine, sparse tensor representation, or GPU device-memory manager.
External contract

The ONNX IR specification defines tensors by values plus shape, distinguishes scalar shape [] from a one-element vector, and requires top-level graph inputs and outputs to carry rank information even when individual dimensions are symbolic. When an ONNX model is imported, the internal tensor representation must preserve those distinctions instead of flattening everything into an untyped byte blob.
Primary reference: https://onnx.ai/onnx/repo-docs/IR.html
Failure probes

A tensor-runtime implementation should deliberately test integer overflow while multiplying dimensions, out-of-range indexing, zero-sized dimensions, rank-zero scalars, incompatible broadcasting, views whose strides are not contiguous, aliased mutation, negative or unsupported strides if the API exposes them, and CPU/GPU disagreement over element size or alignment.
The central reconstruction question is: given only shape, strides, element size and an index tuple, can you prove which byte is being accessed and whether that byte remains alive?
Related: Shader buffer ABI, Quantization and compressed weights, ONNX graph import and lowering, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime.

Appendix.title: DCC adapters and engine publication
Appendix.Content: DCC adapters and engine publication

A production pipeline should not let every DCC application define a different engine truth. Blender, Maya, Houdini and Nuke expose different object models, dependency systems and scripting APIs, but the engine-facing publication contract can remain host-neutral.
The useful separation is:

Content.Strong: Host adapter → normalized asset description → validation → deterministic build plan → staged publication → engine-side verification.

Appendix.Content: The host adapter owns how to read the authoring application. The normalized core owns what the engine requires. Publication owns filesystem and identity guarantees. Engine verification proves that the published result can actually be consumed.
Blender boundary

Blender’s Python API exposes application data through the bpy module, including data access, context, operators, types, utilities and path helpers. A production exporter should prefer direct data access for deterministic inspection and use context-sensitive operators only when their context requirements are understood.

An adapter should establish which evaluated scene state it exports, how collections and object visibility are interpreted, which transforms are baked, and which external dependencies are copied or referenced. Exporting the editable authoring graph and exporting evaluated geometry are different contracts.
Primary reference: https://docs.blender.org/api/main/index.html
Maya boundary

Maya exposes both scripting commands and C++/Python APIs, with explicit dependency-graph and DAG plug-in concepts. A Maya adapter should distinguish scene hierarchy from dependency relationships and should make attribute/default/reference semantics explicit rather than flattening everything into names.
Primary reference: https://help.autodesk.com/view/MAYADEV/2026/ENU/
Houdini boundary

Houdini’s Object Model exposes nodes and geometry through the hou package. SOP networks generate geometry, while ROP networks can describe render/output dependencies. Geometry references can also depend on node cook state, so an adapter must decide when data is evaluated and copied into the host-neutral representation.

SideFX documentation explicitly distinguishes node families such as SOP geometry, LOP/USD scene description, ROP output networks and TOP task workflows. A pipeline should use those semantics instead of treating every node graph as the same kind of data.
Primary references: - https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/hom/ - https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/
Nuke boundary

Nuke publication often involves image nodes, knobs, file paths and frame ranges rather than mesh topology. The engine-neutral contract should therefore represent sequence ranges and missing-frame policy explicitly. Frame range syntax can represent contiguous and stepped ranges, so “first and last frame exist” is not sufficient validation.
Primary reference: https://learn.foundry.com/nuke/content/getting_started/managing_scripts/defining_frame_ranges.html
Host-neutral core
A normalized publication record should carry at least:

ListItem.Content: • logical asset identity;
• schema version;
• source provenance;
• normalized relative input/output paths;
• declared coordinate/unit/color-space conventions where relevant;
• dependencies;
• content identity or cryptographic digest;
• frame range or subresource inventory;
• tool/version information when reproducibility depends on it;
• deterministic diagnostics.

Appendix.Content: The core should not contain live bpy, Maya, hou or Nuke objects. Those are host-lifetime objects. Convert them into owned normalized data before asynchronous work or engine publication.
Validation before mutation

A dry-run plan should be complete before writing outputs. Validate path traversal, duplicate output destinations, missing dependencies, unsupported schema versions, frame gaps and identity collisions first.

Then write to staging locations. Only after every staged artifact passes validation should publication become visible. On filesystems where atomic replacement is relied upon, that property needs an actual platform/filesystem test; a logical transaction model does not prove disk semantics.
Executable witness

tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp implements the host-neutral part of this design. It validates a portable relative-path grammar, rejects parent traversal, checks schema and SHA-256 string shape, produces a deterministic sorted publication plan, checks output collisions, models idempotent publication, and verifies contiguous frame sequences.
It deliberately does not claim real Blender/Maya/Houdini/Nuke execution, SHA-256 computation, symlink resolution, atomic rename behavior or render-farm integration.
Related: Atomic publication and durability, Binary format contracts, Interface contracts and publication.
Executed Blender boundary

The host-neutral adapter contract now has one real DCC execution path. tools/dcc/blender_contract.py runs inside Blender in background mode, creates mesh/collection/object datablocks without UI interaction, attaches logical publication metadata, saves a .blend, exports a binary glTF/GLB with extras, validates the GLB header/JSON chunk, resets Blender, re-imports the GLB and verifies mesh identity plus custom publication fields.

The GitHub workflow .github/workflows/blender-dcc-contract.yml installs Blender on Linux and executes that round trip headlessly. This changes the Blender portion from “API described” to “host executed in CI.” It does not upgrade Maya, Houdini or Nuke: their adapters remain host-neutral contracts until a licensed/current host can execute them. It also does not prove arbitrary production scenes, armatures, materials, texture packaging or current Kairo import parity.

Current Blender documentation explicitly supports background Python execution and glTF export; the repository test treats those host APIs as an external boundary and validates the exported artifact rather than assuming an operator call succeeded.

Appendix.title: Differentiation rules and chain rule
Appendix.Content: Differentiation rules and chain rule
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Differentiation rules let us build derivatives from simpler functions. Linearity handles sums and constant factors; the product and quotient rules account for both factors changing; the chain rule handles nested mappings. For a composition, the derivative of the outer function is evaluated at the inner output and multiplied by the derivative of the inner function. In multiple dimensions, this becomes matrix multiplication of Jacobians in composition order. Elementary rules for powers, exponentials, logarithms, trigonometric functions, and inverse trigonometric functions follow from limits and implicit relations. These rules are the local sensitivity algebra used by automatic differentiation and gradient-based fitting. Each rule has a domain: quotient denominators must be nonzero, logarithms require positive arguments, and inverse trigonometric derivatives can become singular at boundary values.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: • Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images
• Limits and continuity

Appendix.title: ONNX graph import and lowering
Appendix.Content: ONNX graph import and lowering

ONNX is a graph interchange format, not a command stream to execute blindly. Import therefore has two separate responsibilities: decode the normative serialized model, then lower its graph semantics into the engine’s own validated intermediate representation.

The ONNX IR describes a graph as a side-effect-free computation containing model parameters and a topologically ordered list of nodes. Node outputs obey single-static-assignment: an output value name is produced once. Inputs, outputs and initializers have declared types and shapes, and symbolic dimensions can constrain values across the graph.
Primary reference: https://onnx.ai/onnx/repo-docs/IR.html
Import pipeline
Parse. Decode Protocol Buffers into ONNX model objects. Reject malformed serialization before graph reasoning begins.
Validate names and versions. Check IR version, opset imports, graph name, duplicate names and unsupported domains.
Resolve value contracts. Establish element type, rank and known or symbolic dimensions for graph inputs, outputs, initializers and intermediate values.
Validate graph order and SSA. Every consumed value must either be a graph input, initializer or output of an earlier node; every node output must be unique in its namespace.
Normalize operators. Convert ONNX attributes and optional inputs into an internal operator description whose defaults are explicit.
Infer and verify shapes. Propagate shapes where operator rules permit it, while keeping an unknown dimension distinct from an invented concrete dimension.
Lower. Translate supported operators into backend-neutral internal nodes. Unsupported operations must produce a deterministic diagnostic, not fall through to an unrelated kernel.
Plan execution. Topologically schedule nodes, assign storage and lifetimes, select kernels by capabilities, and insert device transfers or fallback boundaries deliberately.
Why an internal IR matters

If Vulkan, Metal and CPU code each interpret ONNX attributes independently, the repository effectively owns multiple importers with multiple chances to disagree. The importer should instead produce one small semantic IR: tensors, operators, attributes, shapes, constants and explicit capability requirements. Backends lower that IR.

This creates a testable seam. A CPU reference kernel and a Metal kernel can receive the same normalized MatMul or Softmax node. Their numerical agreement can then be tested without re-testing protobuf parsing.
Executable graph contract

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp does not parse protobuf and labels that limitation explicitly. It models the post-decode internal graph boundary and verifies that inputs and initializers are available before use and that node outputs satisfy SSA uniqueness. Negative cases reject use-before-definition and duplicate outputs.

That is deliberately narrower than ONNX support. Full support requires actual protobuf decoding, opset semantics, operator-specific validation, shape inference and numerical parity against a trusted runtime.
Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime, Interface contracts and publication.
Real protobuf and official reference-runtime witness

The internal graph contract is now complemented by tools/ml/onnx_contract.py, which uses the official ONNX package instead of modeling the interchange format by hand. The witness builds a ModelProto with MatMul → Add → Relu, named initializers and symbolic batch dimension, serializes it to a real .onnx protobuf, reloads it, runs the official model checker, invokes shape inference, and executes the graph with ONNX’s reference evaluator.

The expected numerical result is independently computed with NumPy before comparison. A second deliberately invalid model reuses a node-output name and must be rejected by the official checker, exercising the SSA constraint at the actual interchange boundary.

This changes the evidence level for the ONNX file/IR boundary, not for a production inference backend. Dynamic control flow, nested subgraphs, arbitrary opsets, external tensor data, quantized operators, custom domains, ONNX Runtime/device execution and current KairoONNX lowering still need separate proofs.

Appendix.title: Transformer attention and KV cache runtime
Appendix.source: Concepts/Transformer attention and KV cache runtime.md
Appendix.Content: Transformer attention and KV cache runtime
A transformer runtime becomes understandable when tensor shapes remain visible. For one attention head, let a token representation produce query, key and value vectors
For a query attending to keys , the scaled score is
followed by a stable softmax
and the output is
Subtracting does not change the distribution because the same factor appears in numerator and denominator, but it prevents overflow when logits are large.
Causal masking

For autoregressive decoding at token position , a query must not observe keys and values from future positions. In a batch attention matrix this is represented by a causal mask before softmax. During incremental decoding, a correctly managed KV cache gives the same structural guarantee: only keys and values through the current token have been appended.

The cache exists because recomputing all earlier K/V projections every token is wasteful. If each layer has key/value vectors of head width , number of KV heads , sequence length , and element size , the rough storage per layer is
bytes before allocator and alignment overhead. Cache datatype, paging strategy and maximum context length are therefore memory-system decisions.
Multi-head and grouped-query attention

Multiple heads perform the same mechanism with separate projected subspaces. Grouped-query attention may use fewer key/value heads than query heads; the mapping from query head to KV head must be explicit. GGUF metadata commonly carries head-count and key/value dimension information, so model loading and runtime shape validation meet at this boundary.
Residual, normalization, and feed-forward structure

Attention is only one sublayer. A complete transformer block also needs residual paths, normalization, and a feed-forward network or architecture-specific alternative. The order—pre-norm versus post-norm, RMSNorm versus LayerNorm, activation and gating choice—is part of the model architecture and must come from the model contract rather than a generic “transformer” assumption.
Executable witness

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp implements stable softmax and a small incremental KV cache. Two keys with distinct values make the weighting observable; a single-token case proves that incremental causal attention cannot see a future token that has not been appended.

It intentionally does not claim multi-head batching, rotary position embeddings, grouped-query attention, tokenizer behavior, paged KV caches, fused kernels or production-model parity. Those are separate implementation milestones.
Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, GGUF binary model loading, ONNX graph import and lowering, Quantized matvec and dequantization.

Appendix.title: Interface contracts and publication
Appendix.Content: Interface contracts and publication
An interface contract says more than which function name to call. It defines the states in which an operation is valid and what becomes true when it succeeds.
A complete contract should state:

ListItem.Content: • valid input domain and units;
• ownership and lifetime of arguments/results;
• mutation and aliasing;
• failure representation and exception/error guarantees;
• thread/concurrency rules;
• timing: immediate, deferred or asynchronous;
• invalidation;
• observability/publication point.

Appendix.Content: Publication is a state transition

A producer may construct a resource privately and then publish it so consumers can rely on it. Before publication, partial state can remain invisible. After publication, every documented invariant must hold.
For CPU concurrency, release/acquire synchronization is one possible publication mechanism when the memory model requirements fit the data structure.
For asynchronous assets, “decode finished” does not mean “GPU resource is safe to sample.” A useful state machine may distinguish:
requested → decoded → upload recorded → submitted → GPU-ready → published.
Similarly, an obsolete request must not publish after a newer generation has replaced it. Generation IDs or request tokens protect the destination identity.
Ownership versus readiness

A reference can be alive but not ready. A GPU buffer wrapper can exist while its upload is still in flight. Conversely, a resource can be GPU-ready while the CPU owner is about to destroy it unless retirement is deferred until all GPU use completes.
Lifetime and synchronization are independent axes.
Failure guarantees

If publication is atomic, consumers should observe either the old valid version or the new valid version, not a half-updated mixture. That promise requires implementation evidence appropriate to the domain: atomics/locks for CPU state, transaction/staging for files, semaphore/fence/queue dependencies for GPU work.
Evidence

tools/labs/threaded_asset_publication_lab.cpp and tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp exercise two different publication domains: concurrent asset decoding/publication and deterministic staged production publication.
Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#An API is a promise about an operation.
Related: Atomic publication and durability, Production manifests and transactional publication, Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions.

Appendix.title: Limits and continuity
Appendix.Content: Limits and continuity
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

A limit describes the value a function approaches as its input approaches a point, even when the function is undefined or assigned a different value there. Continuity at a point adds the requirement that the function value equal that limit. Epsilon-delta language makes this precise: every requested output tolerance can be met by choosing a sufficiently small input neighborhood. Continuity rules out finite jumps but does not guarantee a derivative; the absolute-value function is continuous at zero yet has a corner there. Limits expose removable singularities such as a cancelled factor, while one-sided limits reveal boundaries and discontinuities. In numerical software, local smoothness matters because derivative-based approximations rely on nearby inputs producing controlled output changes. Domain restrictions, branch conditions, and singular denominators must be checked before applying derivative formulas.

Appendix.title: GGUF binary model loading
Appendix.Content: GGUF binary model loading

GGUF is a binary container used by GGML-family inference runtimes. Treating it as “a file full of weights” is too vague for a safe loader. A loader must first establish a byte-level contract: magic, format version, tensor count, metadata count, typed metadata records, tensor descriptors, alignment, tensor-data offsets, and bounds. Only after those checks can tensor bytes become runtime values.

The first four bytes identify the format as GGUF. Multi-byte fields must be decoded according to the file format instead of reinterpreting an arbitrary file buffer as a C++ struct. Native C++ structs inherit compiler padding, alignment and host-representation assumptions that a binary file does not owe the process reading it.
A useful loading pipeline is:

ListItem.Content: 1. Read and validate the fixed prefix.
2. Parse metadata key/value records with checked lengths.
3. Parse tensor descriptors: name, rank and shape, data type, and relative data offset.
4. Compute the aligned start of the tensor-data section.
5. Validate every tensor interval against file length and arithmetic overflow.
6. Keep file or mapping ownership alive for every lazy tensor view.
7. Convert the file tensor type into an internal runtime type only after the descriptor is validated.
8. Dispatch dequantization or quantized kernels from that internal type rather than from filename assumptions.

Appendix.Content: The official GGUF documentation describes the format as a single-file, extensible model container and defines architecture metadata, tensor data layout information, and attention metadata such as head counts and key/value dimensions. Those metadata values affect runtime shape contracts; they are not merely labels.
Primary reference: https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md
Prefix witness

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp parses the GGUF magic, version, tensor count and metadata count from an explicit byte vector using checked little-endian reads. It has a negative case for invalid magic.

That witness intentionally stops at the prefix. It proves that the repository now owns the boundary between raw bytes and validated scalar header fields; it does not pretend that the entire GGUF metadata type system or quantized tensor catalog has already been implemented.
What a full loader must prove

A production reader must defend against truncated strings, absurd ranks, shape-product overflow, unsupported quantization types, alignment overflow, tensor intervals outside the file, duplicate or contradictory metadata, offsets that alias unintentionally, and files whose declared architecture cannot be executed by the runtime.

For memory mapping, “the pointer is valid” is not enough. The mapping object and file lifetime must outlive every lazy tensor view. Page faults also become part of performance: a model that technically maps instantly can still stall during first use if access order faults pages unpredictably.
Quantized execution boundary

GGUF storage type and execution type are separate decisions. A block-quantized format normally stores scale or other metadata together with packed codes. A portable reference path should decode or dot-product those blocks in a simple scalar implementation first. SIMD or Metal kernels then have an independent oracle. If the optimized path disagrees, the scalar path is evidence; if both paths share the same unpacking bug, the test is not independent enough.
Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, Quantized matvec and dequantization, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime, Binary format contracts.
Metadata and tensor-descriptor witness

The earlier prefix-only boundary has now been extended by tools/labs/gguf_metadata_tensor_lab.cpp. The subset parser validates GGUF v3 magic and counts, parses typed UINT32 and STRING metadata, consumes general.alignment, reads tensor names/ranks/dimensions/type IDs/relative offsets, computes the aligned tensor-data start, and rejects truncation or invalid alignment.

The parser remains deliberately incomplete rather than permissive. Unsupported metadata types are rejected instead of skipped with guessed sizes. It does not yet implement arrays, every GGUF value type, every GGML quantized tensor block, tokenizer metadata, endian conversion for big-endian files, or payload interval validation for all tensor types. That is the correct boundary for an independent reference: a small loader should fail loudly outside the subset it actually understands.

Appendix.title: Quantized matvec and dequantization
Appendix.Content: Quantized matvec and dequantization

Quantization trades representation precision for storage and bandwidth. The runtime question is not merely “how many bits per weight?” It is what mathematical value each stored code represents, where its scale or zero-point metadata lives, and how the dot product is accumulated without silently changing the model.
For a simple symmetric per-row signed 8-bit scheme,
with clamping to the representable range. The reconstructed value is
A reference matrix-vector product can therefore compute
That scalar implementation is not necessarily fast, but it creates an oracle for SIMD or GPU fused dequantization-and-dot kernels.

Before clamping, the scalar reconstruction error for ordinary round-to-nearest is bounded by roughly half a quantization step. The output error is workload-dependent because the dot product combines weight errors with input magnitudes. An accuracy report therefore needs representative activations or a model-level metric, not only weight reconstruction error.
Zero rows and exceptional values

When all weights in a block are zero, dividing by the maximum absolute value would produce an invalid scale. The format and runtime need an explicit zero-block representation. Non-finite input weights should be rejected or handled by a documented conversion policy instead of entering integer casts accidentally.

Groupwise 4-bit formats add another trade-off. Smaller groups let the scale adapt more locally but spend more bytes on metadata and may increase metadata bandwidth. Larger groups reduce metadata overhead but make each scale describe a wider distribution.
Reference versus optimized execution

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp implements a checked per-row Q8 reference and compares its dot product against the original floating-point row under a stated error budget. The point is not to advertise Q8 as the final format; it is to establish the proof pattern:
stored codes plus metadata → scalar interpretation → reference result → optimized kernel → measured error and performance.

A Metal or SIMD kernel should be judged against that reference on adversarial widths, tails, zero blocks, extreme scales and random vectors. SIMD lane packing is an implementation detail; the dequantized mathematical contract remains the same.
Related: Quantization and compressed weights, GGUF binary model loading, Tensor runtime layout and views.

Appendix.title: Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions
Appendix.Content: Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions

Vulkan synchronization is not “put a barrier between two passes.” A dependency has to connect a real producer access to a real consumer access with execution and memory scopes that cover both operations.

Vulkan 1.3 includes the synchronization2 model promoted from VK_KHR_synchronization2. It places stage and access masks together in the version-2 barrier structures and uses commands such as vkCmdPipelineBarrier2 and vkQueueSubmit2.
Primary references: - https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/extensions/VK_KHR_synchronization2.html - https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/synchronization.html
Producer → consumer reasoning
For every hazard, write the transition in words first.
Example:
A transfer command writes a storage buffer. A later compute shader reads that buffer.
The producer execution stage is transfer. The producer access is transfer write. The consumer execution stage is compute shader. The consumer access is shader storage read.
An abstract memory barrier therefore needs to cover:
source stage = TRANSFER source access = TRANSFER_WRITE destination stage = COMPUTE_SHADER destination access = SHADER_STORAGE_READ.

Using ALL_COMMANDS and MEMORY_READ/WRITE everywhere may accidentally work but destroys precision and can hide misunderstanding. Using a destination stage that never performs the consumer access is not made correct by a broad access mask.
Image transitions add a layout contract

Images have another state dimension: layout. An image memory barrier can both synchronize accesses and transition from oldLayout to newLayout. The old layout must describe the state established by prior use unless the contents are intentionally discarded under the rules that permit that.
A render graph therefore needs more than “read” and “write.” For each image subresource it eventually needs:

ListItem.Content: • stage/access usage;
• required layout;
• aspect;
• mip range;
• array-layer range;
• queue ownership when queues/families differ.

Appendix.Content: A whole-image state tracker is a valid early implementation but cannot claim correct independent mip/layer scheduling.
Queue submission and timeline semaphores

Synchronization2 also modernizes queue submission through VkSubmitInfo2 and related structures. Timeline semaphores carry monotonically increasing integer values and are useful for expressing ordered completion points across submissions. A timeline value is not a memory barrier by itself; the signal/wait operations participate in dependencies whose scopes must still match the work.
Native witness now in the repository
tools/native/vulkan_sync_smoke.cpp is compiled and executed in the dedicated native graphics workflow on Ubuntu with a Vulkan implementation and validation layer packages. It:

ListItem.Content: • creates a Vulkan 1.3 instance;
• finds a device exposing synchronization2;
• creates a queue/device with the feature enabled;
• records a VkMemoryBarrier2 through vkCmdPipelineBarrier2;
• submits the command buffer using vkQueueSubmit2;
• waits for fence completion;
• fails on validation-layer errors when the layer is available.

Appendix.Content: That materially raises the evidence level from a CPU-only logical graph.

It still does not prove a resource-specific RAW transition, image layout transition, queue-family transfer, timeline protocol, transient aliasing, physical-GPU performance, or current Kairo/Vulkax integration. Each of those needs its own captured witness.
Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, Rendering history validity, Render graph barrier lowering.

Appendix.title: Render graph barrier lowering
Appendix.Content: Render graph barrier lowering
A logical render graph and an API synchronization plan are different layers.
The logical graph answers:

ListItem.Content: • which pass reads or writes each resource;
• which hazards create ordering edges;
• whether the pass dependency graph is acyclic;
• when a logical resource is first and last used.

Appendix.Content: API lowering answers:

ListItem.Content: • what concrete stage/access state each use requires;
• what image layout or resource state is required;
• which subresources are affected;
• which queue executes each pass;
• what barrier, semaphore, fence/event, or encoder boundary realizes the dependency.

Appendix.Content: The repository already has tools/labs/render_graph_contract_lab.cpp for the first layer. That CPU witness proves RAW/WAR/WAW edge construction, deterministic topological order and several invalid-graph cases. It does not prove Vulkan or Metal memory visibility.
State machine per resource version
A practical compiler treats each write as producing a new logical version. A read consumes a particular version. For every concrete resource/subresource, track the last known backend state:
producer pass queue stage/access layout or storage state version.
When the next use requires an incompatible state, emit a transition whose source scope covers the prior access and whose destination scope covers the next access.
This versioned model prevents an important bug: a pass can read “history texture” while the graph accidentally associates it with the current-frame version rather than the previous-frame version.
Subresource granularity

Whole-resource tracking is simple but can over-synchronize. Independent mip levels, array layers or depth/stencil aspects may be used by different passes. Moving to subresource tracking requires interval/range splitting and merging so that state for mip 0 does not overwrite the state of mip 5.
The first correct implementation should prefer conservative whole-resource barriers over an incorrect fine-grained optimizer. Fine granularity is an optimization after invariants are tested.
Vulkan lowering

For Vulkan synchronization2, a transition record eventually becomes VkBufferMemoryBarrier2, VkImageMemoryBarrier2 or VkMemoryBarrier2 inside VkDependencyInfo, possibly combined with queue submission dependencies.
See Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions.
Metal lowering

Metal does not mirror Vulkan’s barrier vocabulary one-for-one. The backend should lower the same logical dependency into Metal’s encoder ordering, resource hazard mode, fences/events where required, and heap/lifetime rules rather than forcing Metal to imitate Vulkan object names.
See Metal heaps memoryless resources and hazards.
Verification ladder
A render-graph compiler should be verified in layers:

ListItem.Content: 1. dependency graph against a CPU oracle;
2. resource-state transition plan against hand-written traces;
3. Vulkan execution with validation enabled;
4. Metal execution with GPU capture;
5. cross-backend image/data parity;
6. transient aliasing stress with deliberately overlapping and non-overlapping lifetimes;
7. current production-engine integration.

Appendix.Content: The current branch now has stages 1 and a minimal Vulkan synchronization2 execution/Metal compile boundary. The deeper stages remain explicit rather than implied.

Appendix.title: Metal heaps memoryless resources and hazards
Appendix.source: Concepts/Metal heaps memoryless resources and hazards.md
Appendix.Content: Metal heaps, memoryless resources, and hazards

Metal exposes several resource-lifetime tools that matter directly to an engine render graph. Their purpose is not just API convenience; they let the engine state when storage must exist, when bytes may be reused, and who is responsible for synchronization.

Apple documents MTLHeap as a way to create resources from a larger allocation and to alias memory among resources whose lifetimes do not overlap. Apple also documents memoryless textures for temporary render targets whose contents can remain in tile memory rather than occupying ordinary persistent system/GPU memory.
Primary references: - https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metal/memory-heaps - https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metal/reducing-the-memory-footprint-of-metal-apps
Heap aliasing is a lifetime proof

If resources A and B use overlapping heap memory, the engine must prove that A is dead before B begins using the same bytes. “They are in different render passes” is not enough when command encoding/execution overlap or when a resource is consumed asynchronously later.
A render graph can perform interval analysis:
A lifetime = [first use, last use] B lifetime = [first use, last use].
Only non-overlapping lifetimes are candidates for aliasing, and compatibility constraints such as size/alignment/storage mode still apply.
The allocator also needs to keep the heap itself alive for every resource created from it.
Hazard tracking mode

Metal heap resources can use tracked or untracked hazard behavior. Apple’s heap documentation explicitly notes that Metal synchronizes heap-created resources when their hazard tracking mode is tracked. Choosing untracked mode transfers more responsibility to the application. That decision should therefore exist in the backend state model rather than being an incidental resource flag.
Memoryless attachments

Memoryless texture storage is suited to temporary render-target contents that do not need to survive beyond the render-pass/tile use for which they are created. A later pass that samples the image needs persistent storage; marking such a resource memoryless would contradict the data-flow graph.
The render graph can infer memoryless eligibility only after it understands whether the produced contents escape the render-pass lifetime.
Argument buffers and residency

Argument buffers can reduce CPU binding overhead and can reference many resources. That also makes lifetime/residency reasoning more indirect: the resource referenced by an argument buffer must remain valid for the encoded GPU work even if the CPU-side wrapper is no longer visible.
Current evidence
tools/native/metal_compile_smoke.metal is compiled to AIR and metallib on the macOS CI job. This proves that the repository owns a real MSL compile boundary instead of only pseudocode.

Compile success is not GPU execution evidence. It does not prove heap aliasing, tracked/untracked hazard behavior, memoryless attachment correctness, argument-buffer residency, command-buffer timing or Apple-GPU performance. Those require a Metal execution/capture on suitable hardware.
Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, Render graph barrier lowering, Interface contracts and publication.
